FURNESS ABBEY. Majestic ruin of a long-past day. Soul-stirring, massive, and sublimely grand! Hail to thy ancient walls with ivy decked! Hail to thy grass-grown corridors, where once Solemnly paced the reverend monks of eld ! Hail to thy towers, which once ambitious reared Their turrets to the clouds, and bold defied The stormy buffetings of Boreas stern, Till he, unable by fair fight to gain The day, employed foul means andstraightway sent The treacherous Decay within thy walls, And they were vanquished. Stealthily the foe Despoiled their sijength, and, slow but ever smtre, They yielded to The spoiler's power; and now, Grown weary of incessant strife, would seem To court the earth, majestic in defeat. The tired sun sinks to rest, And darts his farewell rays upon thy walls, • ! ancient Abbey! Fair at all times thou, But faire,* far when the bright Day King bastes To reach h ; couch behind the western hills! Tinged will a golden hue thy walls appear • To gain new life, and, for a time, to cast Aside theigarb of deep solemnity That well becomes them, noble edifice! He were, indeed, an artist who could paint That tranquil scene,—he who could reproduce From Nature's sketch-book such a lovely gem,— And he, in truth, a poet who could write An ode describing truly all its beauty. The zephyr sighs amid the foliage green Of neighbouring trees—sighs gently evermore For faded grandeur and for glory gone. Once stood an Abbey, noble and complete, Here where Queen Desolation holds her court. The now deserted chapel once was filled With venerable monks, who chanted low Their Latin hymns; at Matins rose the sound of holy singing, and at Evensong The vespers chimed and called the monks to prayer. Once ruled an Abbot o'er the goodly land, And once tired travellers, journeying from afar, Found here a comfortable shelter. Monks :Vied each with each in hospitality, And food and wine were soon supplied; no lack Was there, in truth, of aught that could be asked; And when sweet Morn ched darksome Night away, And Luna fled in fear from mightier Sol, The once-tired traveller, now refreshed and strengthened, Was wished" God-speed," and bade the monks farewell. But now the scene is changed. The grass grows green Upon the chapel floor; where once was heard The sound of sacred singing all is still, Save when the voice of some bold traveller breaks The mystic charm of solitude; the rook, Startljd, flies quickly from his peaceful nest, And, from a distance, views with questioning gaze The being who thus rashly dares to break The stillness weird. The vespers chime no more. The Abbot sleeps within the silent tomb, Alai the good monks have long since left their labours, No more in earthly choirs to chant God's praise. Jove, m'ghty Thunderer ! spare this Abbey old, And IA thy storms pass gently over it ! Time, hoary Father Time! "who changes all," Be thou indulgent to this edifice ! Let the long-standing wall, still longer stand, A monument of days that long hare fled, An ornament to Britain, and au heirloom For coming generations to admire, To guard, to cherish as their fathers did! —Preston, March, 1886.

VANITY OF THE GREEKS.—A marked characteristic o. the Greeks is their vanity. No country is comparable with Greece, and naturally in their own esteem the Greeks are more than comparable with any other people. In their relations democracy of the fullest kind prevails, and, as Professor Mahaffy remarks, every common mule ' boy is a gentleman and fully your equal, sitting in the room at meals, and joining in the conv.ersation at dinner. Every one, high or low, is his "brother," and to the tra- veller accustomed for a social inferior to keeep in his "proper station," it is at first a little irritating to be ad- dressed as " Adelphe" by a stranger, perhaps not very honegt, and unquestionably very dirty. To these traits in their character—to their egotism and love of ostenta- tion—may be due the circumstance that the Greek, though temperate in his dietary, is a much more expen- sive person as regards his clothing and household goods I than either the Turk or the Bulgarian. No Greek who can afford a coat of fine cloth, with stockings and shoes, I would submit to wear a coarse oba and a sheepskin gee ['la, and if he can at all compass them, will make a point of having tables, table linen, knives, and forks. Nor, except in the humbler establishments, does the bedding consist solely of rags, as among the Bulgarians, and their houses, if often lacking much in the way of ' cleanliness and comfort, are usually better built and I more pretentious than those of their neighbours.— ' Peoples of the World. BALLAD SINGING.—I would impress on amateurs who may be interested in the art of singing a ballad that be- fore the chief essential, "speech in song," can be arrived at, the proper production of vocal tone must be mas- tered.. To begin with, I would have my readers think of • the singing voice as of a marvellous musical instrument which is placed in the throat. It is a natural combina- tion of many manufactured instruments, but chiefly it is to be considered as partaking of the nature of a wind and a reed instrument—that is to say, the air, propelled , by an invisible but distinct force from the lungs, is di- rected against the vocal cords or ligaments, where ; sound is produced. In order that this sound may not be impeded in its efforts to reach the outer air, the throat must allow itself to open. It must open passively; the sound then escapes, and finding free passage, it di- rects itself against another part of the instrument, I which is the sounding-board, or resonator, of the voice, and is known to us as the hard palate, just above the top front teeth. Hero the sound is intensified, or minimised, ' and manap:ecl as the artist chooses, and when perfected it may be clothed in speech, and so produced finally in sone..." "Speech in song" means, to my mind, that ! the sound which is uttered is so enveloped by the word, that "word and sound," so combined and perfected, end lin being "song." It will be seen, then, that to sing an I English ballad requires an unusual combination of : forces in the singer, and it is this very necessary com- bination which makes the true artist so rare.=Cassell's How MARRIAGES ARE MADE AMONG CAPE BRETON FOLK.—Courtship is by no means a necessary preliminary to marriage. The wedding just then under discussion was a little more eventful than common in the number, ; but not in the kind, of incidents. To begin at the be- ginning: When a young man decides that he will marry, he often first builds a house; and it is no trivial matter ; here, where most of the lumber is sawn by hand in a I pit. A man may be said to be in earnest when he begins his suit with months of such hard labour—and that, too, ; from a disinterested motive, not having the faintest idea, perhaps, as to who will be the mistress of the house. We ; saw a number of such expectant buildings, in all states I and of many ages ; for some, failing to get a tenant, stood without windows or doors, the image of a desolate and empty heart. John ----, a young man duly prepared and determined to marry, had set out the previous week I with his spokesman to get a wife. He had no particular preference for any one, but they decided to go first to the house of Mary —, one of the brightest girls of the I parish, whom he had often noted, but with whom he had never spoken. When they entered the house a hint of 1 their object was given to Mary, :and she retired from the sitting room. The spokesman then delivered his ! speech, in which he praised the personal qualities, the ; fortune, the social position, of his friend, and asked the I hand of Mary for him. As the father had no objection ; to the offer, lie at once consented to leave the matter to his daughter. She was called in, and the spokesman conferred quietly a while with her in a corner, and she consented to the marriage. The spokesman (then led her out to the middle of the .floor, and John came from i his corner and took her by the hand; thus the "con- tract" was accepted, under the usual penalty of forfeit- ing twenty dollars in case the engagement was broken. That evening was spent in dancing; but if any of the deacons had had wind of the affair, it is probable that they would have come and changed the festivity into a prayer meeting. The young man afterward engaged the priest to publish the banns for the first and last time on I the following Sabbath. But Mary had her own plans in all this: she knew that the affair would reach the ears of Sandy —, for whom she had a strong preference, and perhaps bring him promptly to a proposal. Sandy did come, and the upshot of it was that he and his father went late on Saturday night, roused the priest, and had Sandy's name substituted in the banns for that of appli- cant number one. I'll give ye the upper farm this minute. Go, get ver brother, see the giro.lw, and happened nheedr home here. Well keep her safe." N that Malcolm was the richest of the three applicants, besides being, I will suppose for charity's sake, a good fellow. Suffice it to say that they brought the girl home, bag and baggage, by stealth, that Sunday night, and mounted a guard that prevented the success of any stratagem on either her part or the part of others, and they were married on the following Tuesday. These ; persons were by no means of the lower ranks; the girl was described to me by an old fisherman as a " noble- minded-lookin' girl, sir; a fine specimen of the Highland craft." A man is all the more highly esteemed for such a feat. The rejected fellow does not lose heart; he generally keeps on with his negotiations, day after day, house after house, until he finds a partner. An intelli- gent woman, while admitting the general predominance of worldly interests in these matters, and the suddenness with which marriages were often made, said that un- happy families are nevertheless rare among this people. —Hai-per's 3fagazine.

A coat without a button.—A coat of paint. "Our house was entered last night and robbed of all the valuables, including the silver plate," he telegraphed to his wife. "Good gracious," she exclaimed, "I hope they didn't take the gold fish!" A Cheshite auctioneer, while engaged in his avocation, this exalted the merits of a carpet: "Gentlemen and ladies, some folks sell carpets for Brussels which are not Brussels; but I can most positively assure you that this most elegant article was made by Mr. Brussels himself." "Where were you engaged last?" asked a lady of the new coloured cook. " Yer oughten'ter ax me dat, lady." "Well, I just want to know, as it may tend do give you character." "Wall, lady, I was engaged ter Bob Phillips, de triflingestryaller men I eber seed. Why, lady, dat man stole my year-rings and runned away! How many times wus yerself engaged, lady ?" TWO GRUMBLERS. A monkey, as free as his forest air, Found little to eat, for the fruit trees were bare, So he grumbled away in a royal rage; ' While his brother, who lived upon daintiest fare, Grumbled because he was fast in a cage. We're much like the monkeys admit it or not ; We grumble ant grumble, whatever our lot. —" Little Folks' Maga:ine" for March. THE TOWER OF REPENTANCE,—There is a place called Hoddam Castle in Scotland, and near it is a tower called Repenta-ace. Many years ago a well-known writer named Sir Richard Steele was walking in that neighbourhood. He suddenly caught sight of a little boy who was lying on the ground reading. When Sir Richard came near enough, he saw that the boy was studying the Bible, and thinking to find out how much the boy understood of what he was reading, he said, "Can you tell me the way to heaven, my liose?" " Yes, sir," was the ready answer; "you must go by that tower." And the boy . was right, for repentance is the only guide to heaven.— Little Folks' Magazine. Gloomy Siberia has furnished a joke of her own that ' has made all the Russias laugh. Ivan Petroff, a mer- chant and Mayor of the city of Gorki, of the Tomsk Pro- vince, died a while ago. The citizens raised 200 roubles to procure a painting of the dead Mayor. They sent the money to Mr. Skotti, a well-known painter of Moscow, asking him to produce a portrait of the Mayor. They did not enclose any photograph, but gave this descrip- tion: "Age, 52 years and six months; stature, five feet six inches; hair and eye-brows, auburn; eyes, gray; nose, mouth, and chin, ordinary ; face, clean. He had no special traits, except stammering." The artist laughed, and gave the curious order to one of his young pupils, Astra,khoff, who in a few days painted the portrait of the stammering Mayor, and sent it to Siberia. In a few weeks Skotti received a letter ,Irom the Ghorkians, say- " The relatives of the late Mr. Petroff and the rest of citizens believe that no better likeness could have been painted." MR_ MC.VICAR AND THE YOUNG PRETENDER.—111 1745, after the victory of the Highlanders at Prestonpans, a message was sent to the ministers of the city, in the name of "Charles, Prince Regent," desiring them to preach next day, Sunday, as usual; but many, alarmed by the defeat of Cope, sought refuge in the country, and no public worship was performed within the city, save by a clergyman named Hose at the Tron. It was other- wise, however, at St. Cuthbert's, the incumbent of which was then the Rev. Neil Mc.Vicar, who preached to a crowded congregation, many of whom were armed Highlanders, before whom he prayed for George 11., and also for Charles Edward in a fashion of his own, re- corded thus by Ray, in his history of the time, and others :—" Bless the king! Thou knowest what king I mean_ May the crown sit long on his head. As for that young man who has come among us to seek an earthly crown, we beseech Thee to take him to Thyself and give him a crown of glory." It is said that when the prince heard of Mc.Vicar's prayer he laughed heartily, and ex- pressed himself quite satisfied.—F7'o77l " Cassell' s old New Edinburgh?' for March. STAGE ELEMENTS.—The French have a proverb that Nothing is sacred to a sapper," but there is nothing that your stage carpenters cannot grapple with and mimic. Earthquakes, storms, thunderbolts, fires, water- falls, animals, steam-engines, ships, &c. he is ready for them all, and on the whole succeeds wonderfully. How is the roll of thunder contrived? Formerly, a large sheet of iron, hung up at the wing, was rattled ; it sounds exactly as one would expect it would, that is, as unlike thunder as possible, and very like striking a tea-tray. But there is "another way," as Mrs. Glasse' would have it, more terrible and effective. In the larger theatres the property-room is placed over the audience. Here is :wheeled along a sort of truck laden with round shot, which tilts over on a hinge, and sends the balls tumbling over each other, to be followed by a hollow sound as they roll over the floor. For lightning a long tin tube with a spirit lamp is used. A powder is then blown through, which takes fire as it passes by the spirit and gives out a vivid flash. The most effective, though most troublesome, mode is to cut out of the scene zigzag strips in imitation of forked lightning; these are covered with varnished calico and painted. Rain is imitated by the rolling of peas in a long tube; wind, by revolving a roller against a rough cloth. These are not quite as im- pressive as they might be. The most absurd attemnt at usion, and which is still retained at first-rate theatres, is the attempt to represent any crash, such as the break- ing open of a door or falling downstairs. Tradition re- quires that this should invariably be done by springine a rattle, accompanied by a loud stroke of the drum with perhaps a heap of broken glass emptied from a I), asini Anything more absurd cap: stebe imagined, especially -the. The severe depression in Scotch agriculture was shown by the fact that on Saturday, in a newspaper published in the North of Scotland, 47 country mansions, with 245,000 acres of shootings attached, were adyer- tised.to ler.

RAILWAY RATES.—An influential meeting of cattle traders has been held at Aberdeen, at which it was re- solved that the time had now arrived when railway rates for home dead meat should not exceed those levied on foreign meat, and that, in any case, preferential rates in favour of foreign traffic over that of our own country was most unfair and unpatriotic. It was afterwards agreed to approach the railway companies by memorial, asking them to reduce their rates. GRASS SEEDS WITH BARLEY.—" .1. A." writes :—" Hav- ing already sown barley land intended to be Laid down withltalia,n rye grass and clover for one year's ley,vrhen should the grass mixture be sown, and what is the best method of covering the seed? Will it be injurious to the young barley plant to harrow it ?" It will do quite well after the barley is up; if sown sooner it might smother the crop. A very light harrow must be used to cover in, or, better still, a brush-harrow, made by fasten- ' ing bushes into a hurdle. PLANTING. LARGE v. SMALL POTATOES.—At the New York Experimental Station potatoes were taken for seed from the most productive hill, and planted the next spring in regular and registered order. The result was that the largest tubers from the productive hill exceeded by 16 per cent, the product of the Largest tubers from the least productive hill, and the smallest tubers from the productive hill yielded slightly more th'an the largest iubers from the least productive hill. The conclusion is therefore drawn that it is best, in digging potatoes for seed, to select from the most productive hills. The results of such experiments would doubtless vary much with the condition of the soil, depth of planting, and the mois- ture and dryness of the season. BUTaER FACTORIES.—Professor Sheldon is writing a series of articles in an agricultural contemporary on dairy questions. His last was on the proposal to establish a number of butter factories in Ireland. In it he says : "Assuming that things go smoothly, and that the manager is master of his job, I have no hesitation in say- ing that butter factories will pay. No one can make butter of fine quality and perfect character unless the Milk he handl,es is everything it ought to be, and so it follows that the measure of success secured by any manager will be governed by the character of the milk which is placed in his hands, so far as the raw material is concerned. The one great feature of factory butter is its uniformity of character, and in this it has a consider- able advantage over an equivalent number of farmhouses. This question of uniformity, indeed, is one of first-rate importance. The competition, whether it be butter or butterine, which is cutting farmhouse butter so keenly, finds its leverage less in superior quality than in superior uniformity, and it is obvious that the butter from a number of farmhouses cannot be uniform in character. French butters and Dutch butterine combine excellent quality with uniformity ot character, and these are fea- tures which ought to be found in factory-made butter, if in any butter at all. It is likely, indeed, that butter factories will do great good in Ireland, but we must not forget that such institutions require very careful and competent management." UNSHOD HORSES.—The Mark Lane Express of last week contains an interesting article on unshod horses. They say :—" From time to time evidence has been cropping up to the effect that horses have been used unshod for years, in all kinds of town and country work, by various individuals, with more or less success. Sometimes the success has been complete and sometimes partial, but there can be little doubt that a case has been made out against the ordinary horse shoe and against our ordinary methods of treating the foot of the horse." The Rev. J

G. Wood, in a work.he has written against horse shoeing, after explaining the structure of the hoof of the horse, calls attention to the fact that the frog comes first to the ground in a state of nature, and so prevents any jar to the legs and body. Not only so, out it fills the cavity of the hoof almost entirely, and thus would prevent the horse getting stones in its feet if it were left alone. "An unshod horse which has perfect hoofs cannot pick up a stone because there is no room for it," says the author; and then he shows how the sole is pared, the walls cut down, the bars cut away, the heels, "opened," and the frog "pared to stimulate its growth," until the horse's foot presents a perfect appearance. "It is diffi- cult," says the Rev. Mr. Wood, "to persuade many people that the Creator really did know how to make a horse, and that divine handiwork cannot very well be im- proved by man. But a horse whose hoof is left as Nature made it cares nothing about pebbles, or even broken flints, but can gallop among them without being even aware of their presence, so dense and strong is the horn of the sole."

DAIRY HINTS.-Mr. Primrose APConnell, in an able article on dairy management, says :—" The general treat- ment of cattle is to keep them as comfortable as possible; shield from heat in summer, and keep warm in winter. The temperature of the cowhouse ought to be about 60 deg. N.; under this there is a loss of food in keeping up ttie heat of the body; above this the animals tend to perspire too freely, while, of course, ventilation without draughts must be attended to. The production of milk in winter, all the year round, or in the summer only, for cheese, butter, or for new milk, will each of them re- quire a system of management to suit, both in the feed- ing and timing of the dropping of the calves. Where an all the year round supply is required, it is best to have the cows calving during winter or spring time. They naturally tend to go dry in the autumn, and those which have had their young in summer will lessen their flow at the usual season, although they may not have been giving milk for more than a few months. On the other hand, those which commence during the winter will take a new start when put out to grass. Unfortunately, however, we are generally short of supply about August. Food must be given at regular intervals and warmed a little if possible in the winter time; while—as cows are very much creatures of habit—everything ought to be done regularly at its own particular time every day, a state of matters to which the animals will very soon learn to accommodate themselves. Milking is one of the most important and difficult jobs on a dairy, and it is one which is usually touched upon very lightly by our various authorities. Very few attendants become good milkers unless they have started when young, and have had every inducement to improve themselves. It is best done by piecework, and the quicker it is done the better, as it is seldom that a quick milker is a bad one. The number allotted to each atten- dant is usually ten, and when in full milk it is quite pos- sible to do this number in one hour. We have had regular experience of this being done, and two gallons drawn from each cow in the time; but more ordinarily it will be found that about half this number will be

nearer the mark in practice, and any master who can get eight cows milked per hour is very well off. It should be done regularly, quietly, and thoroughly, no scolding or beating, and the last drop to be extracted. There is nothing which tends to lessen the yield of a cow so much as illusage or bad milking, and where there are a number of attendants they ought to take the cows in turn, so that the good milkers will tend to counteract the bad effects of the inferior milkers. Cows cannot inten- tionally and deliberately hold up their milk, but if they are frightened the nervousness which is induced has a reflex action, and the tissues of the milk vessels are tightened, so that the milk will not flow so easily. Every- thing ought to be done to keep the milk as clean as pos- sible, so that the udders ought to be brushed over if at all dirty before commencing; the attendants ought to wash their hands and keep their nails pared. The last drop should be extracted, and for this purpose some re- sponsible person ought to go round after the regular hands and "strip " them out. These " strippings" are the richest part of the milk, and will amount to about one gallon to every 25 cows. Good milking stimulates the yield of an inferior cow, besides enabling a good animal to do her best. We should very much like to see a com- petition of this kind inaugurated at our dairy shows, to encourage attendants to excel. For sore and injured teats the little silver milking tube is invaluable if care- fully used, but no really efficient milking machine has been yet invented.

TENANT RIGHT TO HOUSEHOLDET, 25.-olle of the strong- est arguments for giving tenant-right to householders is afforded by the monstrous injustice commonly practised of levying black mail on a tenant who is compelled to stay in the house because he has built up a good busi- ness in connection with it. In such cases it is usual to screw the rent up to the utmost endurance of the unfor- tunate tenant, and the landlord thus obtains enormous rents to which he has not just claim. This is a form of renting tenants on their own improvements that ought to be put down by law.-3fark-Lane Express. AGRICULTURAL EXPERIMENTS.-Mr. James Howard has recommended to the Royal Agricultural Society that they should determine upon a course of experiments, practical and scientific. He suggests, "in respect of the scientific portion, the consulting chemists of the various agricultural societies should be invited to a conference and be asked to prepare for the consideration of the Council a list of field experiments and experiments in the feeding of animals which they recommended should be carried out. In respect of the practical portion, the Special Experiments Committee will doubtless be able to deal."

! CLOVER SEEDS.—" A. MI." says :—" I have a valuable field of fine loamy soil, on which the seeds, one year's Icy, are much too thin. The seeds were manured in the autumn with ,c,ood short dung, which will shortly be chain harrowed. Can anything be sown on now to fill up the crop, and if so, what?" If the land is in good heart, and the short dung to be presently chain-harrowed be a liberal dressing, we should be inclined to sow two bushels of Italian rye grass per acre on the land before it is harrowed and rolled. If the weather suits, you would probably have a considerable addition to the swathe in July, and great improvement in the aftermath.

The point wherein the majority of chicken raisers fail is with respect to feeding. One of the most difficult matters to instil into the minds of poultry keepers is that the feeding of their stock must be very carefully and systematically done. Overfeeding is the cause of nearly all the diseases that poultry both old and young are sub- ject to. Thus it will be at once apparent that if it is im- portant to feed adult fowls in the right manner, it is especially so in the case of young chickens. The former may under certain conditions throw off the evil effeales of bad feeding, but this is scarcely possible in the case of young and growing stock at the time when the frame is 1 being formed. The very desire to feed the birds suffi- ciently very often leads to the giving of either too much or too rich food. The delicate stomach of the little things need food that shall be of a suitable nature, and full of nourishment. This very fact leads to error. Rich food is not necessarily nourishing, and rice versd. Chickens do not require any food during the first 24 hours after they are hatched. The contents of the yolk- bag,which bag is absorbed into the stomach immediately before the hatching takes place, canthins sufficient nourish- ment for the first day, and any attempt to compel the chick to swallow other food is most likely to do more harm than good by the derangement of the digestive system. There will be no difficulty in getting the chicks to eat if they are simply left alone for the first 24 hours, after they make their debit into the world. All such practices as the giving of a pepper-corn to the newly-hatched chick are most objectionable, and are founded either on superstition or ignorance. Such pungent things as pee- per-corns must be very trying indeed to a delicate organ like the stomach of a young chick, That still more ob- jectionable practice of tearing off the horn or scale which nature has placed on the beak of chicks to enable them to break open their prison house, combines cruelty with other things, for this scale will drop off itself within a few days. The less chickens are interfered with the bet- ter during the early stages of their growth. The first food should consist of hard-boiled eggs, chopped fine, and mixed with twice their bulk of bread crumbs. Those eggs which have been sat on for a week and proved to be infertile answer capitally for feeding the chickens. Failing these we should purchase duck eggs in preference to using the fresh eggs from the hens, unless the latter are exceptionally plentiful. Only as much of the egg and bread crumbs should be prepared as will serve two or three times, as it soon loses its fresh- ness, and if sour will cause scouring. It should be slightly moistened with milk, but very slightly, just sufficient to damp it. Much depends on the way in which the bread crumbs are prepared. The way we have always adopted has been to rub the bread—stale bread is to be preferred—through a fine seive turned up- side down. In this way they are not only speedily made, but are fine and even, which is almost impossible to secure if simply rubbed in the hands. On cold or wet mornings it will do good to add a little seasoning to the mixture, such as aromatic compound, and the same thing is desirable with the soft food afterwards, and bone meal should always be mixed with the food of chickens. The egg and bread crumbs should be continued for about a'week when the alternate feeds may be of some such food as Spratt's poultry meal, which, without hesitation, we have found to be the best thing for rear- ing chicks that has come under our notice, that is, as al soft food, for we should never think of giving that or any other soft food alone. It seems to be a combination of just what chickens require, and yet it is not unduly stimulative. It can be fed for the -whole period of a chicken's life without the least fear of injury or evil effects. When the chicks are eight or nine days old they may have the egg and bread crumbs discontinued, in place of which may be given a little boiled rice, but not much of that, and some oatmeal mixed with barley or wheat meal, or, if it can be obtained, in plan of the oat- meal, some ground oats. When the birds are about a fortnight old a little crushed buckwheat may be put down to them, as they will not be able to manage the whole corn until they are older. From the time we have already stated they may be gradually accustomed to a plainer diet, until four months old in the case of the more rapid growing breeds, and five months in the others, when they will require no different treatment to the older fowls.

An important matter to be considered is the times of feeding, for the most inexperienced will see that young animals and birds need smaller quantities, but at shorter intervals than adults. The following may be regarded as a very good table for the periods at which chickens should be fed :—For the first week or ten days, every two hours; from ten days to a month old, every three hours; ' after that, five times a day; and when two months 'old four times a day. It is most desirable that the times of feeding be as equally divided as possible and be .strictly observed. Doctors say that there is nothing worse for children than irregular meal times, and this is just as injurious in the case of chickens. The first feed should be early in the morning, say, about an hour after daybreak. This may necessitate early rising on the part of someone, but that grace is a most essential one for the chicken raiser. It can scarcely be expected that chickens which have to run about hungry for hours after they are astir will thrive properly. Some leave a little hempseed over night, so that the birds can help themselves in the morning. This is undoubtedly better than nothing; but they will be more likely to do well if they have a warm feed first of all. Then until the chicks are a month old they should have a feed about nine or ten o'clock at night. This entails trouble, but it will re- pay any trouble involved. Food should be fed sparingly and never left for long. The system of feeding we have found best of all is to only give as much as is eaten readily. Lately there have been those who have written in favour of always having food so that the birds, both old and young, can help themselves, but we do believe it is the better method. A hungry chick is a thriving one. Much contention has been raised as to whether chickens should have water or not. As to whether they can be raised without liquid needs no discussion. That has often been proved possible. lint what is possible is not always advisable, and we think it is most desirable that the chickens should have access to water. They will only drink as much of it as their system requires. At one time we used a flat shallow dish with rings so that the chicks could not drown, which they are most likely to do in an ordinary dish. But a fountain that has recently been introduced by Spratt's Patent is much better. The cup is inside instead of outside, as is usually the case with fountains, and yet the chicks cannot get bodily into it. One most important thing in the feeding of chickens is a supply of green food. If they are being reared on a nice piece of juicy grass they can do with- out anything else; but even then a supply of fresh let- tuces will be to their benefit. Should there not be good grass the lettuces become indispensable. It is necessary to remind the reader that the directions given here for the feeding of chickens refer to those that ' are intended to be kept as layers or as stock birds. If to be fattened as speedily as possible and killed off, then another course should be adopted. Under these circum- stances the food should be such as will develop flesh and not bone. For this purpose boiled rice and Indian corn should form the staple food. Eggs are very scarce at the present time in consequence of the severe weather we have had this winter. In some cases the production of eggs has been reduced by hue i half, and a calculation was recently published .n southern paper to the effect that if this proportion is universal throughout the country it has involved a. loss since Christmas of more than a quarter of a million pounds to the farmers. This is veryserious if it be true, and, whether entirely or partially true, there can be no doubt that the loss has been a serious one. In winter, laying fowls need to be kept warm and comfortable, to be fed well, and to be made to work. But with the large elimination of heat through the cold, it cannot be ex- pected that they will lay as well in winter as at other times of the year. -3:

THE SHIP CANAL BILL. The result of the poll of the ratepayers and owners of property in Salford, on the proposal that the Corporation should become shareholders in Ow Manchester Ship Canal Company to an extent of .C 250,000 was declared on Saturday eyening,. The proposal was approved by 16,653 votes, against 2,443. Thirty thousand papers were distributed, and 20,800 were collectod, but of these over 4,000 'Were unmarked.

A report has been issued which says that " it is proposed by the Manchester Ship Canal Bill to amend the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885, by anthorising the Manchester Ship Canal Company to pay interest during the period of seven years allowed by their Act of 1885 to the shareholders of the company on the amount from time to time paid up on the shares allotted to or held by them respec- tively from the respective times of such payments." A clause enabling them to pay interest during con- struction was inserted in each of their bills by the promoters, but it was struck out by the House of Lords. In 1882 a Select Committee of the House of Commons recommended that companies should be permitted to pay interest upon capital during the sonstruction of railways or tramways, subject to ' certain conditions which were inserted in Standing Order 167 at the end of session 1883. These condi- ‘iotis are in force in the House of Commons, but not in the House of Lords. The report concludes-- "The provision proposed to be made by this clause with regard to the mode of raising the capital for the construction of this canal appears to the Board of Trade to be deserving of the favour- able consideration of Parliament.

Some difficulty was experienced at the Regina trials in Canada in making the Indian prisoners understand the legal terms in which their offences were set forth. For instance, no term could be found to convey to the un- tutored mind the idea of the Queen's Crown, which the prisoners were charged with conspiring against. This was explained to One Arrow as being "the Great Mother's big bonnet with feathers in it." A candidate for the honour of representing four Fife Burghs in Parliament, calling upon an honest shoemaker for his vote and influence, took the liberty of kissing the gude wife, who was a middle-aged woman; and, in doing so, he took the further liberty of slipping a couple of guineas out of his own mouth into that of the ;matron. Instead of being offended by such a breach of decorum, the lady slily said, as she pocketed the two shining pieces, "Gin ye like, sir, ye may kiss my dochter too." A party of Bedouins were di,puting respecting the sanity of Lady Hester Stanhope, one party strenuously maintaining that it as impossible a lady so charitable, so munificent, could be otherwise than in full possession of her faculties. Their opponents alleged acts as proofs to the contrary. An old man called for silence. "She is mad !" said he; and, lowering • his voice to a whisper, as if fearful such an outrage against established custom should spread beyond his circle, he added: "She puts sugar to her coffee !" This was conclusive. This anecdote is related by Mr. Barnum in illustration (:o the axiom that drinking is a habit that grows. "Last winter two of my elephants began shaking with chills one lir:ming. The keepers ran down into the village and got sik gallons of whisky. Hastily returnimg, three gallons were given to each elephant. Fortunately it cured them. They liked the artificial -.Tarmtli it sup' er- induced. Next morning, when the keeper came to them, he found both elephants shaking with might and main. No, you don't!' he. shouted. You are well enough to-day;' and they stopped shaking." •
Public Analysts have submitted CADErsuy'S COCOA. to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. .Bos'aro of Imitations.— Advt.

div.head: SECOND READING PASSED IN THE HOUSE OF
div.p: SECOND READING PASSED IN THE HOUSE OF

COMMONS. Mr. HOLDSWORTFI, in supporting the second reading of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill in the House of Commons on Tsesday, stated that the object was to give effect to an Act passed during last session for the construction of a ship canal between Manchester and the sea. It was felt by the promoters that the powers asked for in the bill Went necessary in order to carry out the construction of a work which was sanctioned by Parliament last year. The bill provided that interest should be paid during construction until any portion of the works becomes profitable. These powers were not pressed for in the original bill, because it only passed, on the 30th July, and it was therefore impos- sible ea press for, those powers without sacrificing the whole bill. The promoters preferred half a loaf to no bread. The hon. member cited the case of Indian railways, where in- terest was paid flaring construction. In France the con- structors were actually bouni to pay interest. Should the second reading be granted, the promoters would be ready to meet the opponents in Committee. The Act passed last session would, be believed, be inoperative unless this bill received the sanction of Par- liament.

Lord C. HAMILTON, in moving the rejection of the bill, pointed out that the clause in the bill of 1883 for the pay- ment of interest out of capital was struck out by the House of Lords, and that in the Dill of 1886 most stringent provi- sion was made to guard against such an arrangement. The protnoter4, in making the proposil they now did, were, com- mitting a breach of a solemn avreement entered into by them with a Committee of the Commons. They proposed to reduce the capital by the amotnit of £750,000, and he hoped that if the House passed the second reading of this bill they would at least allow the petitioners, who were the Corporation and people of Liverpool, to be heard against it.

Sir H. THOIIPSON seconded the amendment. Mr. MUNDELLA. said be would give the reasons why, in the vieve of the Government, this Bill ought to receive the assent of the House. In 1883 the Manchester Ship Canal Bill passed the House of Commons with this clause in it. (Hear, hear.) The next year tie. Bill was hrouebt in in the House of Lords, and it was in deference to Lord Reties- dale, the Chairman of Committees in that House, that the clause was not inserted. In 1885 the clause was taken out of the bill because the Standing Order was forced upon the promoters by the Chairman of Committees. Ho would point out that that Standing Order really applied t) railways and not to canals at all, and he thought it was hard measure to force it upon a canal company. It was said that great berm was likely to result from the present proposal, but he ceuld quote high authorities to show that the Standing Order was a great restriction upon enterprise, and had done a great deal to help monopoly. This canal scheme was not like a railway, which could be opened in sections, for the whole undertaking must be completed before any profit conld be received. (Hear, hear.) These were not times when men were prepared to lock up capital for seven years before they received a farthing in return. The Standing Order was of doubtful advantage—(hear, hear)—it existed in no other country in the world, and in France ccmpanies had to pay 4 per cent, during construction, and ado it to the capital, for practically it was part of the cost. (Hear, hear.) What had been the effect of the enterprise? It was impossible to deny that, coincident with the Canal Bill, the railway rates between Manchester and Liverpool had been reduced 25 per cent., and although it might be said that this reduction would have taken place if the scheme had never been b(oached, he ttaougstit it was the broaching of the scheme that had helped the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce to get the reduction. On this occa'sion the House would do well to relax the Standing Order. With reference to sending the bill to a Select Committee, heel there not been enough money wasted in Committees? (Hear, hear.) He thought that an enterprise which was believed to be of great public utility should not he ob;iged to pit itself in Committees against rich companies like the London and North-Western. He trusted the House would pass the bill, and he would observe that when the Ship Canal Bill was rejected in the last Parliatrieut the noble lord the member tor Paddington went straight to Manchester and declared that there was no greater proof of the incompetence of the House of Com- mons than that it had rejected the bill. (Cheers and laughter.) Sir R. PEEL supported the second reading, observing that six Committees had already sat on the Canal Bill. Mr. BRAND reminded the House that the Committee to whom this question of the Standing Order was referred im 1882 recommended that exceptions should be made in special cases, and that each case should be decided by the House upon its own merits. In this instanee he thought the House should consent to the second reading, but sug- gested that it should then be referred to a Private Bill Com- mittee to consider whether the company, having had leave to pay interest during the construction of the works, should not increase its own capital.. Mr. GIBSON (Walton Division of Liverpool) submittal that where a Select Committee bad sanctioned a bill on certain terms, the House ought not to take upon it- self the very serious responsibility of saying that Cease terms should be varied without any inquiry by a Com- mittee. Mr. COURTNEY, while wholly averse to the motion that this bill should be rejected now, was in favour of remitting the bill to a Committee in the ordinary way, restricting their attention entirely to that alteration in the financial basis of the bill. (" Hear, hear," and uNo.") He would be prepared to make a motion to that effect. Sir J. MOWBRAY doubted whether this course would not lead to the whole queetion being reopened. (Hear, hear.) Mr. L. COHEN (North Paddington) contended that the question was one which it was quite competent for the House to decide itself. Lord C. J: ITAMiLToN intimated that if the House agreed to adopt the suggestion of the Chairman of Wsys and Means, be should be willing to limit the reference to finance, excluding the commercial and engineering ques- tions. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER hoped the House would take upon itself the duty of deciding the ques- tion of financial principle without sending the bill to a committee. After remarks from Mr. SCLATER-BOOTH and Mr. A. FORWOOD, Mr. SEXTON stated that be held in his band a list of 15 members who occupied the position of directors ef the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire, the London and North-Western, the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire, and the Midland Railways, all of which companies were interested in oppos- ing the present scheme. He wished to ask the Speaker whether these gentlemen would be entitled to vote in the approaching division. The SPEAKER: That matter is entirely on 3 for the in- dividual judgment of the members concerned, of course al- ways bearing in mind the fact that it is a question of the directness of the interests cencerned. Mr. SEXTON: I beg to give notice that if I see any of them coming out of the divieion lobby--(Loud laughter, in which the remainder of the hon. gentleman's remarks was lost.) The bill was then read a second time, the challenge to the Speaker's decision that the ayes had it not being plea- 1 sed to a division.

Lord C. HAMILTON then moved that the bill be referred to a committee, to be nominated by the Committee of Selection. Sir J. FERGUSON and Sir J. ATOWI3RAY Objected to the proposal, the latter urging that the bill should take the or- dinary course. The House divided— For the motion ............... 61 Against ........................ 385-314 Kr. SErrox moved that the vote of Mr. Plunket be dis- allowed. Mr. TIPPING rose and said that he also went into the lobby, and he was a director of the London and North-Western Rail way. Mr. SEXTON said that Mr. Plunket was also a director of that railway, and he preatunA the two gentlemen received pecuniary Compensation for their services. ThAt constitu- ted a sufficient reason why neither of them should intervene in this division.

Lord C. HAMILTON called attention to the fact that Mr. flouldsworth, who was a director of the Manchester Ship Canal, told in the division. (Laughter) Mr. PLUNKET, submitting to the House, stated that in his case a similar question was decided in his favour three years ago. Mr. TIPPING looked upon the observa,ion of the hon. member below the gangway (Mr. Sexton) as. a species of boycotting. (Laughter.) He should go into the lobby again under similar circumstances. • Sir W. Hencounv cited authority to show that on sravernl occasions since 1846 the Houss bad allowed votes of this kind. If the votes of opOonents wore disallowed, the votes

of prompters who went into the lobby should be disallowed. He should think, under these circumstances, there might be a truce. (Laughter.) The House divided. For Mr. Sexton's motion Bl Against The Ship Canal 13111 is still retained in the group which was formed before the bill was read a second time. The de- cision of the House not to refer the Bill to a Select Com- mittee does not affect the duties which the Private Bill Committee will have to discharge. If an objection be taken by the promoters to the three petitioners, the Court of Referees would have to decide the question, and it is believed they would refuse to grant a locus. In that event the Bill would then become unopposed, and be referred to the Chair- an of Ways and Means.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

To write instructions how to proceed witlt outdoor gardening operations savours of the burlesque when the ground is covered with from 6 inches to a foot of snow. We hope, however, that it will not remain many days, and that before we have to write again we shall be ac- tively engaged preparing for sowing peas and beaus; also planting kidney potatoes. Celery: A box or nail of this should be sown at once, and placed in a frame or greenhouse if early plants are required. The compost should be light and rich, and the portion used to cover the seed should be passed through a *in. mesh riddle. Watering must be done with a fine rose on the water- pot, or the seeds will be disturbed by the force of the water against them.

TEE FRONT GARDEN.—The Ivy: From now to the end of the month is a good time to trim this plant, where it covers the dwelling or any other building. Those who cut it in autumn or mid-winter are forced to gaze for several weeks or months ma a more dreary surface than the bare brick wall would be, whilst those who cut it at the end of March will have it green and cheerful in a fortnight or so. We like to clip the leaves as well as the young growth close to the wall, as it gives an oppor- tunity to clear it of dead leaves and other rubbish, and the ivy seems to approve of this treatment, for its whole surface becomes quickly covered with young growth as vigorous as before. We have in this column combated the notion that ivy encourages damp in walls that may be covered with it. Those who are still sceptical on this point have only to inspect ivy-covered walls during rainy periods,, and they will be convinced of the fallacy of this antiquated opinion. If peoiale persist in cutting the ivy at the wrong time, they have themselves to blame, and not the ivy. It is plain that those who cut it in the autumn expose the wall to the rain, which is readily absorbed by the porous bricks, and before the heat of summer dries it up the wall is covered with young leaves, which will to some extent account for the inside damp. The ivy should at all times be kept clear of the spouting, for [if pieces are allowed to enter it or lap over it they interfere with the flow of the water, and they act as conductors to carry it down the surface of the wall. We have also seen it permitted to ~row partly up the roof, and when such is the case the shoots thrust themselves under the slates or tiles, and widen the laps, which let in the rain when it comes from the point the roof faces.

THE GREENHOUSE.—Tomatoes : Early in the present year a correspondent addressed to us some queries re- specting the cultureof the Tomato in a greenhouse. We briefly replied at the time, and promised details later on, or at the time the seeds may be safely sown in a green- house. The season has now arrived, and two or three seeds may be inserted in a not 3in. diameter, containing light and moderately rich soil. The seeds should be placed in a triangle in the centre of the pot, about half an inch distant, and as soon as they are an inch or two high pinch off the two weakest. This plan will obviate breaking the roots, as is the case when a nnmber of seedlings are turned out of a pot and separated, and somewhat clumsily pricked out. It is true we sacrifice two plants to get one, but we take the seeds to be of less Importance than the time that would be taken up in filling so many more pots, in order to ensure the requi- site number of plants, as the same number of pots should be sown as there are plants required. Those who choose to trust to the one seed and .one pot may do so, and insert it in the centre, and cover it with a quarter of an inch of fine soil. After the seeds are sown and the covering slightly sprinkled with tepid water, they should be placed in the warmest part of the greenhouse till the seeds are up; then they must be elevated on a shelf near the glass, to prevent them drawing. When the roots show themselves outside the pot through the hole at the bottom, they will require transferring into another pot 2in. larger, and the soil should be moderately fresh loam, chopped or pulled to pieces, to which should be added one-fourth leaf-mould or decayed manure. Soil in which cucumbers have done well will also answer very well, as the plant at this stage is not fastidious as to soil, but, at the same time, thrives better in that which is good than in bad. Pot moderately firm, by pressing the soil dewn with a flat, blunt stick. If the soil is moderately' moist, water will not be required for a day or two, but this will to a great extent depend upon what power the sun has on those particular days. It is best to keep them on the dry side, so as to ensure short- jointed, sturdy growth, and at the same time have their: tops nearly touching the glass. At this stage each plant should be provided with a stake to support it, lest by the process of watering, or in some other way, it may got bent, and consequently bruised. Those who may not have time to raise their own plants can always purchase them in small pots in April and May.

1 THE FABLE OF THE CLOCK.—"Ah," sighed an old faith- ful clock, which I had in my room, "what a burden is life! These weights wear me out.. With much pleasure would I say, 'Tick, tick,' and strike as is my duty, if I only need not carry these dreadful heavy weights; I am not free from them one single hour." So it sighed daily, till I was moved with pity to my dear old faithful clock, and took away its weights; its complaints stopped; but it has given me no sign of gratitude since, and is silent as the -grave. So I have taken the moral to myself, and perhaps I sigh needlessly when I think that it would be so with many of us if we were without our daiiy bur- dens; they are needful to our life, although, perhaps, often heavy and wearisome. DESPERATE ENCOUNTER WITH A BURGLAIL-012 Satur- day night, at Shorne, between Rochester and Gravesend, a desperate affray took place between a policeman and a sup- . posed burglar. Sergt. Button, noticing a suspicious-looking character carrying a sack, accosted hirn.l The man imme- ' diately dropped the sack and ran. Sergt. Button wt,nt in pursuit, and, after running about a mile, the man suddaily turned round and attacked the constable with a large knife. Batton drew his stag, and a desperate struggle ensued. Sergeant Button succeeded in striking the man several severe blows on the head, but was himself severely st,blied, and became weak and faint from loss of blood. Finding his opponent getting the better of him he blew his wriist!e several times. Fortunately a farm bailiff and one or two labourers recognised the whistle and hastened to the spot. They found the officer and man struggling on the ground. They secured the man, who was subsequently recognised as a notorious thief, named, Patrick Lynch. The officer lies in a serious condition.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 13. 188 g.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 13. 188 g.

that the Speaker's chaplan were;te utter a sentence in Welsh. The Welsh quotation was given and received at first with laughter—a laughter, however, followed by a striking silence when it became clear that the Welsh words were A portion of the Lord's Prayer. Taking advantage of this solemn calm, the hon. member impressed upon tha House the moral with which he had introduced his bold quotation. —At a late hour the CHANCELLOR of the EXCH*UER ad- mitted that a case had been made out which had hardly been disputed by the Opposition, but excused the Govern- ment from supporting the motion on the ground that the church in Wales was so much an integral part cf the church in England that it was impossible to raise disestablishment in Wales and in England as separate questions. The Govern- ment were further precluded from taking up the dieestab- lishment qaestion by general elect4oo pledees.—W R. Cron concluded the debate, and at one the house divided. By the aid of Opposition votes the amendment was first adopted by WI to 229 and became a substantive resolution. A division was, however, taken before leave was obtained to put it to the House in this form. Finally, on a third division, ltfr. Grey's proposal was rejected by 34(1 to 4. The net result, therefore, was that both resolution and amendment were rejected. The reading of the figures cauaed some laughter. The Freshwater Fisheries (Eels) Bill and the Glebe Loans (Ireland) Acts Continuance Bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at ten minutes past two o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WIiDetBSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes after two o'clock. AMENDMEET OF THI PUBLIC HEALTH ACT.—The mend reading of the Public Health Acts (Improvement) Expenses Bill was moved by Mr. Dodds, and Mr. Chamberlain hav- ing accepted it as a very usesul measure and asked that the committee stage might be postponed fur a fortnight, the bill Was read a second time. THE SALE OF LIQUORS ON SUNDAY.—Mr. JOSEPH PEASE moved the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill, which seeks to provide that Lon- don public-houses shall be opened from seven to ten o'clock on Sunday evenings instead of from six to eleven, and in other towns and populous places from seven to nine in the evening instead of from six to ten.—Mr. J. C. STEVENSON supported the second reading, though he thought the bill was not equal to the demands of public opinion.—The re- jection of the bill was moved by Mr. ADDISON, who asserted that in reality only a very small minority of the people were in favour of the proposal, and contended that the only way in which good could really be done from the point of view of the temporance reformer was to prohibit the menu- facture or importation of intoxicating drinks altogether; but that was impossible.—Mr. Toecexersos, who seconded the amendment, thought something might be done in the direction of promoting temperance by stopping the adulteration of beer and by preventing the sale of immature spirits. Mr. -Meceleeet attribu- ted his return for Oldham to his refusal to have anything to do wit'e either local option or Sunday closing. Mr. CHILDERS stated that the Government would be prepared to support the pro- posal with retard to the Metroplis and large towns, but with regard to the application of.the measure to small towns and rural district' they coasidered that modifications were required. The Government would be prepared to accept the priociple laid down in the resolution passed by the House in 180. Whatever was done, it must be borne in mind that it could only be passed with the distinct understanding that the lecal authorities to be created by the reform of county government would have power given them, within certain limits, to deal with this question.—Mr. A. J. BAL- FOUR held that the bill would satisfy neither the extreme temperance people nor those who desired the law to remain as it was. The late Government were prepared to give the several districts themselves, with proper restrictions and due regard to the interests of the trade, power to make their own regulations for dealing with the question, and no time should be lost in bringing forward a Local Government Bill, for until that was done there could be no final settle- ment of the question.—Mr. H. FOWLER remarked that no- thing in the bill would interfere with the provisions of, a Local Government Bill.—Mr. Iduntz spoke amidst loud cries for a division and other manifestations of impatience from the Mieisterialists, and continued his remarks until a quarter to six, when according to the rules of the House the debate was adjourned. MISCELLANEOUS.—On the motion of Sir R. Cross, the House went into Cemmittee on the Coal Mines Bill, and progress was immediately reported.—Mr. J. Cowen brought in a bill to make provision for the assessment and collection of \municipal rates., Mr. Warrningham a bill to amend the Commissioners Clauses Act, 1847, and for other purposes, and Mr. J Ellis a bill to facilitate the acquisition of sites for places of religious worship. The House adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUsiii OF LORDS.--THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat me the woolsack shortly after 4 0 o'clock. THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY moved that a Select Committee be appointed to join with a Committee of the Commons to inquire into the opera- tion of certain Act" of Parliament for the better govern- ment of India. The noble earl stated that though it was not desirable to question the direct rule of the Queen in India, many changes had occurred there during recent years, mainly owing to the introduction of railways, which made it desiiable that the affairs of the country should be reviewed. Tha system of administration was sound, but there were various details in which amendment and change might be desirable. Lord CRANBROOK had no objection to offer to the motion, which was agreed to. Their Lordships adjourned at five minutes to five o'clock.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QuESTIONS,—Sir H. ROSCOE asked whether, in view of the success said to have attended M. Pasteur's treatment of hydrophobia, the Government would appoint a Commit- tee to communicate with the Committee of the French Academy of Sciences as to the exact position of the ques- tion, to obtain investigations as to the reliability of M. Pasteur'slenethod, and advise as to its applicability to this country.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN replied that the information at present possessed by his department was too vague and incomplete to afford material for a full appreciation of the process. He would consider hew an inquiry could be most satisfactorily conducted, and would confer with the Chancellor of the Exchequer with reference to the question of expense. He hoped to be able to arrange such an inves- tigation as would enable a just estimate to be formed of M. Pasteur's method and its applicability to this country.— The ATTORNEY-CTENERAL stated that the Government had no intention of taking proceedings against Mr. Bradlaugh for sitting and voting in the House this session.—Sir Juereal GOLDSMID inquired as to the accuracy of a state- ment made by Lord R. Churchill at Manchester to tl'e effect that Lord Salisbury had sent instructions to our agents abroad to assist British commerce.—Mr. BRYCE replied that, with the exception of the instructions sent to Her Majesty's re- presentatives in China and Japan to support British com- mercial interests where foreign representatives interfered to their detriment, no instructions whatever appeared to have been given by Lord Salisbury to our agents abroad re- lating to the promotion of British commerce.—Sir L PLAY- rent stated that the question of intermediate education in Wales was so mixed up with the Educational Endowments Act, which was now the subject of inquiry by a Select Committee that the Government could not promise to in- troduce a bill this session. THE SHIP CANAL BILL.—MT. BADEN-POWELL, referring to the second reading of the Manchester Ship Cannl Bill authorising the payment of interest out of capital, asked the President of the Board of Trade if he intended to amend the standing order so that it might apply to companies other than railway, tramway, or subway companies, and if he intended to amend the Joint-stock Companies Act so as to abrogate the rule that no dividend should be paid except out of the profits arising from the business of the company. —Mr. Mum:meta replied that he did not intend to extend the standing order, which would still hold good, as it did not appear to have any bearing upon this particular ques- tion. He added that be had no intention of amending the Joint-stock Companies Act. SUPPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply upon the Civil Service Estimates there was an animated debate upon the vote of £112,619 for the Royal parks and public gardens in the Metropolis.—Mr. LADDIJOHERE moved to reduce the vote by £50,000. the charge for the mainten- ance of certain of these parks.—Mr. CHILDERS agreed that the local parks ought to be kept out of the rates, but said at present there was nobody to whom they could hand them over.—Mr. RTLANNS argued that the result of refusing the vote would be to compel the Government to undertake legis- lation upon the subjeet.—Mr. H. FOWLER said he was not going to recede from a single opinion he had expressed on this subject when he was in a very small minority. He should now be perfectly satisfied to abide by the decision of the House.—Upon a division the numbers were—for the re- duced vote 131, against 114, a result which was received with much cheering.—When progress was reported, Mr. MIIN- DELLA. explained the provisions of his Railway and Canal Traffic Bill, which alters the constitution of the Railway Commission, making it a permanent Court of Record pre- sided over by an English, Scotch, or Irish judge, laccord- ing as it has to deal with English, Scotch, cr Irish com- plaints.—After some general discussion of a friendly tone towards the bill, it was read a first time.—The House ad- journed at ten minutes past two o'clock.

TRAGEDY NELB DERDY.—ILI the course of Thursday night a dreadful tragedy was committed at Quorndon, Bear Derby. A labouring man named William Wagstaff made an attack upon his eon, who was in bed ill with brain fever. Wagstaff's cousin, a woman named Morrell, tried to pull him off, when he turned upon her and beat her about the head with a piece of a chair, killing her in a few minutes. He is a respectable man, and there is no doubt he had gone madr Another account says Wagstaff attacked the young man and then the nurse, Mrs. Morrell. He strangled the woman and tore open her jaw. The other members of the family fled. A sudden paroxysm of mad- ness is alleged as the cause of the crime. Wagstaff has bseu remanded.

GREAT MILL FIRE AT MOSSLIST.—At Moasley, on Tues- day afternoon, the large mill of the Brunswick Cotten Spin- ning Company, Limited, was completely destroyed by tire. The mill was 26 windows long and five storeys high, and contained about 60,000 spindles. The less is estimated at over £60,000, and is only partially covered by insurance. Be- tween 200 and 300 hands will be thrown out of employ- ment, as the mill was in-autl work. Many of the workpeople had very narrow escapes in getting out of the burning band- ing, and in the hurry they had to leave their clothes and other articles behind. ALLEGED MuRDER OF A POLICEXAN.---John Airey, aged 19, labourer, was remanded at the Kendal Police Court on Monday, on a charge of murdering P.C. Groves. Prisoner was being conveyed to the police station for being drunk and disorderly at the Salvation Army Barracks. Groves was kneeling over the prisoner, Who was strimglieg upon the ground, when the prisoner kicked him upon the temple. Groves fell and immediately died in the street. At Kendal, on Tuesday, Airey was committed for trial charged eith murdering P.C. Groves during a dasturbance at the Salva- tion Army Hall on Sunday. Freeman, 60, brickmaker, was repairing his braces. using a sharp pocket knife for the purpose, when his son Henry, aged 14 years, laughed at him. The father ran after the boy, and gave him a blow with his hand. He was goiieg to strike him again, when the lad ran in towards his father, and the knife, which was pointed outwards, entered the breast and penetrated his heart, causing death in a few moments. The father was taken into custody, but he pro- tested that the affair was only an Resident, and the other people in the house also testify that it was so. Street, Leek, was found upon the fire grate shockingly burned about the breast, head, and face. Lying upon a sofa close to the grate was a paralysed old woman named Mary V9hieldon, aged 91, whose cries of terror upon seeing her friend ablaze, and being unable to help her, ultimately, brought assistance from the street. On being rescued medi- cal aid was procured, but the injured woman succumbed on Tuesday morning. The shock to Whieldon, who was almost suffocated by the stench of bursing flesh and clothes, was so great that she is not expected to live. The two wo- men were old maids, and had lived together on most affec- tionate terms for about 30 years. ALLEGED INTIMIDATION AT THE GENERAL ELECTION. —On Saturday, at the Huntingdon Divisional Bench, Jas. Hall, farmer, of Bythorn, Hants, was summoned for alleged intimidation at the South Hants election in November to- wards two labourers employed on his farm. The evidence went to show that Mr. Hall was heard to say that he would discharge any of his men who went against him at that election. He is a Conservative, and two men on his farm were Liberals. A short time after the election the men had notice to leave his service. The theory of the prosecution was that they were dismissed because they voted for the Liberal candidate. The Bench held that a prima facie case had been made out, and decided to send the case fur trial at the assizes. The defence was reserved, and the defendant was admitted to bail. RECKLESSNESS WITH DYNAIIITE.—At Chester Castle, on Saturday, Richard C. Briscoe, explosive manufacterer, was eummened for causing a ton ef dynamite to be removed from his magazine at Mold to Ellesmere Port in a cart, in which were a number of iron bolts which had not been properly covered, on February 23rd. One of the bolts had penetrated from a quarter to half an inch into one of the cases of dynamite, and the box was with difficulty removed. Several of the other cases were also " dinged" by the bolts. The defence was that the offence had been due to the carelessness of Mr. Briscoe's men. The Bench thought defendant's recklessness utterly inexcusable. De- fendant bad been fined on four previous occasions, and it was extremely fortunate that there had been no explosion. He was now fined the maximum penalty of 10 and costs.

(Loud cheers.) PRESENTATION TO LORD IDDESLEIGII.—Lord Iddesleigh was, on Monday evening, entertained at a banquet and pre- sented with a testimonial at Willis's Room, London. The testimony—a magnificent silver centrepiece, four dessert , stands, and two candelabra of most ornate design and beautiful workmanship—was subscribed for by members of both political parties, many of whom were present. The Lord Chancellor presented the testimonial, making refer- ence to Lord Iddesleigh's eminent public services, and par- ticularly to the unfailing courtesy with which he had car- ried on political controversy. Lord Iddesleigh expressed his sincere pleasure at finding himself surrounded even by men to whom he had been strongly opposed in Politics. He spoke of the interest with which he lead watched the struggles in the House of Commons, of an oc- casional longing to be engaged in them again, and to be threshing out the questions of the day. But amongst the men who represent the opinions and idiosyncrasies of the nation politics, he pointed out, were not all, for there was much otherwise to be done by men of leisure, education, and experience for the benefit of the country. FAtEIGN NEWS. THE BURNIALI DIFFICULTY.—A Biansa GARRISON SURROUNDED. MANDALAY, FRlDAY.—Geueral Prendergast has issued a proclammation offering an amnesty to all persons, with the exception of murderers and notorious dacoits, who volun- tarily surrender to the British before June 30th next. Col. Sladen will remain in Upper Burn:rah. He strongly advo- cates the construction of railways and pulic works with a view to relieving the prevailing distress and to Prevent dacoity. Ealsooom, MormAY.—Yemethen, a place to the north of Mymgyan, which was recently occupied by the British, and garrisoned by 300 troops, has been surrounded by about 9,000 rebels. The garrison has been ordered to entrench themselves, and not to attempt to move out of the place. General Prendergast; who is at Jounghoo, will leave for Yemetiien to-morrow, escorted by a small force of 100 men. It is believed that he will have to fight his way, and a severe engagement may ba looked for in a few days when the general arrives at Yemethen. A column of troops is being despatched from Mandalay to relieve the beleaguered garrison.

THE CONQUEST OF BURNIAH. RANGOON, 111IIESDA.T.—N0 serious apprehension is felt by the authorities in regard to the position of the British garrison at Yemethen, the Indian military department hav- ing been forewarned some weeks ago of the danger to be apprehended from a concentration of dacoits in that region, and havinßaccordingly forwarded reinforcements. DiSESTABLISHMENT IN WALES. Mr. DittwYsi's opportunity did not arrive till after eight o'clock. He then moved—" That. as the Church of Rug- Ind in Wales had failed to fulfil its professed object as a means of promoting the religious ifiterests of the Welsh people, and ministers to only a small minority of the popu- lation. its ointinuance as an Established Church in the Principality is an anomaly and an injustice which Aught no longer to exist." By statistics the hon, member claimed to prove that churchmen were in a minority of 1 to 8 in Wales. He assured the House of the thorough earnestness of the Welsh people on this subject, and urged the House to act towards Wales its the spirit of the golden rule.—\lr. WESTON SHANTERS T. FELODSILMIS ROVERS.—This return fixture was played at Weston, and resulted in a win for the home team by one goal, one try, and five minors to one try and one minor. The visitors arrived one short, but found an excellent substitute in Pendlebury, who scored the try and played a good game throughout, receiving good assist- ance from the brothers Rogers and Nixon. For the home team all the backs played well, W. Tudor gaining the try, and G. A. Tudor, by a splendid run and drop, landed the goal. Teams:—Shanters: Full back, G. A. Tudbr ; three- quarters, Brookes, Webster, and Moores; half-hacks, W. Tudor and Hollingsworth; forwards, Farrall (captain), Beckett, Lawrinson, Molineaux. CUP TIE, WEST LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWNS UNION.
WARRINGTON V. LYINIM AND OUGHTRINGTON.

These teams met on Saturday last on the club ground, Wilderepool Causeway, to compete in the first rouno for the above trophy. The weather was cold, hut still when the teams arrived on the field upwerds of 2,000 persons had as- sembled together to witness the encounter. During the early part of the week the ground was covered with snow to the depth of some inches, but an efficient staff of men under the superintendence of Captain Fair and his Joll(e)y assistant had been engaged, speedily cleared the field of its white mantle, but their work was somewhat marred by the further downfall on the Friday night previous to the match. The ground at the time of action was rather hard and slip- pery, therefore to some extent good running and passing was rather hindered. Both sides expressing their willing- ness to play, F. Turner commenced hostilities by kicking off, and there being no return, play for sometime was con- fined to the visitors' 25. Before three minutes had elaps,d, a good pass by Speakman to Barnes, and then re-passed to Jolley let in the latter player, Gilbert failing at goal. The backs exchanged kicks, and then Fair Turner came through with a dribble, and Povey picking up crossed the line, Fair Turner failing to improve. A minor was registered for the home team from the kick out, being immediately rushed over. Allen kicked off from the 25, Turner returning. Jol- ley now got hold, but was tackled on the line. From the scrimmage Speakman passed to Barnes, who kicked wide to Jolley-who ran a short distance and then droeped a splendid goal, which evpked loud cheering. Th,e visitors' forwards worked the ball up the field from tbe kick out, but Povey put an 'end to their hopes by taking it back to the usual quarter, v.z., the visitors' 25. Allen stopped Jolley on the line, and soon after Speakman passed to Barnes, who unselfishly passed to Massey, who galloped over the line, Turner missing at the place. Allen kicked out and Miller improved [natters by a run te half-way, but F air Turner and Aebton equalised matters by dribbling it back aoain to the .goal-line, Speakman from the scrimmage, dashing over for try number four. Turner failing. From the kick out Gil- bert was seen to advantage by a good run and ki'4' to touch. A kick by Barnes caused another minor totle re- gistered. Play was next confined to neutral ground for some time. but Ashton was not to be denied his share in the try-getting, for knocking aside all opposition, ground the oval over the line. Turner being unsucoessful at goal. Ashton stopped the kick out. but the visitors dribbled to half-way, Rigby rushing it back to the visitors' quarters, where some exciting scrimmages took place. Eventually Davies got held, passed to Turner, who passed with good judgment to Rigby, who,comnleted the try, Speakman kick- ing a goal which brought about half-time. • The second half was merely a repetition of the first, if anything, the passing was better. It would only be monotonous to give all the play as it took place, suffice to give the tries, &ea and the manner they were obtained :—let try l‘laseer after a good- pass by Jolley, Speakman failing at goal ; Jolley next dropped another goal amidst much applause; 2nd try Barnes, after a dice run, Turner failing at goal; 3rd try Fair Turner, after a dashing run, upsetting He opponents like ninepins, the game player failing at goal ; 4th try Maesev, Speakman kicking a goal sth and last try by Ash- ton, after a run three-quarters of the field. Speakman being unsuccessful at goal. Davies in this half made a brilliant rim, being collared on the line, Ashton, Povev, Rigby, and Turner also beirag conspicuous. The full score at the close being Warrington : 4 goals, 9 tries, 6 minors to nil. Warren and Buxton were unable to take their position in the team. ' For Warrington Hewitt at full-back got in his kicks with good judgment, but is rather weak in tackling. Jolley was the best of a good lot of three-quarters. Gilbert played well until he was hurt and had to retire at half-time. Speakman shewed good judgment in his passieg. Of 'the forwards too much cannot be said in praise, as they played an excellent combined game; Fair Turner, Ashton, Rigby, Povey, and Davies were perhape most prominent. Allen, Miller, and Ho]t (backs) played well for Lymm ; the for- wards were completely overpowered, and taking all into consideration, a better game on the Warrington part has not ben seen on the Warrington ground. Teams :—War- rington—Back, Hewitt; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half-backs, Gilboa and Speakman ; for- wards, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Ashton, Heyes, Rigby, Dillon, Davies. and Povey (captain.) Lymm and Ouglitrirgton—Back, Gleave; three-quarter backs, Thoma- son, Miller, and Allen ; half-backs, Chantler mad Holt ; forwards, Gosling (captain), Kirke, Brazendale, Gibbons, Hart, Kay, Shaw, Clarke, and Forster. Referee, Mr. Nay- lor, Wigan.
