EARLESTOWN OLYMPIC V. SANKEY REFINERS —These teams met on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and a good game resulted in a draw, 2 goals each. The Olym- pians played a pressing game throughout, while in the first half the leather was continually in the Refiners quarters. Swift, W. Tarton, Simon, Powell, and the goal keeper played well for the visitors, while Toole (centre forward) and Percival (goal) were most conspicuous for the home team.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The initial round of the West Lancashire and Border Town Cup was inaugurated on Siturdav, but unfortunately only twelve clubs played their ties, the weather not being of that propitious character which has hitherto favoured the Union Extures.

Of the winning teams .the first we deal with is the War- rington. That they would win was hardly doubted, but by the enormous total of 4 goals, 9 tries, and 5 minors cer- tainly was beyond the most ardent supporters' anticipa- tions. Warren was on the sick list, and Buxton also cried off at the last moment, Hewitt filling the vacancy. The ground was very hard, and at the start some 3,000 Persons were present. Throughout both (40's) forties the" villagers" were on the defensive, but their efforts were of no avail, as try followed try in rapid succession. Sixty-nine points to nil is a facer, yet every point was honestly deserved. Hewitt, what little he had to do, was done well. Jolley was in great form ; one of the two goals he dropped was a beauty, and in addition to securing a try he again ran the ball over the line, but lost possession, Massey touching down and recorded his third try. Barnes is deserving of mention foe his unselfishness, and it is to be hoped he will endeavour to cultivate the style of play he exhibited on Saturday. Gilbert was unfortunately crippled early in the I game. Povey took his place, and in consort with Speak- man performed very creditably. The combination of the forward division was grand, passing neatly and with preci- sion. Their following up was good, and they tackled splendidly. There was nothing striking in the display of the Lymmites, Miller and Holt being the pick. Runcorn 2nd beat Sutton a few weeks ago, consequently the latter were aware it was only a question of how many points; 70 to 1 was the result, and Runcorn enter the second round. Widnes sat on the Recreations by 53 to nil, Edgehill beat Lowton by 21 points to 6, St. Helens Recrea- tion 35 points to Blundelleande 4, LitherlaDd 18 to New Brighton Olympic nil. Oldham fought shy of meeting the Hornets at Rochdale; the rivalry between these clubs is as great as Runcorn and Warrington. Several of the second round of the Yorkshire Cup ties came ell, the most notable being Hull beating Ovenden by 3 goals, 6 tries, and 6 minors. A meeting of the Executive Committee of the West Lan- cashire Rugby Football Union was held at Liverpool on Saturday, when it was unanimously resolved that the second lround of the cup competition be played on Saturday, March 20th, and the remaining contests in the first round to be decided (s-day (Saturday). The following is the draw for the second round :—Leign or Kirkdale v. Runcorn; referee, Mr. H. Hibbert, Chorley. .Bootle or Walton v. Wavertree or St. Helens; referee, Mr. H. Bell, Liverpool Old Boys. Blackrod or Wigan v. Edge Hill ; referee, Mr. G.W. Vickers, Salford. Litberland v. St Helens Recreation; referee, Mr. J. Jackson, Salford. Pagefield or Newton v. Southport Olympic or Aspull ; referee, Mr. A. B. Dewhurst. 'War- tington v. Widnes; referee; J. T. Seddon, Swinton. Bon. secretaries of clubs will take notice that the cup competition for next season mill commence on the first Saturday in March, 1837. The success which has attended the efforts of the origin- ators of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Union of Rugby clubs since its forma:ion in 1834 has led to the establishment of a challenge cup competition, in which the winners of the final tie will have the honour of bolding for twelve months a handsome trophy. In one respect the con- ditions of the contest will differ from those which gener- ally govern matches played according to the Rugby Union code of rules, and will meet the strong objections welch are frequently raised against the injustice of allowing a goal (either placed or dropped) to beat any number of tries. The Rugby Union rules, as regards the play, will have force in this competition, but the points gained will be anPreised at the following valet& :—A goal placed after a try will count eight points, a goal kicked from the field of play six points, a try four points, and all minor points one each; a majority of three points being necessary to secure a victory.

FRESCO' RURAL SANITARY AUrtIORITY. EXTRAORDINARY " 6CENE." A special meeting of the Prescot Moon Rural Sanitary Authority was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, to consider the proposed sewerage scheme for the Eccleston (Rural) township. There were present Messrs. John Leatherbarrow (chairman), J. T. Hall, W. Newsome, E. Syder, John Kenwright, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).— The Clerk said the meeting had been called to consider a letter from the Local Government Board with respect to the Eccleston sefferage scheme. The letter from the Local Government Board was dated March sth, and they trusted the Rim' Sanitary Authority would euhmit their mo4ifi..d proposals ?,.'4h r°spßt tr..) tt4 ,”WeTtiZt Accl disposal of it sewage of the contributory place of Eccleston at a very early date. The Board were advised that eorks of sewerage and sewage diepae,ll were macti seeded for certain parts ,of the place, and having regard to the time which ' had elapsed since their views on the original applica- tion were communieated to the Authority, the Board toought the details of a revised scheme should be d:finitely settled ' without further delay.—Continuing, the Clerk said it would be recollected Messrs. Hall and De Rance were employed by the St. Helens Corporation to report upon certain portions of the scheme, and a copy of the report had been sent to each member.—Mr. Newsome asked hoer the matter had been brought forward. He considered Eccleston Rural was the most healthy portion of the Union of Preecot. It migat be there were some busybolies making themselves conspicu- ous with bringing forward the matter.—The Clerk said the Sanitary Authority had previously agreed to have a sewer- age scheme for that part of Eccleston township in the Au- thority's district, and an inquiry into the subject was • held by one of the Local Government Board's inspectors,and the Local Government Board, had said there were cer- tain parts of the township e which required a sewerage scheme. Mr. Hall proceeded to ask the Clerk as to how the matter tirst arose.—Mr. Newsome said that was extraordin- ary, when Mr. Hall a short time previously professed to have nothing to do with it. Many members thought he had not. He (Mr. Hall) was a disinterested party, and not a ratepayer, and he (Mr. Newsome) did not see why he should bring the scheme on them.—Mr. hall said he wished Ito know why the original scheme had been altered.—The Clerk pointed out that the Local Government Board con- sidered the scheme too elaborate for tare present needs' of . the district, and the Authority, while adopting the whole scheme decided to proceed with only a portion at a time.— Mr. Hall asked if one portion was proceeded with would the whole township have to contribute towards the cost.— The Clerk replied that the whole of Ecclesron Rural would have to pay its share. Mr. Hall asked if they considered it was fair and honest. The Clerk : It is a matter of Jaw.— In reply to Mr. Newseme, the Clerk said the sewage scheme bad been under consideration since Decembet, 1879.—Mr. Newsome said his contention was that if the Sanitary Au- thority bad done their duty then in regard to buildings there would have been no necessi!y for the scheme now.—Mr. Hall considered its sin that persons who would never get any benefit should have to contribute for the sake of Eccleston Park and the Lane Ends. He did not think personal re- marks by Mr. Newsome ought to have been made, and.he would not have them.—Mr. Newsome did not think Mr.. Hall had a right to be on the Authority. He was one who had fostered the scheme.—Mr. Hall : I have a right and I am here.—The Chairman: Order, one at a time.—Mr. New- some (to Mr. Hall) : You don't pay —Mr. Hall: I have my say in the matter.—Mr. Newsome: You do not pay at all. —Mr. Hall : I will not have it. That has been decided and the Local Government Board have said I have a tight to sit here, and I will sit here independent of rod or anybody else. Mr. Newsome and Mr. Hall continued speaking to each ether, Mr. Hall ulti- mately rising and taking his hat, el-clared that Mr. New- some was " a —lrishman ; that's what he is and nothing else."—The Clerk: Mr. Hall, will you vote on this ques- tion ?—Mr. Newsome: He has no right.—The Clerk, in reply to Mr. Hall, said Mr. Hall had a right to be present and vote.—Mr. Hall (speaking to M. Newsome): I wilt sit here independent of you or anybode else, you " bloom- I hie Irishtnan."—The Clerk: You have a right to be here. —Mr. Hall : I will not allow an Ir.shman like Mr. New- some to stop me.—The Chairman : It you have no respect for yourself, kindly have some respect for the committee you are among.—Mr. Newsome: He rnieht take his bat off. The Chairman: The langtage you are using is not fit to be used anywhere—Mr. teall: He broualit it on.—The Chairman: *Well, uso your language outside, but don't bring it here.—Mr. Hall: I will not be insulted by a fellow like that.—The Chairman again drew attention to the business before them, and Mr. Hall ultimately moved that the cle7rk should write a letter to the Local Government Board acknowledging rt.. ceipt of the communication with reference to the proposad, scheme, and asking if they endorsed the opinion of the in- spector, Mr. Arnold Taylor, that the possibility of pollution of the water in either tee well or the borehole of the Cor- poration water supply was so remote as ID be tmworthy of consideration. In the event of the reply being in the affir- mative, the Authority would at once negotiate for the necetee rary land. Mr. Newsome remarked that there were always some persons very ready to spend a lot of money they had no interest in.—The Clerk, replying i to Mr. hen right. said the charge would only be upon that portion of the Union affected by the sewerage scheme. It weuld be a special charge upon that portion of Ecclaston not within the borough of Sr. Helens. It was absolutely necessary that he saould send a reply, ad Mr. Kenwriglat thereupon secanded Mr. Hall's proposition.—The resolution was passed unanimously. the Ch.irinan remarking there were certain times in the hietory of men's lives when they made use of lananage that was not Parliamentary, ard for , the use of which they were aftereards oorry.—Mr. New. seine: And liae other occasions ibey will regret it.—This concluded the business a

The re-opening last week of !Ile Warrington Library and Museum will : • ve done something, it is to be hoped, to tusect the attention of the people of this dis- I. to the fact that, although Warrington , as one of the first, if not the very first, u,oroughs to bring into operation the Libra- • s Act of 1850, it does not yet possess a Free I....ibrary in the true acceptation of the term; ,tsitors are free to read at the reading-room Bold street, but if they desire to take a ,b°ook away they are confronted with a charge. 4.his, as it seems to us, is an antiouated.and 9diculous remnant of the days of the War- rington Subscription - Library, and, as we also believe it to be, a breach of the law, We trust that the ratepayers will not let the niatter rest until justice is done to them by the abolition of the obnoxious impost. We have just received a copy of a valuable work "Free Public Libraries, their organisa- uses, and management," by Mr. 4hornas Greenwood, F.R.G.S. It is a sub- tantial and instructive volume, and we do , nOt hesitate to say that if each Town Conn-' • in the kingdom were to furnish himself 'with a copy the reproach would ere long be I,lzeri away from us of having 133 Free Pub- ; Libraries only as compared with France,: o• r instance, witn x,OOO. We find from the \ork in question that what is known as Wart's Libraries Act of 1850 has been re- Pealed, and its place taken by the Libraries A:ct of 1855, which, with amendments enacted .BL!rice, governs the proceedings of existing ; .„'ree Library Committees in connection with 40\vn Councils. We have looked carefully Over this Act and these amendments, and we cannot find one word which gives authorityl for making a charge for the loan of books ; 811C11 as is imposed at the Warrington Library. On the contrary, clause 25 says :—!' The ad- r9ission to all Libraries and Museums estab- lished under this Act shall be open to the ! Public free of all charge." It would be Possible, of course, to contend that "admis- sion "to Warrington Library is free, and that the borrowing of books is a different matter. .uut we submit that the whole tenor of the i e• t is clearly in the direction of the Library oeing free to the ratepayers even when booksl a, re "lent out." Clause is provides that t• he amount of the rate to be levied in any ' oorough, district, or parish, in any one year,i for the purposes of this Act shall not exceedl he sum of one penny in the pound." There I Is. nothing said about further funds being ' talsed by way of a second charge upon the ratepayers. Authority is nowhere given for Inaking such a charge; and, as no corporatel uodv can act outside its statutary powers, there can be no question that the imposition • a subscription is illegal. Clause 21, which deals with "general management," gives the committee power to "make rules ard regulations for the safety and use of the Libraries. and Museums, and Schools, and r.or the admission of tile public ;" and what :Is meant by this is revealed in "Appendix 11.,.," where a model code of rules is set lorth. These rules make ample provision for the safety" and " use " of the books, not o.tuitting fines for keeping books beyond the tine specified; but there is nothing about a libscription or chargé of any kind for books 9orrowed. On the other hand, it is dis, tnictly stated that "persons enrotled as bur- ,gesses of the borough shall be entitled to norrow books on their own- responsibility. Persons not so enrolled shall be required to Obtain the signature of one burgess to the '''cher, which must be renewed annually."i granted that a Free Library Committee s IlOt under obligation to adopt this particular k:ody of rules, we ask—where is the authority 'Or making a charge? It is a burlesque t'Pon what is being done in other towns with a, Penny in the pound under the Act to take the full penny in the pound in Warrington, then ask the ratepayer who has met all 'dues and demands" required by the law to 1?43' in addition a subscription of eighteen- pence a quarter, or five shillings a year, be- -I,e he can be allowed to read his own looks T. If there is a select class of people 1,11 the town who want a select class of books, h• ere can be no objection to. their forming a 131thscription Library; but they will .not be entitled to ask for a subvention from the I:ates. The books purchased out of the rates are the property of the ratepayers, !rid, as such, they should be lent to the rate Payers without charge, as is the custom in Other towns. It is not sufficient to say—

" They are free to read al the Library, if they like, and there are many who avail them- selves of the privilege." Granted this is so, how many more are there, we would ask, who would be glad to take books home and read them, as they have a right to do? It is not enough that people should be able to get a drink at the well; they want now-a-days to be able to draw water at home—just when they most need it. We understand that it is urged. as a reason for not doing the right thing, that one penny in the £ is not sufficient to keep the Library, Museum, and Art Gallery going. As to this, we have to say that institutions of this kind can be kept going on £soo or on £5,000 a year. The coat has to be cut ac- cording to the cloth, and the " cloth " pro- vided by the Legislature is a matter of the penny in the £ on the rateable value, which in Warrington means £530 a year. The sub- scribers who at present have a monopoly in the loan of of the ratepayers' books contribute less than £ so ; and we have not the slightest doubt that, by a little of the pinching which is being generally resorted to these hard times, the Committee could dispense with the £l5O and declare the Library really free. They would not require to touch salaries, which do not amount in the aggregate to more than £zzs ; and, after paying neces. sary expenses, they would still have some- thing for new books, though as to that— since there are 20,000 volumes in stock— the public would not starve if for oie year no new book was placed upon the shelves. What we object to is the starving, intellec- tually, which is going on at the present moment in so many households, and amongst people who have contributed their full share to the well-stored granary which is stationed in their midst. There is such a thing as book hunger, and there are books in abundance to meet it. Let them be placed where they ought to be—in the hands of the people, and let the people enjoy them by their own firesides.

THE Presentation, on Monday evening, to the Earl of IDDESLEIGH of a magnificent tes- timonial subscribed for by noblemen and gen- ilemen of both political parties is agfeeably suggestive of the fact that politicians are not so black as they are sometimes painted. Thrre are few men, however, who have been as much to the front as Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE was for so many years in the House of Commons who have preserved so well all that is regarded as finest in the character of an English gentleman. In the description which is given of the testimonials it is stated that two of the accessory.figures represent "forti- tude and gentleness as characteristics of Lord IDDEsLEIGH's life," which would go to show that the work is as excellent in design as it is beautiful in execution. Some of the fiercer spirits of the Tory party thought " the gentle Sir STAFFORD" was "lacking in go ;" but it is all to his credit that he would not " go " into anything unless with the ap- proval of conscience and judgment. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL contrived to make the bulk of the Conservative party believe that they would get along much better if Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE were deposed. But have they? They have certainly made more stir, made more noise, and thrown more mud, but nobody can honestly say they are any better for it. It was fittini . that the pre- sentation should be made by a Liberal Lord Chancellor, who could truly say that his lord- ship had secured— that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends. Indeed the Lord Chancellor went so far as to say he had' troops of friends and not a single enemy." Lord IDDESLEIGH confessed that he had felt the separation from the House of Commons a great deal more than he thought he should, and he added The House of Commons was, after all, the ex- pression of the meaning, sentiments, will, and power of the nation, and it maintained its position amongst us because it was a thoroughly representative body." His lord- ship, although now a member of the House of Lords, is not disposed to exalt his n w sphere at the expense of the old. Perhaps he feels, as Lord BEACONSFIELD expressed it, that in going into the House of Lords he was being buried alive. Well, he has had thirty years of work and turmoil in the House of Commons, and, as he is not strong—it is stated that he has a weakness of the heart— it will, it is to be hoped. prolong his life to "go to grass "amongst the drones. He has, to quote his own words, "leisure and educa- tion and experience ;" and we wish he may long be spared to follow his scholarly tastes, while still proving of service to his QUEEN and country. •

THE Manchester Ship Canal Bill, brought forward to enable the promoters to pay inter- est out of c,anital during the course of con- struction, had something like a triumph in the House of Commons on Tuesday. The opposition can hardly be said to have been in the running. Lord CLAUD HAMILTON started boldly as a Liverpool representative to get rid of the measure altogether; but, finding that he was on the wrong horse, he was glad to snatch at a proposal to refer the matter to Committee. Another Committee, forsooth, when not less than a QUARTER OF A MILLION has been already spent in Com- mittee work in deciding the main issue The House felt that the question of finance was one that could be settled there and then; and Lord CLAUD HAMILTON having withdrawn his motion "that the Bill be read a second time that day six months," the proposal to refer the Bill to a Committee was rejected by 375 to 61. It was pretty evident during the course of the debate that the opposition had no case; and, seeing that there was the precedent of the Regent's Canal, the argument was greatly in favour of the Bill. Mr. AIUNDELLA was careful to point out that there was a wide difference between making a railway and making a canal. A railway could be partially con- structed and opened in sections; but a canal was useless until finished from end to end. Four per cent is not a great deal to pay; but on the other hand it is natural that people who have invested their money should • want some return during a course of years. If there was a likelihood of investors being taken in by the facts of the case being kept from them, there would of course be .strong ground of objection; but it is provided that the prospectus., or 'share certificate, shall set forth the fact that the interest is for a certain period to be paid out of capital. Looking at the least promising ;aspect of the case, it is surely no worse sink- ing eight or ten millions in the construction of a canal, which will; at least keep a large !number of Englishmen at work foryears, than investing as many millions in foreign bonds which so often pass away and "leave not a rack behind." Taking all the circumstances of previous struggles into account, the House of Commons has done no more than its duty in declining to refer the Bill to a Cummi“ee.

RE-ASSESSMENT OF MANSIONS IN CHESHIRE.— The Nantwich Assessment Committee are now deal- ing with mansions in Cheshire, and great interest is felt in the proceedings. The following increases were reported to-day :—Cholmondeley Castle raised from £489 rateable to £1,300; Peckforten .4.',425\t0 £1,200; Crewe Hall, £425 to £7OO. The total increase of assessments already made, includ- ing Crewe Works, is nearly £200,000.

sntERT A.&iDtNT AT Wltnlas.—As Mr 3. of James Murray, one of the foremen at the works of Messrs. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Present—Messrs. Littler (chairman), Rogerson, Whittaker, and Salkeld (clerk). It was reported that the interments for the eleven months endittg Febru- ary 25th were 313, corresponding period last year. 335; decrease, 22. The fees received during the same period amminted to 305 14s 10d, being a decrease of -£56 16i 9d. Accounts amounting to £53 Sc, including £l9 6s for in- terest, were passed. It was decided to give the overseers notice to call a vestry meeting for the purpose of appoint- ing auditors to the Board. __•

WIDNES TEMPERANCE AND BAND OF HOPE UNION.—A meeting under the auspices of this union was held in Malin's Hall, Simm's Cross, on Wednesday evening. There was moderate attendance. Mr. J. R. Hudson pre- sided, and referred to the objects for which the union had been formed. Speeches were made by Messrs. Hargrnves, Gibbs, Fairhurst, and Reay, upon the advantages to be gainen by total abstinence from intoxicating liTior. Glees were sung by a choir composed of members of the various temperance organisations in the town, and the proceedings were of a pleasant description. _

WIDNES CATHOLIC CHORAL SOCIETY.—The Widnes and District Catholic Choral Society gave a concert in the As- sembly Rooms (Baths) on Monday evening to a fair audi- ence. The first part consisted of a cantata entitled May Queen," and the various songs and choruses were sung in admiral9le style the effect being improved by an efficient string band. The second part was of a miscellaneous char- acter. Miss Jameson, Miss Oakdea, and Mr. Finn were each encored for their capital vocalisation; and Mrs. O'Keeffe, Messrs..jlanlon, Rafferty, Faulkner, Williamson, and Cullen were also successful in their various efforts. A cornet silo by Mr. J. Stirk, and a violin duet by .Messrs. Gordon and Kiddy were much appreciated. Mr. G. Faulkner was the conductor, and Mies Cullen the accompanist. STRANGE ADVENTURE AT WIDNES.—Mrs. Sennett, of Caroline-street, Widnes, has had a strange adventure. On Saturday night, about ten o'clock, she left the house to fetch a pint of beer fer her husband, who was in a state of great alarm because she did not return. Between six and seven o'clock on Sunday morning she was found lying in the garden attached to the house of Mr. Patten, at Moss Bank, almost frozen to death. She had the can in one hand, and 3d. in the other, tightly clenched. She was re- moved to the engine-shed on the railway, and after being well warmed she was taken home in a cab, and she is now recovering from the effects of her severe exposure. The woman had no idea how she travelled so far, as Mr. Patten's residence is about three.quarters of a utele from her home.

THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.—The triennial election of the Guardians of the Prescot Union will take place dur- ing the next month, and it is considered Mid,' there will be contests in more than one of the townships. The number of guardians to be elected for each township is as follows: —Bold 1, Cronton 1, Ditton 1, Eccleston (urban ward) 2. Eccleston (rural) 1, Hale 1, Halewood 1, anyton-with- Roby 2, Knowsley 1, Parr 2, Prescot 2, Rainford 2. Raiohill Speke 1, Sutton 3, Tarbock 1, Whiston 1, Widnes-with- Appleton 4, Windle (urban) 2, Windle (rural) 1, Little Woolton 1, Much Woolton 2. Nominations must be handed to the clerk (Mr. S. H. Hartley) between thel4th and 26th of March; on the 27th inst the list of nominations will be issued, and if more than the required number of candidates are nominated voting papers will be delivered on the 7th April. and on the following day they will be collected. The counting of the votes will commence on the 9th April.

BWRELOR's TEA PARTY AT WinNEs,---The annual bache- lors' tea party and entertainment took place on Monday evening in the Primitive Methodist School Chapel at Simm's-cross. The proceedings from beginning to end were very diverting. There were about -200 persons pre-. sent. The married men of the congregation —or " ex-bachelors," as they were termed—had to perform all the offices pertaining on such occasiuns to the lair sex, and to make the tea, cut up the viands, lay the tables, and attend upon the bachelors and spinsters, and this they did in a manner which displayed some awkwardness at first, and evoked a consequent amount of merriment. "The " bachelors " were attired in a somewhat hybrid style of cos- tume, wearing mob caps, plentifully " trussed witn rib- bons, white aprons with bibs, fancy skirts, and .over all a swallow-tail, or square-cut black cloth coat. Their appear- ance. as may be surmised, was most ludicrous and mirth- provoking. After tea the Rev. James Calvert (superinten- dent minister) presided, and the benedicts discoursed a programme of songs, recitations, and addresses suited t o the occasion.

EVANGELISTIC SERVICES AT WIDNES—Mr. and Mrs. Wiggan, of London, the gentleman being known as the " Weeping preacher," brought a fortnight's successful tnis- sion work in the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel to a close on Monday. On the previous day Mr. Wiggan preached to good congregations, morning and even- ing, and in the afternoon Mrs. Wiggan related the story of her conversion. At the evening service the following mo- tion MS unanimously carried •—`• That we wish Mr. and I,4rs. Wiggan to so arrange their present engagements as to be able to return from Warrington to Widnes for another fortnight at least before they leave Lancashire for Lincoln- shire, Surrey, or London." A tea party was lAA on Mon- day evening in the chapel, 120 persuos being present. At the subsequent public meeting there was a good audience, and the Rev. J. Calvert, of Warrington, presided. The Chairman related bow he was converted 34 years ago. Ad- dresses were given by Messrs. Wood, Overton,Shuttleworth, and Lewis, and then Mrs. Wiggan spoke. Many flattering references were made to the evangelists who were cordially thanked for their services on the proposition of Mr. Lewis. Mr. Wiggan responded. There were the usual devotional exercises, and the proceedings concluded with the singing of the Doxology.

RUNCARN f'ONS OF TEXIPERANCE.—A meeting in connec- tion with the "Lifeboat Crew' division of the Sons of Tem- perance was beld in the -Regent-street Schoolroom, Run- corn, em Tuesday evening. Mr. F. J. Norman presided, and there was a good attendance. Mr. W. parish, J.P., ex- mayor of Chester, was announced to be present, but was unable to fulfil the engagement owing to indisposition, and his lelece was taken by Mr. Ghiers, Chester city temper- ance missionary, who delivered an able address. Duties- the evening several glees, auartettes, and solos were given by a glee party, under the leadership of Mr. J. Stubbs, Mr. WaGittens being az the harmonium. Addresses were also delivered by the chairetan, Mr. John Withiugten, and Mr. B. 13ishrown. TUNCORN BOARD OS COMMISSIONERS—A special meet- ing of this Board was held yesterday, under the presidency of Mr. P. Speak-man. On the proposition of Mr. Grice., seconded by Mr. Dobesu, Mr, Charles Wigg was unanim- euely re-elected the representative clf the Board on the Upper Mersey Navigation-Commission for the ensuing, three years. The Board then went into committee to consider the "tineatisfactory manner in which the nightsoil cnn- tract was carried out.' by Mr. E. Field. After considerable diecussion a resulution was passed, en the motion of Mr. Leke, seconded by Mr. Harris, to the efect that the Inspec- tor of Nuisances attend on the nightsoil contractor and neke possession of the hoeces and plant used for cerrying out the nightsoil contract, end in case the ,contractor refused to surrender them., that horses and plant be engaeg,ed to clear the asbpits. The cost thereof was to he charged to the .centractor, namely, deducted from the " conrederation -moneys" in the hands of the Comtniscioners. The bonds- men of the contractor are also to be 'notified that the In- spector of Nuizances had certified that the contract war, not being carried out in a satisfactory manner, and of the acreion the Beard proposed to take in the matter. It was sfurther resolved, on the motion of Mr. Lake, seconaed by Mr. Dobson, that .the Health Committee be empowered to carry the foregoing resolution into erect in such a manner asithey considered advisable. A. WIDNES WATCEmAKER AND MS DOG.—Axt,NG CxtegE.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. John Brook, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday., Frederick Hunt, watchmaker, Widnes-'road, was charged with keeping a dog without a license. P.C. Savory and T.C. 1,119 visited the defendant's house and asked if be kept a dog. He replied Ne " and gage them permission to search the house, of which the officers availed themselves, and found a retriever ,chained up in the back yard. He had no license. Tbe de- fendant called his wife-who said the doa was her own eri- vateiproperty.—The defendapt : And neu keep it ageinet my-desire ? Witness:: No.—The defendant slid his house had-been broken into and the thieves never found. His wife considered their lives and property were not safe without some prptectione and she persisted in keeping a Cog for (het Pureoee contrary to his wishes. Under the Married Women's Property Act of I.BBo—(lnughter)—anything belonging to a marriea woman was her sole property, and she was to be acted and proceeded against in all actions at law as though she were a single woman. Under these circumstances he submitted that he was not liable. Ills wife did not know et was necessary te have a license, and there was no inten- tion to avoid payment.—Tke defendant, in reply to M. Lewin, admitted that he was the occupier of the house and that the dog was upon his premises.—The Bench fined him Ss, and costs 12s. A HORSE ENGULPHISD AT NORTIriTICII.—A sud- den and alarming subsidence occurred at Northwich on Sunday at the stables of Messrs. Worthington, salt manufacturers, where, without the least warn- ing, the earth opened under one of the horses. The animal fell into a deep gulpli, and immediately dis- appeared, the water rushing up to within ten feet of the ground level. The stable boy escaped only by grasping the tail of the farthest horse. The inhabitants ot the immediate vicinity were greatly alarmed, and some families deserted their homes in terror.

PAGE LANE MISSION, WIDNES —ln the LOOM Of this mission on Saturday evening, a successful entertainment was given by Messrs. E. Carey, J. Morrison, C. Driffield, H. W. Deacon, S. Kidd, IL Cookson, F. Scott, and G. Barker. The choir assisted.

ROYALTIES AND THE MINING • INDUSTRY.—A number of members of Parliament interested in the mining industry met on Wednesday at Westminster and discussed the question of leases and royalties, with special reference to the bill of Mr. Conybeare, which at present only relates to Cornwall. Mr. Conybeare, who presided, said the principle affected the whole country. The mining industry was hampered by the landowners, who could deal with the minerals underlying their property as they liked. He thought it desirable that there should be fixity of tenure in relation to leased mines, and that a competent tribunal should be entrusted with the adjustment of a fair scale of royalties, which at , present were arbitrary. Several members present advocated the establishment of a Mining Commis- sion, but some difficulty was foreseen in the settle- ment of what a fair royalty ought to be. After considerable discussion it was agreed that the Go- vernment should be urged to grant a Ccinmission of Inquiry into the system of royalties and dues, and Mr. Conybeare promised, if that request were un- successsul, to go on with his bill at the earliest date possible.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

At a recent meeting of the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority language was used "Un- mentionable to ears polite.' The Chairman did his best to preserve order; but, if disorder is to be the order of the day, he will require to be provided with a " chucker- out."

The New Zealander is marching on. Taw- hiao has prohibited the sale of intoxicating liquor in his territory. This is one of the advantages of ruling without Parliament; no need to 'wait, debate, and hesitate." It looks as if Macaulay's pet were preparing himself for that sketch of St. Paul's from the ruins of London Bridge.

The Rector of Warrington can hardly be called a man of peace. He has. quar- relled with curates. churchwardens, and parish clerk, and now he is at odds with the School Building Committee. Pity he doesn't see what a relief it would be to himtelf and other people if he would re- sign, and take it easy for the rest of his days.

The Liberals of the North wich Division are in a festive frame of mind. At their next meeting the Executive of the Council will consider a proposal to hold a series ot soirees in the division. There is hardly any doubt that the idea will be carried out, or that Runcorn will be the scene of one of the gatherings. Why shouldn't poli.ics and social enjoyment go hand in hand? The franchise never was conferred to make our pleasures less.

Mr. Latham, M.P., is recovering nicely at Southport. He is none the worse for know- ing that a kind friend has paid his election expenses. Mr. E. K. Muspratt is also re- covering' from the illness which prostrated him at the beginning of the week. It was a sore disappointment that he could not preside at the soiree at Widnes on Tuesday. It is hoped that he will keep in trim for the next electoral battle, which will be a success- ful otit,,

The ratepayers of St. Helens may be ex- cused for showing themselves a trifle nervous at the proposal to borrow, all at once, £24,000 for the extension of the gas works, and Err,ooo for the site of the proposed Park. Important matters of that kind should not be entered upon without the fullest in- quiry. At the same time, if a bargain is to be made in securing land, the Corporation should not throw a chance away because times are hard. It will be pleasant to stroll in the Park in the good time coming.

Mr. John Morley is showing great aptitude for his work in Parliament as Chief Secretary for Ireland. He manages to keep the golden mean in the cross fire of questions between Orangemen and Nationalists, encouraging neither the one nor the other. But, when it comes to matter of real importance—such as the distress in the West of Ireland—the short speech which he made on Monday shows that he has deep sympathy and that he is quick to act.

The members of the Earlestown Liberal Club are all alive and debating. When it is stated that the subject under consideration on Wednesday evening was "The Taxation of Ireland," it will be readily understood that there is no topic that they are afraid to tackle. They are setting a good example; there is too much of "the three B's "—beer, 'bacca, and billiards—at Liberal as well as Conserva- tive Clubs. It is a sign of improvement when people take to thinking rather than thinking as a means of diversion.
Punch has put on record, as follows, "What working-men think of the Wolff Mission "
We feel, at a season when work runs so short And where taxes fall hard on the labouring poor, What's expended in keeping a Wolff at the Porte, Might assist us in keeping the Wolf from the door.

Particulars of a touching instancepf "the short and simple annals of the poor" is given in another column. A clerk out of employ- ment, 4.0 years of age, and in delicate health, went to reside with his daughter, aged ro, in the poor neighbourhood of Pocket Nook, St. Helens. Feeling very ill, the other day, he called his little girl to him, asked her to make his bed and then tenderly said— " Good-bye, my dear." Poor fellow ! This was his last good-bye, for he died shortly afterwards, leaving his child, a shilling in the house, and scarcely any furniture.

An inquest was held at Dutton Union Workhouse, on Saturday, on the body of a man who had died from cold and exposure, and who was apparently on the tramp in search of work. The regular tramp knows how to take care of himself and where to beg; but cases of this kind are full of tragic pathos. The long hard frost has done murderous work among "homeless heads and unfed sides."
Alone and unknown—alas, what an end, When Death is thus haled as the poor nian's friend.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, an order was made for a black and tan dog, belonging to William Unsworth, to be destroyed. It had bitten a traveller named Appleton, and Mr. A. B. Mackie gave evidence that it bit him in November last. This "black and tan" has "played at snap," if we mistake not, for some time; but we shall hear of it no more, unless it goes about as a ghost of a dog making a ghost of a snap. if the brute felt that its mission was to bite, why did it not fly at the calf of "Spring- heeled Jack," of whom all the small boys speak just now with bated breath.

Captain Reynolds is to be presented with a testimonial by the Conservative working- men of Warrington and their friends, as a mark of their recognition of his .invaluable services tdtheir cause." It will surprise no one to hear, and it Is no reflection upon Captain Reynolds, that the subscriptions of the working-men are just now of a micros- copic kind; but it is surprising to learn that the Committee couldn't decide whether they would have a death-like bust or a life-like portrait until they got tenders. "The lowest tender" was for a bust, and bust it is to be. They would have liked to honour the Captain ; with cheese, but under the circumstances , they have resolved to give him chalk.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Alford-street, on Tuesday. Present—Mr. Carey (in the chair), Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Wright, Dutton, Heyes, Tay- lor, S. Sadler, Houghton, T. Handley, J. J. Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Carr (engineer).

div.head: TILE FREE LIIIRAItY.
div.p: TILE FREE LIIIRAItY.

Mr. Wright moved the passing of the minutes of the last meeting, with the exception of tbe General Purposes Commit- tee. These minutes sanctioned the utilizing of the Board-room for the purposes of a Free Library, and that £lOO be spent in books.—Nl r. lie.yes seconded the motion. He never under- stood that the minutes were put at the last meeting, and had the chairman declared them c*rried he should have challenged the decisioa.—Tne motion was carricd.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board with regard to the application of the Board to borrow £7OO for the purposes of the Free Library. They intimated that an inquiry into the subject would be held as soon as arrange- ments would permit.

div.head: GAS AND WATER
div.p: GAS AND WATER

The minutes of the Ci-As and Water Committee reported the appointment of Herte-rr. 1,,,es as assistant gas and water manager, at i salary or £9O per annum. The Engineer re- ported that during the last month Dr. Campbell Brown had analyst(' samples of the water of stock's well and Netherley, and rep .rt,d that both were excellent for domestic use. There was a slight decrets.e in the amount of•impurities in the Stock's welt water. The mean rainfall for February bad been 164 inches The water in Stock'zi on February 24th eras 4,215,969 g.llons. The illumin4,lll,r power of the gas during the month had averagA 17 92 candles.—The minutes were pa=sed vu the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. "ray lor.
HIGHW i MATFFIZS.

! Mr. Plerpoint waited upon the Highway C.nr.ntittee and asked that a sewer should he laid in Albert-road to provide for cellar drainage. The committee replied that it was not intended to make a s2wer there at present. Mr. J. White wrote on behalf of the managers of St. Mary's Parish Cbtrei, s:a:ing that they have no funds to pay any ex- pens,s for the making and sewering of Marsh-street. In- struction given to reply that oply plac,s appropiiated to public. reii4ious worship are exempt (ruin such expenses by the P.H. Act, 1675. and that othe- schools have had to pay similar charges. It was recommended that the Board's plant usel io tLe construction of the main sewer be sold Lv pncc 31ti-m—The minutes were adopted on the motion of the Chiirman, seconded by Mr. Houghton. THE ACCIDPST HOSPITLL: PROPOSED CITLN9SE.

:the Heelth Committee's minutes cmtaiued the report of the medical otlic.o for February. Tne births had numbered 84 ; and the deaths 40, being at the rate respectively of '36 65 and 17 45 per 1,000. Zyrnotic diseases caused two !deaths. The receipts from the Market durieg February amounted to £2:20 3.1, being an increase of £6 18s 3d as !compered with February, 1885. A. local tradesman had complained abut the charges for hawking, and suggested Ithe adoption of differential rates for resident and. non-resi- dent hawkers. The matter will be considered at the next I meeting of the committee.—Accident Hosjoita! : No patients !since 24th Decetnhsr. The Matron submitted list of the ,! names of donors of books, papers, flowers, fruit, (t.-,c , received ' clueing the past 12 months. It was recommended that the charge of one shilling per day be Ant enforced ; and that the matron be empewered to call in, when necessary, local medical men in ro atioro to patients ether than pauper, club, or other patients where the patient employs his own medicel man, and that medical men so celled in be paid a :ee upon the sone scale as in Poor Law ewes—Dr. O'Keeffe moved, :and Mr. Heyes seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wright said there was no doubt that an accident hospital was one of the grand institutions of this countryOand to • his mind it ores a misfortune that such an institution should • ever become a burden to the ratepayers, and to; should like ' to know how it was that it was now proposed to abolish the Ifee of a sh'llino per day. It was, he acknowledged, a very ' small item to a large body of ratepayers such as they had in Widnes With regard to the payment of the doctors; this vras the begiening of something they did not know where it would end. When accidents did occur the sooner they relieved suffering humanity the better, but he cer- tainly otiierned to the Board being made responsible for the fees of medied noon ee.Mr. Sadler slid after the three ex- empted cases, what were the other cases in which they were require' to eineley medical assistance P—Dr. O'Keeffe re- plied that there might be a stranger coming into tee town, who might accideneatly break his lege, he would certainly re- quire a medical man to set the leg, and he would not be a pauper. Medical men would not be inclined to attend their patients unless they got such fees as they received from the Poor Law Board. This matter hart been taken up in consequence of some remarks made by Mr. Gaskell, who called the attsntion of the Board to a man who was injured, and who rather then pay the Is per day which would be taken out ef his club money, and consequently front the support of his family—he was transferred to Liverpool, where no charge would be made. The recommendation was simply an experiment, and it was brought before the Board for the purpose of hearing the opinion of the Board whether it would be a benefit to the people of Widnes. He !did not tie.ink it would be any additional expense upon the ' ratepaytre, because during three months of last year the Accident Hoepital was without patients, during the last two moieties there had not been a patient in the institution. They alto found that about •S 0 per cent. of the patients were club patients, and therefore entailed no expense upon the ?ratepayers of Widnes. It was very rarely indeed that any person had been taken in the hospital when a fee had been charged us the rates. As it had been so in the past they might oreeurne and hope that it would be so in the future.—Mr. Heyee slid the committee spent about two hocrs considering this question, and they thrashed it out thoroughly. The conclusion they came to was that it could 'not possibly involve the Board at the worst in ran additional .e.emoenee of £5O a year. When they considered that they bad the hospital on their hands, and could not get rid of it at a considerable annual .expense, it seemed to him as a ,business more the height of folly that it should not be made 1 as useful as poteible to the ratepayers who had to pay for It, all for the sa.ke of a fen pounds more. With regard to the shilling fee, he considered that it was very hard to :charge a poor working-man when he was struck down by an I accident and no longer able to keep his family that he should be called upon to pay one shilling per day out Gf the scanty club pay for the support of the hospital which he , also supported in ate rates. It was a pity that the hospital should he no use to the ratepayers all for fear of risking a few more pounds upon it.—Mr. Dutton said he was on the Hospital Committee for re wo .years,and he found the regula- tions of the hnspitai were very excellent and suites to the wants and requirements of the peesons who needed its as- sistance. Hee denied that at present it was useless. It was there when wanted, and he did not regret it being empty at all. It showed that there were very few acci- dents in the town. He preferred to adhere to tbe eld usages of the hospital for the present.— Mr. Sadler questioned the correctness of the sure mentioned by Mr. Heyes The hospital was now used for prlvate surgical cases and he contended that it was unfair that these oersons ehould be not only found with accommo- dation, but maintained at the expense of the Boara.—The Chairman suggested that the consideration of the subject should be deferred fat a uacnth.—Mr. Taylor moved that the recommendation be referred back to the committee.— Mr. Dutton seconded thee motion, and it was carried.—Dr. O'Keeffe proposed that the hest thanks of the Board be given to those lathes and gentlemen who had given periodicals and flowers.—Mr. Dutton seconded, and it was carried ueattimously.

PRIVATE STREET IMPROVEMENTS. The Finance Committee recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £1,250 for t..:m years for the making of Marsh-street and Witt-road—The Clerk said he had written to the Local • Government Board asking if they would entertain an ar• plication for borrowing power for making streets, the usual notices not having yet been served upon the owners. His object was to save the time of the Board by having one in- quiry instead of two or three. He had received the follow- ing reply :—" lam directed by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter of the 4th lust with regard to . the provsed borrowing by the Widnes Local Board of the , sum of £1,230, £3,400, and £4,500 for works of private street improvement ; and to state that the Board have .no 'objection to considering at the present time an application from the Local Board for sanciion to the borrowing of all these Some. They would not, however, be prepared to sanc- tion the two latter loans !loth the requisite notices had beett given in resptct of the streets to be dealt with and the time ' allowed to the owners for the execution of the works had expired."—lhe Clerk added that the streets in question were Farnniorth-road, James-stleet, West-street, Welling- ton-street, Byron-street, at an estimated cost of £2,000. Then time were Ann-street, Victoria-street, Margaret-street, New-street, Lea-street. Fisher street, Edison-street, Irwell- street, and Viaduct-street, at an estimated cost of £4,800. The plans for the last-mentioned streets were not yet ready, but the surveyor .could have them prepared for the next mecting.—Mr. Handley moved. and Mr. Dutton seconded, that application be made to the Local Govern.

LIBERAL SOIREE AT WIDNES.

Under the auspices of the Widnes Liberal Association, a soiree was held in Lacey-street ecuoolreorn on Tuesday evening, and was in every way a success. About 400 per- sons sat down to the tea provided, and the audience was considerably augmented at the concert which subsequently was given. Mr. E. Carey presided, and amongst those pre- sent were—Captain Brunner, Dr. O'Ketiti, alsssrs. S. K. Muspratt, J Talton, F. Lawrinson, W. Sadler, R. Farrant, J. Robinson, I. Carr, A.. E. Smith, John CSXOO, F. H. Pank- burst, J. Taylor, J. Betney, H. B. Shores (sec), ike.. The Chairman said he very much regretted to inform those present that their president, Mr. E. K. Muepratt, was unable to attend that evening. He would read the letter he had received tram him :—"My dear sir,—l regret extremely that toy cold and bronchitis have become so much worse to-day that I am obliged to remain in bsc, and dare not venture to leave the house in such severe weather. I must therefore ash you to make my apologies to the meeting for my absence. I hope you will carry the resolution in favour of Mr. Gladstone with enthusiasm. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He (Mr. Carey) had not the Eighteet doubt they would carry the resolution with all the enthusiasm that their president could desire. (Hear, hear.) He regretted particularly that Mr. Muspratt was unable to De present that evening, because that was the first meeting of what he might call a new series of gatherings in which they core- blued .some pleasant entertainment with more serious eseliti- cal business. (Hear, hear.) The programme opened with a pianoforte solo skilfully performed by Miss Muspratt, and highly appreciated by the audience. The same lady also recited " God's judgment on a bishop," and in response to an encore gave " Lochin- var." Miss Maria Pemberton, of the Liverpool Philhar- monic concerts, gave an enjoyable iaterprotation of "Sing, sweet bird," and she was recalled. She later favoured the audience with a capital rendering of "The bend of the river." Much amusement was caused by Mr. G. E. Young's recitation of the speech by Sergeant Bozfuz, from Pickwick Papers, given in character. Ha was also success- ful in the recitation " Quaker and the robber." Miss N. Handley, of Runcorn, was extbusiaszica:ly encored for her expressive and musical vocalisation of the song, "Someone's sweetheart," and in response she gave "Fairly caught." In the second part she sang with iouch pathos "Side by side," and was loudly applauded. Mr. C. Crighton gave a studied recital of "Eugene Aram " and sang the " Masher king," a hurnourous son .z that proved very acceptable. Miss Wright, of Rencorn, contributed the ever charming seng "The lost chord," in a manner that earned her a well-merited encore, and she bowed her ac- knowledgments. She also gave a capital rendering of " The children's home." Miss Dainteth, of Ditton, who was suf- fering from a cold. sang successfully the belled "That traitor love." Mr. W. W. Gosoige was loudly encored for a careful rendering of 'Go lovely rose," and he responded. Mr. F. Reyes gave forcible and expressive renderings of the songs "Wapping old stairs," and "Simon the cellarer." and he was recalled. Mr. E. J. Spragg sang "The boat- swan's story" in acceptable fasaion. A fsature of the evening was the brilliant execution of a violin solo by Mr. S. Gandy, who responded to an enthusiastic encore. Miss 'Johnson officiated as accompanist. During an interval in the programme, Captain Brunner moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting rejoices at the formation of a strong Liberal Government under the Premiership of Mr. Glad- stone—(applause)—and is confident that he will be able to satisfy the desire of, Ireland for self-government without peril to the unity of the Empire." (Applause.) Being all true liberals, be said, this resolution 'nest commend itself to all of them. They rejoiced that a Liberal 'Government had been formed because they knew that a Liberal Govern- ment represented the wishes and hopes of the vast majority of the people of this couatry—(applause)—an I they looked to a Liberal Government to pass such measures as should ha for the benefit not of the Liberal party only bat the nation at large. (Applause.) They also rejoiced that a.measure was to be brought forward for Ireland. (Hear, hear) Knowing in whose hands that measure was they might be quite satis- fied that the measure would be a just and a generous one— (hear, hear)—and as they hoped that it would lead to the granting to the Irish nation of as full as passible a measure of self-government. (Hear, hear.) We in this country were proud to make our own laws, and he for one could not see why the same ceastitutional right should not be exten- ded to the sister cotantry. (Applause.) He believed that the grantines of a large tneaeure of self- government to Ireland would he, not injurious to the integrity of the Empire—hear. hear)—and ho con- sidered that it would lead to peece and prosteeiity amongs- us all ' • and that in the enjoyment by the Irish people oft the right to make their own laws, we should not only have an unit,:d kingdom in name, but in reality. (Loud ap- plause.)

Mr. I. Morrison seconded the resolution with great plea- sure. Mr. Gladstone deserved not only their support, but their warmest sympathy for undertaking at his time of life —to chase his illustrious career by passing for Ireland legis- lative independtece in accDrdance with the NN idhes and as. pirations of the great bulk of the people. (Hear, bear, and applause) He recommended all those who took an interest in this question to study Irish history for the last century, or since the Act of Union. He was sure that those who did so earnestly, must c.rnie to the conclusion that the gtwern- ment of Ireland could not possibly to worse than it Lad been during that period, and that there turret ultimately be a change. Many people thought the Act of I.7Pion took place many hundred years ago, and that it would be a dreadful affair to interfere with it. As a matter of fact it took place only 88 years ago, which in the history of a , nation was a comparatively recent date; and was passed by such abominable means that one of the Eaglish historians said that it stood a monument of the infamy of the legis- lators of that period. It was, he thought the more necessary to read history, as the Conservative party would use all their power to excite the minds of the English people against self-government. Lord Randolph Churchill and Lord Harris did not hesitare to say that if legislative independence were granted to Ireland that what they called the Loyalists of Ulster would rise in rebellion against it, and they inferred and many more people suppose,' that the Loyalists of Ulster were in a large majority, whereas they were in a considerable minority. (Hear. hear.) Therefore they need not be afraid that the Orange faction of Ulster would march at Vie head of fifty thousand troops, as Major Sanderson had threatened, be- cause it was simply the bluster of such men as Johnson of Ballvkillig, and keen of Belfast, who only within the last few 'days had used language with regard to Mr. Gladstone which was not fit to mention in respectable c)mpany. Hoe for one did not believe that the granting to Ireland of self- government would in the slightest degree jeopardise the in— tegrity of the Empire, but that it would tend to consolidate it, and make Ireland and England a truly united kingibm. (Loud applause.) Mr. Poulson supported the resolution as a working-man, and eulogised Mr. Gladstone.

The Chairman, in putting the resolntion to th, meeting, said they ought to have had their president in Parliament to assist Mr. Gladstone--(hear, hear, and applause)—and if they did their duty at the next election, he went fultber and said they would have him in Parliament. (Loud ap- plause,) •

The resolution was carried unanimously, and the Chair- Man intimated that it would be forwarded to the Premier. On the motion of Mr. Morrison, a cordial vote of thanks was given to the ladies and gentlemen who had entertained them so ably that evening. A similar compliment to the chairman conclu,7.ed the pro- ceedings.

LYMM. There have been no prisoners brought before the Lynne magistrates during the past week. THE MASSEY BROOK WORKS—It is proposed to hold a maes meeting of working-men regarding this question, which is becoming a vexed one. Some dissatisfaction is expressed amongst certain classes that the Local Board did not finally decide it at their last meeting. THE FROST.—The weather during the past week has been severe at Lymm, the frost having been so keen that the darn has become frozen, and a few venturesome lovers of skating have bad the hardihood to try the ice. The water of the dam is deep and great caution snould be used. ForerncoetterG LOCAL BOARD ELECTlON.—Nominations for the coming election of members of the Lymtn Local Board are to be handed in by the 24th March. The voting papers will be delivered on the 29th March, collected on the 2nd April, and the casting up will commence on the follow- ing day. Mr. Dewhurst is the returning officer. FlRE.—Shortly before half-post four o'clock yesterday afternoon a message was received at Lymm Police Station thee a fire had broken out at the Saracen's Head public- house at Heatley. The fire-bell was immediately rung and tSra manual engine brought out into the roadway in front of the offices of the Local Board. Before a start was. made, however, a second messenger arrived with the news that the engine would not be required, the fire h ,ring been got under. It had originated in the rafters of the roof, near the chimney, and was net of a serious nature. LYrNi VOLUNTEERS —A quadrille party, promoted by members of the Shooting Club of the Lynnet Company (3rd Cheshire) Rifle Volunteer Corps, was held in the Drill Hall, Brookfield, Lynam, on Monday evening. 'rue party was just large enough to be comfortaole. D tncreg coins rnenced at 8 p.m., and was kept up with spirit until about four o'clock on Tuesday morning, everyone present seeming to enter into the fan with retnarkalole zest. Tne M.C.'s were Privates J. Rovrson, A. Eustance, and FL Broweing, who arranged an excellent programme, and whose energy and tact did much to ensure the thorough ettjeyment of every memder of the party. The refreshments were dis- peneed by Lance-Sergeant S. Jackson and Private T. WARP.INGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. .310NDAY.—Be10re the Mayer (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. altscennatemous.—Charles McNalty was fined 5s and costs for being drunk in Foundry-street on Saturday after- nooo.--John Mitchell, John Marveion, William Farrell, Thomas Monoghan, William Foy, and a young man named Gavin, were charged with being disorderly in Bank-etreet on the 28th ult., and were each ordered to pay 24 6d to- wards the cests. Defendants were playing football on the street on the Snudav evening in question.--Wiliiam Cotton, a youth, was -fined 58, incluling costs, fete throwing snowballs in Lythgoe'e-lare3 OEI the 2nd March. Vioneeerce: AND DenNet.—A. young man named John Jef- fries was charged with .being drunk and disorderly at Market-gate, on Saturday, and with assaulting Police-con- stables Bruen, Hennessey, and Singleton. The °Meters en- deavonred to disperse a nis9rderly crowd at Market-gate, and defendant refuse to go away and threatened Is break Singleton's jaw if he went near him. Defendant was then taken into cnstody, and assaulted the three officers on the way to the station.—A fine of 103 and costs was imposed SCEOOL ATTRND/4±,ICNI CASES.—The following persons were eummoned by Mr. George Riley kr not sending their chil- dren to school .—John Roony (fifth time), fined 55; John Lee, forgeroan, Ce4hedge (second time). 73 di for two children; John Naylor, fergernan. It appeared . . that Byrnes had been in the Old Crow Inn, when the de- fendant aud her brother came into the same apartment, and the former throw a glass at Byrne which struck and cut his fweheacl. THERSDIY.—BeforcI Major Litton. BEGGING.—James Jackson and George Smith, stranfrers, were each sent to prison for seven days for begging in Wil- son-Patten and Bold-street on the previous evening.

LEcrunE.—Miss Kevan, of the London Scientific Dress Catting Association, delivered a lecture in the Hnyton Park schoolroom to a gathering of ladies on Saturday afternoon. The lecture was illustrated with coloured diagrams and practical demonstration. C.E.T.S (lIMETON BRANCII.)—The meeting en Monday evening was addressed by the Rev. A. T. Scott, Bootie, and )107 an entertainment, vocal and instrumental, was given Mesdames Evans and Scott, Miss Evans, Messts. p. Wester, R. Evans, and S. Lamble. The vicar, Canon Penrhyn, occupied the chair. TRIIPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—On Tuesday evening there was a good assemblage at the Huyton Park School, when an address was delivered by the Rev. C. H. Bradbury, of Teasley Cross, on the " Fducatiin of the nation in the tem- perance cause." Mr. E. S. Eccles was in the chair, and songs and readings were contributed by Mrs. Eccles and Mr. Stoba. Miss Turner presided at the pianoforte. Ac-cmzerr.—As Mr. and Mrs. Brown, of the Blue Bell Hotel, Huyton, were driving ha their trap to Liverpool on Wednesday afternoon, when near Fairfield the horse took fright and upset the vehicle, throwing the occupants to the ground. Mr. Brown we e for some time insensible, and suffered injury to hie aim; and Mrs. rown received a severe cut on the forehead which had to be sewn. Mr. Webster, who rode at the back, escaped with a severe shaking.

DEATH BEFORE DISITONOUR.—A painful tragedy occurred at Vienna on Saturday. Capt. Gerstel, of the Artillery, an officer who was most ponular amongst his comrades, was aumraoned before a court-martial for some slight offenco against discipline, and sentenced to imprisonment for a short period, without &privation of rank 6)r any other loss of honour. Capt. GerstQl heard his sentence with composure, and bowed to the court, but on leaving the room he fired two ehot s from his revolver, both directed against his head. The first shot roiseed, but the second proved fatal. The un- fortunate orficer was the son of a Vienna phTsician, and was only 35 years obi,
