THE STATE OF IRELAND.

A FARMER FOUND DBLD.—A farmer, named James Nee.nan, of Kilrush, was found dead on TOunday morning in a field near Cree. He was at Miltown Fair, on Wednes- day, and it is not known what caused his death. During the progress of festivities in celebration of his wedding, some hours previously, on Wednesday, Mr. Pat- rick Walsh, a farmer and millowner, of Holly brook, near Skihbereen, was taken suddenly ill, and died in the arms of his bride. SUPPOSED INCENDIARISM.—A !catch mill in Coalisland, County Tyrone, took fire on Sunday, and the entire place was gutted. A large quantity of flax belonging to the Roan Spinning Company was destroyed. The proprietor of the mill, named Eckliss, has sworn information the fire was malicious.

DIABOLICAL OUTRAGB.—A house containing 10 caws, 10 goats, and 15 tons of hay was burned to the ground within a mile of the police hut near Listowel, on 'Sunday night. It was the property of a farmer he:ding land from which a tenant had been evicted. The National League held a meeting at the place on Sunday. MOONLIOIIIING —CAptAn Chute, J.P., whilst proceeding home on Saturday nieht was waylaid aboat a mile from Tralee by a party of men, who severely maltreated him and :Meld his pockets. Captain Chute had been under , police protection until recently. Other cases of moon- lighting occurred in county Kerry on Saturday night. HOPE FOR. IRELAND'S FUTURH.—Replying to an address or welcome, on Tuesday, from non-subscribing Presbyterians, the Lard-Lieutenant said he was sanguine to hope that the outcome of the present crisis will inaugurate happier days for Ireland, and he indulged in the hope that he would wit- ness the establishment of mutual confidence, harmony, and tranquility throughout the land. S'IRIPEING AND TA.BRING AN IRISH BAlLlFF—lntelli- gence from Youghal, says a process-server named Ahern, going to serve summonses near Villierntown, County Water- ford, en fishermen who refused to pay more than 103 each en their 30s fislainz licenses, was stopped by a number of men, dressed as women, who deprived him of his papers, stripped him, tarred him all over, and then let him go. MURDER AND SUICIDH—A very tragical occurrence took place in Enniscarthy on Monday. John Somers, the man- ager of a business established in the town, heti recently married a niece of the proprietor. He had returned to Enniscirthy on Monday from his wedding tour, and was cros3ing the town bricge, when a youeg man ran up, and fired two shots at him from a revolver. One bullet pierced him through the heart, and be fell dead. His assailant, Daniel Jordan, then shot himself dead. The motive for the crime is alleged to he jealousy. Petocees SERVER HUNIED BY Doas.—George Gharton, a process-server, proceeded recently to Bellyeughly, near Rostrevor, to serve some ejectment processes on the ten- ants of Mr. Batt's estate. He served a few, but the alarm baying been raisell, horns were blown and crowds gathered, and Wharton, seeing that he was likely to get beaten, re- treated. This is the second occasion on which Wharton has had to tly for his life while endeavouring to serve ejectment processes. In the same district about three weeks ago, while serving processes in the townland of Kncckbaragh, he was attacked and dogs hunted him. SHOOTING BY A MAGISTRATIL—A report which reached

Cork en Sunday night of a serious shooting affair near Bantry, in which a magistrate, Mr. John Onaen Payne, JP., is seriously implicated, turns out to be quit d true. M. Payne is in custody, and has been lodged in the county gaol ; and the wounded man, Ildichsel Lynch, mason, is ly- ing in a precarious state in the Bantry Efospital with a bul- let wound in the side. The allegation is that Mr. Payne invited Lynch to drink, and that after sundry potations some words passed,and that a revolver-shot was tired by Mr. Payne, the bullet entering Lynch's side. It is feared -the injuries may be fatal, and the deposilions of Lynch kayo been taken. _ _

PAINFUL PIIOCEEDII4GS AT A FUNBRAL.—The remains of Finlay, the murdered process-server, were interred on Sat- urday at Woodford, County Galway. 8,-sides a large force of police there was no one present except the widow, Mr. Lewis, J.P.. his brother, and Mr. Lewis's stewart, Mr. Dow- ney. Great difficulty was experienced in procuring inter- ' ment. The remains were not allowed into any of the Roman Catholic burial grounds, and it was found necessary to dig a grave in the old grave yard attached to Ballingar house. It was almost impossible to procure a spa4e for the purpose of aliggirey the grave. Those who openly rejoiced in the muttler of the unfortunate man conducted themselves dis- gracefully. The coffin had to he carried by a baalrway from the house, as the police feared 'a hostile demonstration at the funeral. ROMAN CATHOLIC BISHOPS ON THE POLITICAL SUVA- TlON.—Archbishop Croke, replying to an address presented to him at Lismore, said when next he visited the town he hoped that the Irish cause would have wonderfully pro- gressed, and that the great statesman who had already gran- ted them almost everything they had received in the way of advancement of Ireland would have not only perman- ently and satisfacterily settled the land question, put An end to evictions, and restored the soil of Ireland to the Irish people, but would also have carried through Parliament the approaching changes now at hand which would lead to the e:nancipition of Ireland and the restoration to her of her native Parliament —A pastoral from Archbishop Walsh was read in the Roman Catholic chapels of the Dublin Diocese on Sunday. The document concluded as follows: —" With singular unanimity the leaders of all parties in the State have come at length to recognise the pressing need of a substantial reconstruction of the system of governmeat under which we at present live. So much is certain, nut beyond this all is shrouded from our view in the uncertainty of the future. The minds of many amongst us are agitated ; all around us are heard the expressions of

the anxieties, the fears, the hopes of those who speculate as to what the next few .•weeks may bring forth. Amid all this uncertainty it is assuredly our special duty '.te turn to the throne of the Almighty and All.wis Ruler of the universe in earnest supplication that the light of the heav• enkr wisdom by which kings reign and law-givers decree just things may not be wanting to these sta.tesnten and public men by whom the momentous issues now raised will have tl be decided, and one whose prudence in council or action in the public Senate of the Empire the provision to be made for the future protection of so many and such vital interest in the spiritual no less than in the temporal order must so largely depend."

div.head: PADGA.TE WESLEYAN BAZAAR.
div.p: PADGA.TE WESLEYAN BAZAAR.

On Wednesday afternoon a bazaar was opentd in the Bold-street Wesleyan School-room, Warrington, by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., in aid of the building fund for the en- largement of the Padgate Wesleyan School and building new class-rooms in connection therewith. At the time of I the opening there was a good attendance, amongst those ' present, in addition to Mr. McMinnies, -were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P., Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., Mr. W. Bennett, Mr. T. Bennett, Mr. J. Warburton, Mr. E. Richardson, ard the Revs. J. McTurk, G. E. Cutting, J. H. Jones, and M. Rig- gall. The handsome and capacious schoolroom was elaborately and prettily decorated with mottoes, flags and banners, and in the centre was placed an elegant gipsy tent. The stalls were six in nnmber, three of these being laden Iwith an unusually valuable assortment of the fancy and I useful articles commonly seen at bazaars, pictures, photo- graphs, (ie. A " market " stall was well stocked with 1 flowers, plants, and a rich connection of the commodities Isuitable to the character of the stall, and a refreshment stall I also made a dainty and attractive display. The stalls were I under the charge of the following, ladies and their assis- -1 tants, viz. :—Mesdames T. Bennett, J. Bennett, Harris, Wright, W. Bennett, White, Grainger, Richardson, J. Smith, W. Smith, Houghton, Turner, and Misses Andrews, E. Ben- nett, E. Smith, N. Bennett, and E. Richardson. A hymn having been sung, and a prayer offered up by the Rev. G. Coating, the Rev. J. McTurk called upon Mr. IV. BENatErr, who made a statement as to the objects, Sze., of the bazaar. He said that their Wesleyan Chapel and School at Padgate were built in the year 1876, at a total cost of £2,000. At the time the school afforded ample ac- commodation, but now it was crowded every Sunday and the want of class-rooms made it almost impossible to teach with efficiency. It had consequently been decided to make an enlargement, and plans had been prepared, to carry out which about £4OO would be required, and in addition to this some £55 was required by the chapel stewards for heating lighting, painting, dm. The enlargement of the chapel was also rapidly becaming a:matter of urgency. To meet this °expenditure it had been unanimously resolved to hold that bazaar. Mr. Bennett likewise mentioned that the popula- tion of Padgate was increasing, and that the school children had already collected £9. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. C. BeloannansT said he was much pleased to respond to the invitation he received from Mr. Bennett and his friende at Padgate. He did not want to say anything in the shape of flattery, but he had always looked upon the Beanett family as some of the best specimens of English people they had about here. They seemed to him to rather representi that class of people which had become almost ex- tinct n tleis country—tie meant the old English yeoman I class, which not very long ago was the backbone of English society. (Hear, hear.) In consequence of the unfortunate disposition which people now have to congregate in large Cities the representatives of the country seemed not to have sufficient weight in the land, but he hoped that was a state of things which was in the way of being remedied. (dear, hear.) Referring to Wesleyan- lam, Mr. Broadbent said that he happened lately to be read- ing that part of Green's "History of the English People" which related to the early part of the 18th century. Eng- land at that time was in a state of religious decrepitude, there was an absence of religion to an extent that perhaps had never been known before in the history of the country. It was between tbe years 1730 and 1738 when there was corruption in • high places and ..brutality and barbarism amongst the lowest classes that WnitAeld came to the front, and he and Charles and John Wesley seemed to reuse all i England from the lethargy it was n and bring about a re- vival of Christianity and religious feeling. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to be a natural thing to refer to that on the occa- sion of a Wesleyan Methodiet bazaar, to show that those who did not belong to that body should be grateful to ac- knowledge the immense benefit that all England de- rived from the great founders of that religious society. (applause.) The Mayon said he thought they bacia good many bazaars in Warrington although he did not think they bad more than any other town in proportiqn to population, and nnless some ingenious individual would devise some better method of raising money for the same purposes the sooner they recognised the absolute necessity for having bazaars the better, lacause so long as there were schools or chapels to be built or enlarged, so long must money be obtained in come way. (Hear, hear.) There was nothing that would

affect them more materially than the education of their future men and worn-u, and they must not forget that in every sane person there was asa immense depth of intellec- tual wealth which could only be reached by education, perseyerence, and industry, and the object of that bazaar was to provide miens to di fur and obtain these treasures wkich lay buried in the human mind. (Hear, hear, and ' applause.) The Rey. M. RioaALL, who was described by Mr. Mc- Truk as the bishop of Padgat?, next gave a short address in which he stated that he could bear witAees to the fact that exteasion was neede 4at Padgate schraols. It was sometimes almost suffocating work and by no means plea- sant to address a Sunday scbool there on account of the I limits of the schoolroom, and it would be a joy to all who I work there to see a new schoolroom erected.

Mr. R.lGe.sertarr welcemecl Mr. IVleMinniee to that bee•ear and expre-eed the sympathy he felt for the good friends at Pedgete in their nonle work. A "fellow feeling made them wondrous kind," and be might mention that they had the same difficulty at Penketh in regard to their school. They wanted there a school twice the size of their present one, and he did not know how they were to get it. (Laughter.) The aßey. G. E. CurriNG announced that should they' raise £5OO by that bazaar, Mr. W. Bennett would acla another £lOO to it, so that the chapel might be enlarged. (Applause.) Mr. J. G. McMietems, who was received with applause, said that one good reason why he should speak last was that one half of his speech had been already made. He bad now no reason te tell them what the object of that bazaar was, what the circumstances of the Padgate friends were, what they wanted, and of the imperative necessity that their want should b 3 supplied. They had heard that ten years ago the chapel and school had been built at a cost-of £2,000, that at that time the accommodation was sufficient, but that now the congregetion and school had grown until the ac- comtnodation was quite inacicq,uate, and it was becoming essential that the school sad perhaps the chapel should be enlarged. He supposed it was not necessary now-a-days to ray anything in support of bazaars as a moans of raisin.- money for charitable and religious purposes. It used to be quite necessary to no so, and he believed he had given more apologrtic speeches about bazaars than any man in this town. (Laughter.) • But bazaars had won their way, and he thought that everybedy now ayes disposed to admit that they were the best means of raising large sums of money for charitable and religious objects. (Hear, hear.) In fact the only complaint he now heard about them was that there were too many and that they were too popular. Well, that i might be so, but anything that was too popular and came about too frequently did not need any defence. (Hear, hear.) As reearded the object of that bazaar there wet everything that deserved their strong support. They had heard what the Padeate friends had done, and considering that he should say they would agree with him that they had at any rate that claim upon the help of others which consisted in the fact that they helped themselves. (Hear, bear, and applause.) Having referred to the excellent dis- play on the stalls, Mr. McMinniee declared the bazaar open, and the sales were then proceeded with.
THE LATE MR- JOHN BROOKS, M.P.

It is with regret that we record the death of Mr. John Brooke, M.P. for the Altrincham Division of Cheshire, which occurred at a late hour on Monday night. Mr. Brooks, who was in London attend- ing to his Parliamentary duties, is belieied, a few days ago, to have caught a severe chill. Symptoms of inflemmetion of the lungs soon appeared, and as the hon. gentleman rapidly grew worse, Sir Andrew Clark was called in. Ott Monday his *condition was considered to be so serious that a consultation, in which three other physicians took part, was held. He was pronounced to be in a critical state, and his rela- tives in Altrincham und. Manchester were semmoned. They arrived, however, only in time to see the end, for as evening wore on he sank and died. Mr. Brooks was in the House of Commons on the Wednesday, and recorded his vote against the second reading of the Unclaimed Deposits Bill. The deceased gentleman was the only son of the Rev. John Brooks, rector of Walton-le-Dale, Lanca- shire, and was born on April 7, 1866. He had there- fore barely reached his 3oth year. He was sent to Harrow, and in the yeer 1374 entered at Merton Col- lege. Oxford, taking his B. A. degree three years later. When he had been in residence two years Mr. Brooks met with a serious accident while attempting to stop a runaway horse in one of the narrow streets of the University city. As a consequence he was compelled to relinquish his studies for several months, and also to °ease participation in the athletic pastimes of his college, in which he had taken a foremost part. On his recovery, in 1877, he succeeded in winning the Newdigate Prize of the year, and subsequently achieved high honours in the final examination of the University in the School of History and Political Economy. In the Bummer of 1880, having finished his University course, Mr. Brooks was called to the Bar of the Inner Temple, not with the idea of follow- ing that learned profession, but as a means of com- pleting an education which should fit him for the dis- charge of public duties. At the general election of 1380 Mr. Brooks made his first appearance on a political platfo-m, and did good service in advocating the claims of the Conser- vative candidates in the Cheshire divisions. He VMS a good speakt,r, and possessed a frank and genial man- ner which always secured for him a cordial reception. Subsequently he was invited by the Conservatives. of Stockport to become one of their candidates at the next general election, but was unable to comply with the request. Upon the occasion of the bye-election in Mid-Cheshire, which resulted in the return of the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, Mr. Brooks acted as hon. secretary of the Mid-Cheshire Conservative As- sociation, and contributed in no small degree to the Isuccess which his party then achieved. In July, 1883, Mr. P. Egerton-Warburton, one of the members for Mid-Cheshire, signified his intention of retiring from the representation of the Division, and Mr. Brooks was at onee selected as the candidate to take his place upon the dissolution of Parliament. The operation of the Redistribution of Seats Act some- what altered the plans of the political parties, and Mr. Brooks was adopted as the Conservative candi- date for the Altrincham division. In this contest he was opposed by Mr. I. S. Leadam, and the battle was fought with great spirit. At one time the Liberals were sanguine that they would return their candidate, notwithstanding the personal influence and popularity of Mr. Brooks. The result of the polling, however, was to place Mr. Brooks in possession of the seat by a majority of 750 votes, the numbers being— For Mr. Brooks, 4,798; for Mr. Leadam, 4,048 a At the time of his decease Mr. Brooks was promoting, in his Timperley estate, a system of land allotment to cottagers, and with such successful results that he had expressed his intention of extending it. The deceased gentleman was a justice of the peace for Cheshire and also for Berkshire, in which county he had a residence—Farley Hill Court, Swallowfield, Reading. Mr. Brooks took an interest in many of the benevolent and philanthropic institutions in the localities in which he resided. He was a nephew of Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, who for many years re- presented the eastern division of Cheshire in Parlia- ment. The deceased gentleman was unmarried. By his death a vacancy is caused in the representation of the Altrincham division of Cheshire. An Altrincham correspondent says :—The news of Mr. Brooke's death, which was telegraphed at half- past nine on Tuesday morning, created an intense sensation in the town and district immediately upon the deplorable fact becoming known. During Mon- day afternoon and evening telegrams were despatched. from London to Altrincham, but their contents were unknown except to a few friends of the deceased gentleman, so that when the telegram arrived ax- flouncing his death it was praetically the first inti- mation to the public that he had been ill. Tuesday being market day, the farmers from the country dis- tricts were in town, and general sympathy was ex- pressed with Mr. Brooks's aged mother, who took a deep interest in his election last autumn. The ordeal of a contested election under the extended franchise had a marked effect upon the physical condition of the candidate, but he denied himself the rest to which he was so well entitled. Since his return to Parlia- ment Mr. Brooks has several times been entertained by his constituents, and he has also taken part in several meetings of a social character.

Watfill LITERARY AD MITSICAL FESTIcA.L.—The above annual festival, in commemoration of St. David, the patron saint of Wales, was held on Saturday, in the Wes- leyan School, Earlestown (which had been kindly lent by the Chapel Committee), when a very fair attend- ance of Welsh people was secured. Mr. Williams, of Manchester, took the chair, in the absence of the Rev. J. V. Williams, of Liverpool. The Chairman referred to the unjust manner in which the Welsh nation had been libelled by what he called alien judges. The programme, which was of a very interesting nature, was then proceeded with. Pries.) competitions were entered into, Miss Williams espe- cially distinguishing herself. The musical adjudicator said that Miss Williams was a musical genius of no mean order. The meeting, which was a very interesting one, was brought to a close by the usual votes of thanks. TER DEATH OF THE REV. FIiTGII STOWELL BEOWN.— The recent death ef the famous Baptist preacher, the Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, formed the subject of a Special ser- mon preached in the Baptist Chapel, Market-street, Earles- town, on Sunday evening, by Mr. Alexander Pitt, of Liver- pool. The reading desk and communion were appropriately draped in black, and there was a large attentive congrega- tion. Selecting as his text the words, "A good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2nd Timethy, 2 chap., 3rd verse), Mr. Pitt spoke is feeling terms of the great loss the church had sus- tained by the death of Hugh Stowell Brown, and remarked that his death was felt keenly by him (Mr. Pitt) as a long personal friend of the late rev. gentleman. He alluded to the deceased gentleman's high character and labours, and commented on his kind nature and anxious disposition to do what be could for the improvement and benefit of the working. closees. TEE NEW ORGAN AT WARGEAVE CilußCE.—The series of special services in connection with the opening of the new organ at Wargrave Church were continued on Sunday, when the pulpit was oecubied by the Rev. H. S. Byrth, M.A., vicar of Bardesley. The visit of Mr. Byrth occasioned considerable interest among the older portion of the par- ishioners, from the fact that a considerable number of years ago ha officiated as curate of Wargrave Church. line ser- vices were consequently well attended, and Mr. Byrth's ad- dreeses were listened to with the greatest attention. Mr. Dawber, Mus. Doc., presided at the new organ. In the after- noon the Rev. H. S. Byrth, M.A., gave an address to the school children, parents, dec. The collections in aid of the organ fund amounted to about £l. The special services were continued on Thursday evening, when the preacher WAS the Rev. Canon Lefroy, vicar of St. Andrew's Liver- pool. There was a large congregation. GOOD, TENPLlnr.—Brother George E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided at the weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, on Monday evening, when there evil a good attendance. After the usual formal business a communication was read from the Wigan Total Abstinence Society, inviting the lodge to give them an en- tertainment in the Public Hall, Wigan, and the lodge sec- retary was directed to communicate with the society on the subject. Arrangements were completed for a friendly visit to the Leigh Alpha Lodge oh the nth inst. trother John James Wilson, of the Pilot Lodge, Leith, Edinburgh, visited the lodge and explained that he had unfortunately been out of employment since last November. He was recommended to come to England in search of work, bat he had found things in England were quite as bad if not worse than in the neighbourhood from where he started. He give an in- teresting account of his visits to various lodges, and the good temperance work that was being done. The members of the lodge afterwards decided to give him a donation from the lodge funds. An entertainment followed, as stated in another paragraph. THE ANTI-VACCINATION SOCIETY : CANVASS OF HOUSE- EoLDEES —With the view of testing the opinions of all householders in the Newton township upon the question of vaccination, the Earlesrown branch of the National Anti- compulscry Vaccinaticn have decided to take a vote upon the question. A meeting to consider the matter and com- plete the arrangements was held at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, on Wednesday evening, when a large number of members were present, inclading Messrs. John Clark (president), who occupied tire chair; B. Harri- son, J. Edmunds, W. Gilmour. and others. The question Was discussed at some length, and the proposal appeared to meet with general satisfaction. It is proposed that a voting paper will be left at each house in Earlestown, Wargrave, Vulcan, Newton, dtc., and there will be printed thereon the questions—" Are you in favour of vaccination ?" and" Are you in favour of the compul- sory clauses of the Vaccination Acts?" The delivery and collection of the voting papers will be accomplished during the ensuing week. It is estimated that there are over 2000 householders in the district who will be asked to express their opinion upon the subject. CONSERVATIVE ORGLNIsATION =NEWTON Dlv/SION. A well attended meeting of Conservatives was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday evening, for the purpose of electing a district committee and officers in con- nection with the recently formed Conservative Association for the Newton division.. Mr_ M. firown-Varesthead, chair- man of the local Conservative Club, presided, and he was supported by Captain Seton (Lawton), Messrs. W. F. Gooch, J.P., T. Stone, C. F. Borron, and W. B. Viroodnorth, registration agent. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, remarked that although the Conservative cause triumphed at the last general election it was absolutely necessary, In order to make the seat in Newton division safe in the future, to im- prove the organisation, ' • of the party throughout the divi- sion. At a later period of the evening he also said they could not tell when the Prime Minister would cause a dis- solution and rush an election upon the country, but it be- hoved them to be prepared for an election whenever it might come. The meeting afterwards elected a district committee, and Captain Seton was unanimously appointed chairman, and Mr. J. Mnscrop, secretary of the Newton Division Con- servative Association.—A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, who said he thanked the electors 'tor the way they had done their duty on the last occasion, anh he was sure tlAy would de all they could in the future whoever might come forward to claim their suffrages. At the close of the meeting Captain Seton announced that another meet- ing would shortly be held to complete the arrangements.

div.head: NEW. BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW. BOOKS, &c.

"The Voyage of the Aurora " (llessrs. Sampson, Low, and Co.), is a capital sea story by Mr. H. Col. lingwood, author of "Under the Meteor Flag," 96c. It tells the fortunes of the hero, George Leicester, in a style of which Defoe would not have been ashamed. Mr. Oollingwood is thoroughly at home with every- thing that sails the seas, and he ia so realistic in his details that the reader is irresistibly carried The adventures are of the most thrilling kind, and yet there is nothing romanticiu the sense of their being improbah!e. The boys will find plenty to their taste, the girls will be interested in the love story, and the parents will read the book foz its charm of style, good sense, and real interest.

"The King of the Tigers " is the title of another novel from the press of Messrs. Sampson, Low, and Co. It is fi em the pen of Mr. Louis Rousselet, and bears the the stamp of freshneBa and originality. it relates the adventures of Lord Everest, a young Ence'- lishman who is tired of life, until he falls in witha couple of French travellers, who have been all the world over procuring feathers and hides for a French firm. He resolves to join them for the sake of the sport to be had in hunting wild animals, and goes with them to Central India. the scene of the chief events of the story. "The King of the ligers "is a man-eating brute, that gives a deal of trouble, but ultimately finds Lord Everest a wife. A vivid pic- ture is presented of life in India, and in this sense the novel may be read as a fascinating book of travel. The characters of the more important personages in the story are drawn to the life, and do not fail there. 'fore to prove interesting. Both "The King of the Tigers" and "The Voyage of the Aurora" are ad- mirably illuetrated and handsomely bound. They form excellent six-shilling gift- books. " Free Public Libraries, their organisation, uses, and management," is the title of an excellent work published by Messrs. bimpkin, Marshall, and Co., London, and is from the pen of Mr. Thomas Green- wood, F.R.G.S. The volume is capitally illustrated with engravings of the more important Free Libra- ' ries in the country, and of portraits of gentlemen who have been genereus contributors. There is, for in- ' stance, a fine portrait of Mr. Brunner, M.P., with an account of Northwich Free Library and what he has done for it. The information is brought down to the latest date, and there is, therefore a record of the movement which is now being made in Widnes to form a Library. Mr. Greenwood having at one time been a librarian writes with a epccial knowledge, and his hints are exceedingly valuable alike to author- ities that have a Library at work and to those who are wishful to bring the Libraries Act into operation. The statistics which are given seem to have been most carefully compiled ; and the Acts relating to Libra- ries are printed in -full. We trust Mr. Greenwood will find a ready sale for his book. Apart from its usefulness as a work of reference, it is very readable and will serve to encourage those who are engaged in the good work of diffusing useful knowledge. Messrs. Morgan and Scott, London, are feeling the pressure of ths demand for the works of the late Mr. J. B. Gough. When lest in England the great tem- perance orator revised, corrected, and issued a new and copyright edition of his autobiography, which is a thrilling and absorbing narrative. He also pub- lished in a volume the orations which he was at that time delivering in Great Britain, and to which thou- sands then listened with delight. Both these books are, we are glad to say, izsued at the low price of one shilling each. Messrs. Caesma:and Co. have just published the first part of a new issue (price Gd.) of "Familiar Wild Flowers." The coloured plates are marvels of skill, being fac-similes from original paintings made for the work by Mr. F. E. Hulrae, F.L.S.' F.S.A. The shouldletterpress gives all that everybody should know of wild flowers; and, as the paper is exceedingly good, the parts, when completed, will make a delightful volume.

" Cassell's National Library" goes briskly forward —there being, as might be expected, a large demand for the weekly complete works at threepence each. Amongst the more recent issues are "The Man of "Lives of Alexander the Great and Caasar," and "The Castle of Otranto."

"The Miniature Library of the Poets" has passed through Longfellow and Wordsworth, and is procee- ding with Scott in two volumes. Rood is to follow in one volume—and a dainty pocket companion it will make.

Part 2 of the new issue of " Cassell's. Illustrated Shakespeare " completes "The Tempest," and com- mences The two gentlemen of Verona." The illus- trations are for the most part very striking, and those who are familiar with the text will have a special plea- sure in following the notes by "Charles and Mary Cowden Clarke."

"The Magazine of Art" for March has for a frontispiece the picture of Susi—" sweet sixteen" from a painting by Deiregger. It is in the highest style of workmanship, and will be seized upon by those who are looking out for something to frame. There is a very interestimr sketch of Dr.ifregger, with a por- trait of this noted Tyrolese artist. Amongst the more noteworthy articles illustrated are " Slyfield " (surrey), "A Chapter on Fireplaces," "The Tiber," and "'rho Annunciation in Art."

"Cassell's Magaline" is, as usual, full of good things in the shape of story and verse, and chatty, and yet highly instructive papers. The prize story in the current iJsue "In Rhoda Chester's Honeymoon" will be found equal to high expectations.—."fhe Quiver" forataroh is above the average, especially in the way of illustration. Along with the article on "Famous Pictures" there is a fine representation of Correggio's "Boca Homo." There is too a good portrait of Gen. Grant.—Ever-welcome "Little Folks" has a pretty coloured frontispiece in "Elsie and Punchinello, "The Old Jester's Story" is also capitally illustrated. and there are not a few comical sketches. The won- der is how the publishers can give so much for so little money. The parts of "Cassell's Popular Gardening" and the fine art edition of Longfellow are nearing com- pletion; and it is therefore a fictingt time for those who have not had the sections to order the full work. The Encycl.f.,l. cedio, Dictionary (part 26) is occupied with articles under the letter D; the work is indeed an encyclopcedia as well as a dictionary, and it is therefore invaluable to the student. We have also to hand part 22 of " The Look of Health," and part 7 of " Gleaninf,-_7s from Popular Authors" which will, when completed, make the most readable book of the day, 1

The current number of the "English Illustrated Magazine "is... a strong one. There are some power- ful illustraions of an article on Lifeboats and life- boat men." But tb.o feature of the month is a paper

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION.

" IRISH TAXATION." "The Taxation of Ireland" formed the subject of a paper read by Mr. Thomas Walsh, at the weekly meeting of the Discussion Class in connection with the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, on Wednesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. A. B. Neill, of Bold, and there were also present Messrs. M. Birkhead, L. T. Foulkes, Joseph Davies, W. McEvoy, Thoa. Morris (secre- tary), and others.

The Chairman, in introducing the subject, said it waaorre which had occupied a considerable place in politics, and it would be better if the people of this country were to look Irish grievances and their causes in the face, and try to remedy them. When it needed such a large military and. , police force to keep the people in order there roust be some- thing wrong. He did not think the fault rested altogether with the people of Ireland, but more with its Government. England had to govern Ireland with its polcemen and sol- diers, and they could only expect the people to be grum- bling. If the Irish people had a cmse for grumbling the Government should try and remedy it. (Applause.) Mr. Walsh then proceeded with his paper. He said his object was to bring under their notice a grievance that was not sentimental, but of a substantial and practical nature, the financial grievance of Ireland, and to show how Ireland was taxed beyond her relative ability, not in equality with Eegland, and contrary to the articles of union between the two countries. That very substantial injustice remained in force to-day, and was one of the greatest causes of the poverty and desolation of that country, which was not a credit to those who had held the ruling power. He pro- ceed-d to quote several of the articles of agreement signed for the union of England and Ireland, and urged that they had been violated in almost every instance. He quoted figures to show that Ireland had been taxed beyond her ability, and that the debt of Ireland had greatly increased after the union; and remarked that a large ex- penditure for the Irish constabulary ought to rep- pear under the head of "Army Estimates." Of course they must admit the necessity of the police to a cer- tain extent, but it was ridiculous that such large sums , should be brought to bear upon tee Ith'e taxpayer to main- tain an army of occupation. It was the opinion of eminent men that half the present sum should suffice to protect the interests of the country if the management was in the heeds of these who would look to the welfare of the country, and not in the hands of these who were, and always had been, endeavouring to sink her into poverty aed degradation. There were many items in the present expenditure which would be speedily remedied if the Irish were permitted to keep their own books.. In the House of Commons in 1876 Mr. Mitchell Henry stated that in 23 years the Irish taxa- tion had more than doubled, having risen from 4 to 8•• millions, and within the sante period the taxation per head had increased from 9a Cid to £ll2a Gd, while the population

bad decreased by 24 millions; and out of the 81 millions of taxation which the Irish were forced to pay annually about 61 millions were raised by customs and excie.e duties. It therefore came chiefly from the poorer classes. He did not for a moment say that England was not overtaxed, but in comparison to her wealth it was a mere flea bite as compared with Ireland. In concluding an able paper, Mr. Walsh urged that it was time Irishmen strengly protested against the continuance of fiscal injustice, and said if the grievances were not redressed perhaps another Budget would not be allowed to pass without much stronger opposition than for- merly. (Applause.) Mr. Booth thought the !subject was rather a complicated one, and without books of reference it would be difficult for them to understand the figures and statistics given by the lecturer.—Mr. Foulkes commented on previous debates in Parliament upon the question of Irish taxation, mentioning Mr. Mitchell Henry and Mr. Gladstone as having clearly pointed out its injustice. Ireland was undoubtedly taxed too heavily, but:they were all too heavily taxed. He agreed with Mr. Walsh that Ireland paid a larger proportion of taxation than she ought justly to do, and urged that the land did not pay its due preportion of the taxes of the country. He held that all land was national, and that its present owners could only be considered as trustees, and it . should therefore bear the heaviest part of :taxation. He remarked that land at one time paid 25 per cent of the whole taxation, and in some instances more than that, bat land did not now p iy its. proportion, even to the extent of 2 per cent. Where did the difference go? The money that ought to be paid in taxes to maintain the empire now went into the overfilled pockets of the landowners. Am Ireland vitae purely an agri- cultural country, tiee people must really feel the burden of taxation when it was not properly apportioned on the land. He pointed out that Enedand had borne the expense of the national defences of Ireland, and said he weuld go the whole length of the hug with Mr. Walsh in regard to the Irish constabulary being nothing lees than an 'army of occupa- tion and a standing disgrace to the genius of Englishmen who had been unable to govern Ireland without two armies. It did not speak well for the governing powers either from a coercive or a pacific point of view. (Applauee.)— Mr. Connor said if the Irish had paid the taxes to the ex- tent mentioned by Mr. Walsh he considered they were fools. —Mr. Walsh: But compulsion is no choice.—Mr. Connor asked some Voglishrnan to get up and say something about the matten—Mr. Thomas Morris alluded to evictions., and said soldiers who bad been employed in that directien in Ireland bad told him it was very unpleasant, and it mu.i.t have been very unpleesant for the people to have to pay for them. He agreed with Mr. Ffoulkes as to the Irish con- stabulary, and be considered it a disgrace that England had not been able to govern Ireland better. He thought there had been too much coercion used, and the continual presence of the army must have made the people stubborn. He thought tbey were now entering upon a new era, and were beginning to understand thet the Irish had a ereat deal of grievances. Theylound the Liberal party were banded together and meant to contend with the difficulties and t-y to give Ireland some degree of satisfaction. That WAS their duty, and it was their duty to support the Libezal party all they could in their efforts to give Ireland the satisfaction to which they were entitled. (Aoplause.)—Mr. W. McEvoy, c. also spoke, after which Mr. Walsh replied.

div.head: LIBERAL BALL 4T NEWTON.
div.p: LIBERAL BALL 4T NEWTON.

The fist annual ball under the auspices of the Zarlestoten and District Liberal Club was held in the Assemby Room of tbe Town ;Hall, l(ewton, on Monday evening, and it is a pleasure to record that it was of a very successful and en- couraging character.. The gathering was attemded not only by a large number of prominent Liberals, but it was sup- ported by a few gentlemen holding Conservative opinions. Th 6 whole of the arrangements had been carried out by Messrs.. James Ratter, Joseph Davies, W. 1). Byrne, L. Morris, and other members of the committee, along with the energetic secretary (Mr. Thomas Morris). and to them praise is due for the•conifort of the visitor. The hall had been beautifully draped with curtains and red cloth by 11.1 r. E. T. Evans, of Market-street, Earlestown, while a number of plants, kindly lent for the occasion by Colonel George Mc Corquociale, ,31. P from elle conservatories at the Willows, were tastefnliv arranged around the room and coneiderablv finhanc9d its charming appearance. The band engaged was cornprieed of members of Mr. L‘e Jong's celebrated orchestra, under the conductorship of Mr. 8., H. Pear- son, and their performancei gave the greatest possible satis- faction. Dancing commenced about nine o'clock and an excellent programme of music was concluded about half- past three on the following morning, the large company preseat, numbering Over 150 ladies and gentlemen, thoroughly enjoying themselves. The onerous duties of maAers of ceremonies were efficiently carried out by Messrs. James Rutter and George Green. Refreshments of an ex- cellent quality were supplied by Mr. and Mrs. Henry Bib-' bert, of the Blue Bell Inn, Newton. There were separate cloak-rooms for ladies and gentlemen, the former being nn- der the charge of Mrs. Pennington, while Mr. John Linaker • (caretaker of the Earlestown Liberal Club) looked after the gentlemen's department. During the course of the evening Mr. G. W. Rewliws„of Rainhill, ascended the platform and announced that Colonel McCorquodale was very sorry be , was unable to attend Owing to illness. He would very much ; liked to have been present, and he hoped they would have a very pleasant and enjoyable cneeting. Mr. Rawlins also °stated that a telegram had been been received from Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, S.P.„ stating that he was sorry he was unable to attend, as he had been unavoidably detained on business at London. Among the ladies and gentlemen pre- sent at the ball, in addition to those- mentioned, were Mr. and Mrs. E. T. Evans, Mr. and Mrs, W. D. Hurdle, Mr. and Mrs. P. Hall, Mr. and Mrs. S. div.head: IN THE LION'S DEN.
div.p: IN THE LION'S DEN.

"To owners of dogs.—Wanted, a large bitch, as a foster mother to rear lion cube, about the 24th instant.—Apply, Blackpool Aquarium and Menagerie." I read the advertisement, and experienced a certain degree of interest in this idea of getting a "foster mother" for the lion cubs, and in course of time my curiosity was so arousod that I resolved to go and see the process carried out. On Wednesday afternoon I visited the Aquarium and Menagerie, and was not bog in findiag the industrious mananger, Mr. Walmsley. lat once broke the ice by observing, "You have got some lion cubs here which are being reared by a foster mother, I believe."
"No, we haven't," replied Mr. Walmaley, "the bitch came too late, so we had to resort to, otber means."
"Then the lioness has undertaken the task herself, has she?"
"Oh no, not at all. You see her milk fails her, and un- less we took some artificial means of nourishing them we should lose all the cubs."

"Indeed," I replied. "But you will have considerable difficulty in rearing them, won't you, unless you can obtain some description of animal to feed them ?" "Not a bit of it, as I will immediately show you. Corns along this way," and Mr. Walrusley at once conducted me to his own cosy kitchen.

Here a su-rpri-s-e—wvas in store for me. Picking up a basket which, stood near the fire, he carefully removed At wraps, and there was a lion cub, as snug as anything you ever saw in your life. It was four days old, and about the size of a stoutly-built cat. 'There are two others in the cage with the lioness," pro- ceeded Mr. Walmsley, " bat they are being removed up to the kitchen to-morrow, and then we shall have all the three thoroughly in hand. But you shall see those directly. Now, oome this way, and I will show you a substantial specimen of domestic rearing," and together we proceeded to a room where the sounds were very much like those create() by a lion. At length we arrived in front of the den, and there, through the iron bars, you could see a nice young fem Ale lion about the size of a well-fed retriever. This young lady seemed very vivacious and playful, but I felt very well satisfied to remain at the "weather side" of the bare.

"She wouldn't harm a mouse," observed Mr. Walmsley. "1 suppose not," I replied. "But still, at the same time, as discretion is the better part of valour, I do not propose to disturb her in her solitude. Lions, you know, Mr. Walmsley, are nice in books, and look majestil as vie .ved through iron bars, but I fancy it looks like bad taste to go intruding upon their privacy." "Nonsense," laughed my friend. "Why, I dare sleep la the earns room as that animal, without the slightest protec- tion. I tell you she is as harmless and as pla.ylul :Ls a kitten, and would not hurt anyone. Now, come along in with me, and I will jevot show you." . Notwithstanding Mr. Walmsley'S amusement I hesitated. I felt very plainly that I was not " born to be a Daeiel," and felt also that I didn't want to be if it was all the same. This female, in common with others of her sex, was not die- mayed in the slightest at the presence of the sterner sort. No, ehe seemed te be dying with a desire to embrace uz, and although I might have been slightly bolder under other cir- cumstances, I now concluded that my mission in life was to avoid the acquaintance of lions. But still Mr. Waimsley insisted, still the amiable female scratched at the iron bare, and neither seemed disposed to wait until I had settled my affairs and got an extra insurance on my life. Feeling strongly that I was about to perform a daring deed, whiele had not included in my preliminary programme, I stepped across the threshold of that terrible residence, and before I cauld say "Jack Rebinsou," the amiable female already alluded to had me in her loving embrace, and hugged me, oh so fondly! Now what do you think of that for a situa- tion? Striking, wasn't it? Daniel was a lucky man where I came. That lion's friendship sort of took my breath, do you know, and I began to think—well, all sorts .of things, and I took very little time over it, toe. The lien's paws still clasped my tottering frame, her soft, flaxen head was nestling in my bosom quite poetically, and Mr. Walmsley was almost bursting his sides with laughter. I breathed more freely when he trotted over to my companion, with whom she was likewise moat affectionate. In course of time I overcame my nervousness, and then I enjoyed the fun, but I enjoyed it more to step out of the cage. However, the animal, as Mr. Walmsley stated, is quite harmless, and seemed greatly troubled when we departed. As we descendea the staircase my friend informed me that she frequently visited the kitchen, and seemed delighted when. allowed to romp with the children, who in return arc exceedingly fond of their faithful pet. "But how do you manage to rear these animals ? " I asked.
"Oh," repli.d Mr. Walmsley, "ii you will come thie way I will show you," and he led me up to the mena- gerie, where he pointed out to rne the fine Abysciaial; mother.
"You see that.cage which adjoins her's, which la bouded

up in front. Well the two other cribs about which I bale spoken are in there, and if you will get in along with nut you shall see them fed." I didn't so well like the idea of again intruding, for ther! was only a wooden partition between the youngsters an; their parent. However, I got througii the cage door, an" stepped into the presen e of the little strangers without sn3' comments, although I felt them all the same. There in the corner, on a soft bd of straw, the two little cubs nestlea together.

"Now this is how we rear them," observed Mr. WaltaBle7l producing a child's feeding bottle, containing warm cow's milk, and placing the teat in the mouth of the youngsters' they tugged away with nauch energy, and seemed exce&d. ingly fond of the artificial food. Mr. Walmsley then ea' plained to me that they had grown to the fall ditnensions• Mrs. Wahnsley has charge of them during their infancit and lvz.s never vet failed in her object. In one ity, stance this good lady, who must be in the enjoyment „?.. ' i an unusually strong nerve was particularly successful. ' a little Christaaas-day, 1882, sire received into her care .t..be weakly lion cub which she at once began to feed with bottle. By-and-bye he began to grow very fast, and raPiti developed into a fine animal. For twelve months. Wel% he remained the pet of the kitchen, and by the time of hi first anniversary he was larger ,than any St. Bernard. Droll 1 the day-time he was "on view," but at night he was allow to go hack to the kitchen, a favour which he greatly es" teemed. Every evening Mrs. Walmsley used to go and orn. I "Billy's" cage door, and he trotted along "tome bY nue; I side, and if she heppened to stand speaking to anyone way he would quietly lie at her feet and wait until she ts; I a move. As he grow larger he principally confined _Arl a friendship to Mrs. Walmsloy (although he always enjoYe" a romp with the children) until at length, when he was justif year old, he was deprived of his liberty and nernasuenttia I confined. On one occasion, while Billy was allowed to fi'n I the kitchen, a somrwhat amusing , incident haPPeneto ' Thinking there was no one in the menageria, and wishing. go out, Mrs. Wslmsley liberated the lion somewhat earl.lbee than usual, and together they were jogging about W house, when they were met by two ladies. NaturallY ladies were greatly alarmed, and flying for their livee',,e2o I claimed, "there's a lion got out.' Billy of coarse ha' , eye to business, and with his kind mistress lost no tinle reaching his favourite haunt.—Blackpod Herald.

div.head: WESTON POINT MYSTERY.
div.p: THE WESTON POINT MYSTERY.

The inquest upon the body of an unknown sailor -which was found in the Mersey, near Weston Point, on Friday morning, took plaee on Monday. There were wounds upon the head of the man, leading to the suspicion that he had been the victim of foul play. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, con- ducted the inquiry.—Thomas Bostock, labourer, Weston Point, deposed to finding the body, which be described. The deceased was attired in a knitted jacket and a pair of plaid trousers, elastic side boots, gray stockings, and a flannel shirt. In his pocket he had a half an ounce of tobacco and an old clay pipe. lie had also a plaid woollen scarf round his neck.

Dr. 3.lcDeugall said that on Saturday he made a post-taortem examination of the deceased. The body was well nourished, and there were no internal , marks of violence on the body except on the fore- head there were two lacerated wounds, and a star- shaped wound on the crown of the head. These wounds were produced after death. The ordinary ! signs of drowning at the extremities were well marked. He opened the body, and found the usual signs of drowning in the lungs, liver, kidneys, and in the venous system of the brain. He was of opinion that drowning was the cause of death. The body was that of a fully matured person between 30 and 35 years of age. He measured 41t. Sin.; was light complexion and comely features; light short moustache, and beard of about a week's growth. His hair was of a dark brown colour. He had been in the water a few days.—By the foreman: He could not recognise that the deceased had partaken of in- toxicating liquor. The Deputy Coroner said the evidence of Dr. McDougall was most clear, conclusive, and satisfac- tory. Unfortunately the efforts made by the police to identify the body had not been successful. A verdict of found drowned was recorded.

. TEE STEPNEY ELECTION Pumroxr.—The hearing of the Stepney election pttitiott was resumed on Saturday, before Justices Denman and Field. Evidence was given to show that persons acting on behalf of Mr. Isaacson, the unsuc- cessful Conservative candidate and petitioner, distributed cards and handbills hearing a representation of a ballot paper, with the word " Isaacson " printed in large letters, and with a cross opposite to it. Counsel for the Public Prosecutor urged that this was a device calculated to mis- lead voters, and, therefore, an infringement of the Corrupt Practices Act. Fur the petitioner it was contended that if this were ruled to be illegal almost every election in the kingdom could be voided. The card was intended to show voters who were satisfied with Mr. Isaacson how they were to support him, and Mr. Charles, Q C., suggested that it would not deceive even child. Their Lordships informed counsel that the document was capable of bearing the inter- pretation to an ignorant voter that if he did not exactly ob- serve the directions it contained his vote would be lost. Mr. Justice Denman further remarked that the issue of the card was a "dirty, nasty, shabby trick," and that every candi- date who sanctioned its use ought to be disfranchised. Before the court adjourned it was intimated that any deci- sion their Lordships might come to on this point would be carefully considered by the Public Prosecutor with a view to future action. • 4. div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

Masters of freehand drawing.—Pickpockets. Jones: Can you always tell a fool ?—Brown: If he doesn't ask too much; what would you like to know? It has been found that the termination "atic "in the weeds " lunatic " and " fanatic " refers to the upper storey. OF SINGLE BLEssameuss.—lt is better to be laughed at for not being married than to be unable to laugh because you are. What is that which every one wishes to have, and which every one strives to get rid of directly he obtains it ?—A good appetite. "Doing anything now, Bill?' "Oh, yes, I'm busy all the time :" "Ah ! Glad to hear it! What are you doing ?'' "Looking for a job." Artemus Ward, when asked by telegraph on behalf of a Lyceum committee, "What will you take for ten nights ?" replied, "Brandy and water." A juror asked to be excused on the ground of' deafness. The judge asked the jaryman if he had heard the charge. "Yes, your Honour, but I'll be hanged if I could make head or tail of it !" He was excused. A clergyman who married four couples in one hour the other evening remarked to a friend that it was "pretty fast work." "Not very," responded his friend; "only' font' knots an hour." "What amused me most at the Opera," said an Arab chief who had been taken to hear " Faust, "was a musician in the orchestra seated a little higher than the rest, who per- I formed on an invisible instrument with a stick." This is an echo from the outer lobby of the House of Commons—" Look here, Brown—your friend the new mem- ber for Slumpshire is not at all amusing when he speaks !" "I quite agree with you; but it is only fair to say that he is just the same when he says nothing at all." Miss Philadelphia: And se you enjoyed your tour to Europe ?—Miss Boston: Oh, indescribably !—Miss P.: Did you see the aqueducts in Rome ?—Miss B.: Yes; and they swam beautifully.—Miss P.: Swam? What swam ?—Miss B.: The aquaducks, of course! A wife wanted her husband to sympathise with her in a feminine quarrel; but he refused, saying, "I've lived long enough to learn that one woman is just as good as another— if not better !" "And I," retorted his now exasperated wife, "have lived long enough to learn that one man is just as bad as another—if not worse!" How PAT LOOKED AFTER THE RIM—A. Galway bailiff, having been questioned as to whether he had spoken to the jury durirg the night, answered gravely, "No, my lord. They kept calling out for me to bring them whisky; bat I always said, Gentlemen of the jury, it is my duty to tell you that I'm sworn not to spake to you.'" Young wife: No matter how late George comes in, he always tells me where he has spent the evening —Young wife's mother, sarcastically: Indeed! Where was he last night ?—Young wife: At his office, poor fellow, balancing the books. MISIINDERSTOOD.—" Shall I sing that beautiful song, 'Mother is waiting,' for you ?" asked a Bush-street girl of a gentleman making a morning call, and who was a little deaf. " I beg pardon. What was that?" "Mother is waiting." "Excuse me. I'll go then. I saw her hanging out the clothes as I came. Sorry to detain yen from your washing." SATISFIED WITH THE ASSERTION.—Wife: The lareee is empty.—Husband: So is my pocket-book—Wife: The coal is gone —Husband: So is my credit.—Wife: We have no flour in the house.— Husband: And I have no money.— Wife (emphatically): Well, we can't starve.—Husband I relieve): Thank goodness, I was afraid we should have to. ; A gentleman who was visiting one of the public schools ; in a Texas town asked a bright-looking boy, "What prost , is there in the study of ancient history ?" "About fifty I cents, I reckon," was the reply. "What!" "Well, the i teacher makes us buy the books of him, and we have to pay a dollar. I think he gets them for fifty cents apiece; so he has a clear profit of fifty cents, according to my calculation. Some difficulty was esxperienced at the Regina trials in Canecla in making the Indian prisoners understand the legal , terms in which their offences were set forth. For instance, ' no term could be found to convey to the untutored mind the idea of the Queen's Crown, which the prisoners were charged with conspiring against. This was explained to One Arrow as being "the Great Mother's -big bonnet with feathers in it." A. DESIRABLE SON-IN-LAW.—" Rebecca, you shall nod spheak mit dot Moses Levi vonce more." "Oh, fadder, you preak mine heardt ! Ve vas almost engaged. Ves shall I not soheak of him ?" "He haf sheated. He hat shold me a paste diamond for a shenuine Atone." "Oh, fadder, dot shouldt recornmendt him to you as a son-in-law! If he can fool a wise man like you, see vat a fortune he haf in. der chewelry piziness !" "Veil, Rebecca, you vas schmarder as I tought. Get married ven you like. lam ankehious to go in bartnership wit mine son-in-law !" Woesuer awn LADIES.—A couple of young ladies in a railway carriage on a suburban line, while waiting at a junction, were conversing in French after a fashion. Pre- miming that none of their fellow-passengers understood that language, they made some very pointed remarks about a gentleman sitting directly opposite to these. They re- ceived a well-merited lesson in propriety when, in very loud but classical French, the gentleman referred to re- marked to his neighbour, "All grown-up ladies are women, but all women are not ladies." The solemnity of the silence that followed was painful. Too RISICY.—" Hello, Jones, I thought von were going , hunting this week ? " " Well, so I intended, Smith. But I I have abandoned the idea. 'There was too much risk." " Pshaw ! Man! what risk was there ? " "I suppose you know that I have been recently married?" "Yes." "And I you also know that young Blithers was a suitor for the hand of my wife before we were married ? " "So I have I heard." "Well, there is only one life that prevents my I wife from becoming Mrs. Blithers. I tell you this is a critical time, Smith, and a man can't be too careful." Tomete's SACRIFICE.—The minister had preached a ser- mon on "Sacrifice," in which he urged the benefit of giving lup some cherished pleasure for the cause of religion. Little Tommy had listened thoughtfully, and his mother thought she would find out how deep an impression the sermon had made. "Don't you think, Tommy," said she, "that you would feel better if you were to give up some cherished de- light, some pleasure that you value, in so good a cause?' "Yes," said Tommy, "I think perhaps I might." "Well," said the mother, greatly gratified at his religious interest, "well, Tommy, and what pleasure do you think you had better give up ?" "I don't know," said Tommy, thought- fully. "Supposing I should give up going to church ?" A quiet-looking gentleman walked down a railway plat- form in search of a place in a train which was almost full. He stopped before a carriage in which there was a vacant seat—no, not quite vacant; on it stood a small black hand- bag. A stout person sat next beside it in the corner. "Room here?" demanded the quiet gentleman. "No," growled the stout one. "No one is sitting there "—pointieg to the hand I bag. "Got out—coming back—his hand-bag," growled the Istout passenger. The new comer had his own views as to , how far this vague statement was trustworthy, for he said in his quiet tones, "I will sit there until your friend re- turns." The train began to move. "Your friend is late," said the quiet one. The train was fairly in motion. "Your friend has lost the train," exclaimed the quiet one in a tone of BYroPathY ; "but," he added, "he sha'n't lose his pro- perty," and he hurled the black bag out of the window on to ; the platform. The stout traveller made are ineffectual effort , to save the bag. and then burst out into language not that . of blessing. The bag was of coarse his own.

A MAN FROZEN TO DEATH NEAR RUNCORN. Mr. T. ,T. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest on Saturday at Dutton Workhouse, near Runcorn, respecting the death of a wan unknown, who was found in an exhausted condi- tion on the realside at Preston Brook between ten and eleven o'clock on the night of the 3rd instant, by Mr. Al- bert Webb, a clerk, residing at Preston Brook. Police-con- stable Wynn procured a cart, and removed the unfortunate man to Dutton Workhouse. In his evidence Mr. Webb said that on the date in question he was going doing the New- road at Preston Brook, when he heard a groan, and procur- ing a lamp, found deceased sitting on a ledge of a rock, with his bands in his pockets. He appeared insensible.—P.C. Wynne, stationed at Preston Brook, who was told by Webb of the discovery, said that he removed deceased in a cart to the workhouse at Dutton. Deceased was insensible'and his larms were quite stiff; a purse, a key, and two halfpennies I were in his possession. There was also a ride in his pocket., I and his clothes smelt of varnish, which led witness to be- lieve that he was a mechanic. There were no marks of violence on the body. Deceased appeared to be from 60 to 65 years of age, and was about 51t. Bin, in height. The letters " T.E." were tattooed on his left arm. He wore a black coat and vest, corduroy trousers, blucher boots, grey worsted stockings, new black and white plaid shirt, and a new red flannel singlet. He had iron grey whiskers, mous- tache, and beard, and had lost some teeth on the bottom jaw.—A nurse engaged at the workhouse said that deceased died there on the day of his admission, without giving any coherent statement.—Dr. Robinson, Frodsharn, said that in his opinion deceased, who did not appear to have been starved died from cold and exposure, and the jury returned a verdict to that effect.

A STEAMER'S CREW BLOWN TO PIECES. -- On Monday morning the steamtug Rifleman was lying at the West Bute Dock pierhead, Cardiff, with steam up ready to tow a ves- sel to sea when a loud explosion was beard, and those on shore were startled to see fragments of the steamtug boiler and deck flying around in all directions, and among them the bodies of several of the crew. The tug was shattered to pieces, and sank immediately. There were seven persons on board at the time, and of these five were killed outright. The others were blown into the water, but were rescued by boats, one bsing shockingly injured. The shell of the boiler, weighing 5:".i tons, was blown up to a great height, and falling on the stein (if the Italian haiquentine Clotilde 8., killed a pilot who was standing at her stern, cutting off his head as with a knife, and damaging the vessel seriously. Several persons standing on the quays and on the Clotilde , B, which was lying on the opposide side of the basin, were I injured mare or less severely by the flying fragments an 4 Captain Brown, owner of several steam tue-s,-While stand- ing on the deck of ansther tug, was knocked with great 1 violence to the deck, his clothes being partially blown elf. I Be had several ribs broker, and was otherwise injured. Mn. TT. TS. WOOTON. r. THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON. The weekly meeting of the Distress Executive Committee was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Mayor's Parlour, Town Hall. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present the Revs. R. Pilcher, 8.A., J. Yonge, W. R. Parry, S. Wilkinson, and E. C. E. Carleton; Major Litton, and Messrs. J. Greening, T. Sutton, T. Jolley, J. Smethurst, and S. Davies.—The MAYOR mentioned that a cheque for £lB 6s 3d had been received from Colonel Thackwell on behalf of the officers, non- commissioned officers, and men at Orford Barracks. (Hear, hear.) There was also a cheque for ..£5 from Mr. R. Garnett on behalf of his firm, and .E 2 7s 6d from the Postmaster on behalf of the clerical staff of the Post Office. Mr. Cawley, of Messrs. Waring and Co., wrote that he would subscribe .£1 a week as long as it might be deemed necessary. (Hear, hear.) They could not be said to be in an impecu- nious position yet, as there had not been much more than £4O spent, and they had a sum of pretty nearly .E 450 in hand. But of course there was the present week's expenditure going on. He should I tell them that the ladies and others had very liber- ally contributed towards the sewing fund, and the ' ladies were rapidly making and distributing gar- ments to people in need of them.—Mr. StrrroN asked if there were many applications in cases to which relief was not granted.—The MAYOR said they had an inquiry officer, who made it his business to ob- tain particulars as to every person who applied for relief, and then inquired at their house as to their , condition.—Mr. JOLLEY said that 780 families had! been receiving relief, and of these probably more' than 100 would be renewals. On the previous day 1 about 1,300 persons received relief according to 1 their needs.—Mr. SMETHURST remarked that over j 200 tickets had been renewed.—ln answer to an inquiry, the MAYOR said that most of the subscrip- tions had been paid.—Mr. SUTTON thought there , were several other people who would willingly contribute if asked.—Major LITTON mentioned that ; on Saturday 1,293, and on Sunday the same number , of persons had been relieved. He also mentioned , . that Mr. Smethurst had kindly given them a ventilte- i tor, which wos valued at ..£2 Ls., to put over the soup I boilers; and Mr. SMETHURST mentioned that Mr. i R. Davies had requested him to distribute a parcel of clothing, which he had done. lie added that a person living near the Blue Coat School, who did i not wish his name mentioned, had contributed two tons of coals.—Some discussion then took place as to the advisability of granting relief in coals, and it was explained that in cases in which it was , thought desirable such relief was afforded.—Major LrrroN mentioned that 70 per cent of the applicants ! for relief were Irish, and Mr. JOLLEY expressed the opinion that this large percentage of Irish was due to the severe weather. As soon as the weather be- came open a large number of them, he thought, would go out into the country to seek work.—The sub-committee recommended that Messrs. Greening 'and Jolley be appointed to purchase the next quan- tity of goods, and this recommendation was con- firmed.--In answer to the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, it was, stated that the cost of the bread and soup distributed was a little over id per head.—The cheques for the payment of £ll 17s 6d, expenditure incurred by the Ladies' Committee, having been passed, the meeting terminated.
