OUR SELECT LIBRARY. Sir,—We are informed by your neutral contemporary, the favoured medinui for Mr. Beamont's premeditated imr,romp- Ws, that " great discretion was exercised in sending out the invitations to the conversaaione " to celebrate the re-open- ing of V. e museum and library last week. Can one help being of the same opinion as your contemporary that it was a singularly happy idea" to re-open a public build- ing in this way ? There was something peculiarly fitting and in keeping with the library in the whole affair. In the one case the list of guests was, as far as possible, nicely cut and shaped according to personal predilection, while in the other the subscription barrier is just high enough to keep out the vulgar herd, though easily covered by the better-off few. There is just one disadvantage in connection with the mode of re-opening. It might deepen the impression which a few people are foolish enough to entertain that the institution in Bold-street is a publicly paid-for bat a privately - managed concern.—Yeurs, AN UNINVITED ONE.

THE RECTOR'S GRAMMAR. Sir,—Some contention, in which the Rector is taking part, is going on just now about the site of a proposed new school. Might I humbly suggest that the school should be ereced as near the rectory as possible, in order that the Rector might take advartage of the elementary grammar classes. That instruction in this direction is required, a letter which Mr. Quelsett has sent to one of your contem- par aries affords ample proof. The second sentence in that epistle runs as follows :—"I beg to state that on Sunday, September 13th, 1885, I addressed the congregation at the Parish Church. which you printed at length in your paper of September 19th, wherein I mentioned to the churchwar- dens and sidesnien to call at once meeting of the rate- payers to consider the subject of increased school accom- modation, as Crossley-street school was considered by Her Majesty:s Ins.p,ctor not fully adapted for the wants of the neighbourhood." The columns of the "Guardian" are suf- ficiently unreadable in all conscience, but it is only fair to say that it has never printed, either at length or at breadth, anything so intellectually indigestible as "the Parish Church." . PEDAGOGUE. Warrington, March 4th, 1885.

PREVENTION BETTER THAN CURE. Sir,—Walking one day in Victoria-street, Manchester, I saw a gentleman throw a piece of orange peel on the roadway. I went ani requested him not t) do so. He said he never threw it on the pavement, but Crioug'uL it all right to cast it on the carriage way. I showed him that that was the more dangerous place of the two, as people crossing in a hurry, and in front ef a conveyance, or getting off a tram-car, might slip, be run over, and have to be tahen to the infirmary. He saw the danger, and pro- mised to do what I su4gested. viz., in future, when he ate oranges in the streets, to put the peel in his pocket, and throw it in the fire when he returned home; and I hope that all who read this, and all who eat oranges or other fruit in the streets of Warrington, Earlstown, Newton, St. Helen's, Runcorn, Widnes, Golborn, Frodsbam, and wherever your influential journal may be circulated, Will follow that gentleman's example. Meny may read this who do not eat fruit in the streets, who do so whilst travelling by rail. To all each I would suggest—take with you a small basket or bag for the remains of yonr refreshment, and do not throw out of the carriage windows the fruit peelings and other dcbriss of vonr repast, the empty lemonade bottles, (Lc , to the endan- gering of the lives of the platelayers and others at work on the line, who might slip on the former in avoiding the latter, and be knocked down and killed by the passing express. It is elan very dangerous to leave peel, fruit skins, icc., about scaffolding., &c., quays, and steps about canals, mouths of coal pits, quarries, and such like places. A little care is better than a broken leg, or perhaps heis of life. That example is better than precent in the opinion of your corresponden.t. ALEXANDER WADDELL. Sale, Cheshire, March 10, 1886.

WARRINGTON DISTRESS FUND. Sir,—As it will, lam sure, be interesting to those ladies and gentlemen who have already subscribed, as well as to those who intend to subscribe, to the above benevolent ob- ject, to know exactly how matters are progressing, I here- with subjoin a few pirticulars. The Ladies' Sewing Committee have met every day dur- ing the week, in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, (generally from 20 to 30), and have made a large number of useful wares garments for the poor women .and children, whose circuiustances have been fully inquired into, and their destitute condition ascertained beyond all doubt. Some of the poor suffering invalids have also been visited at their own homes by some of the ladies, and relieved with clothes and food. The following numbers of garments have been made and distributed-161 warm skirts, 30 children's hoods or bonnets. and 55 other garments, a goed many pairs of stockings and clogs to the women and children, while four poor destitute girls h,..ve been provided with clothes, and places of service found for them. The following ladies have kindly contributed parcels of useful under-clothing, materials, clogs, &c; Mrs. Parkinson, Latchford ; Miss Kendrick, Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Birth Row- son, Miss Hepherd. Mrs. Frank Roberts. Mrs. Richard Row- son, Mrs. Craig, Miss Clara J. Harvey, Miss Beatrice Cragg, Latchford ; Miss Grime, Thelwall ; Children of the Bank Quay Mission, us 31d for children's clogs; Miss Pierpoint, St. Austin's, a parcel of shawls ; and, in cash, Mrs. Thewlis, £2; Mrs. Thackwell. .£1 is ; Mrs. Broadbent. £1; Mrs. Butterworth, £1 ; Miss Dutton, of Moore, £1; Mrs. Wheeler, of Penketh, £1; anonymous, £1; Mrs. Coates, 103. _ _

The amount already received and promised amounts to £497 145 Da up to last night, and the sum expended in bread and soap and materials for clotbina amounts to Z 94 123, leaving a balarce in hand of about £3OO, which will soon be absorbed, as, I am sorry to say, the number of recipients is fast increasing, and proiably will, so long as the severe weather labts.

On Monday, March Bth, 1,307 men, women, and childred were sapplici with bread and soup, on the 91a 1,443, 10th 1,500, 11th 1.621, and on the 12th I,6ls.—Yours, Ice , J. HARRISON, Mayor, Treasurer. Town Hall, Warrington, March 12th, 1886.

THE CHURCH QUESTION. Sir,—One rney venture to rely on your deserved reputa- tion for impartiality to refer to your comment last week. upon Mr. John Croefield'e remarks on the occasion ef Mr. Tuckwell's recent lecture. You suggest that "it would be in- teresting to kaow who are the extreme people who have pro- posed such an ext-eme thing" as to " have the churches put up to auction and sold to the highest bidders, to he used as music halls,or pulled down and the streets paved with the stones." At the Triennial Conference of the Liberation Societtr, held in London, May let and 2nd, 1877, the prac- tical suggestions of the Special Committee appointed to deal with the subject were adopted. They have been published by the Liberation Society, and scattered broadcast over England. At page 11, under the heading, "The Disposal of Buildings," paragraph 13 reads as follows :—"Both ancient and modern buildings, as well as all endowments . must be regarded as national property, at the disposal of the State " Parag-aph 17 :—" All churches exist- ing at the date of the passing of the first of the Church Buildina: Acts (1818) should be deemed to be ancient parish churches." Paragraph 18 :—"Ancient churches (as de- fined in sec. 17) should be vested in a parochial board, to be elected by the ratepayers, which board should have power to deal with them ; . . . in such ways as it maw determine The power of sale, at a fair valuation, and under proper regulation, should also be given."—Yours respectfully, WM. CARSON. The Warrington Club, Warrington, March 11th, 1886. [Does Mr. Carson wish it to be inferred from the above that the Liberation Society are to be regarded as " the ex- tram!) people who would have the churches pat up to auction and sold to the highest bidders, to be used as music halls, or pulled down and the streets payed with the stones ?" If he does, we must say that the inference is unwarrantable. It cannot be denied that the Legislature has the authority to exercise such powers as it is sug- gested might be given to a Board of Ratepayers, but would that justify Mr. Carson in sug- gesting time members of Parliament (Sir Gilbert Greenall included) were amongst the extreme people who would convert parish churches into ineeic hallo, or pave the streets with them? Surely not. "The Radical Programme" puts a different conetruction on what is meant by this proposed power of sale " under.properre- gulations." The writer, page 163, says :--" It is possible that, under certain circumstances. the Beard would sell the fabric out and out to the Episcopalian or other reli- gious body." There is nothing about music halls or street- paving in either "The Radical Programme" or the "Sug- gestions " of the Liberation Society.—ED. Ex.]

div.head: MIGHT IS Rivar.
div.p: MIGHT IS Rivar.

Sir!—l have read with much interest the correspondence which has appeared in your columns of late on matters of social and political importance. I admired the way in which one of your correspondents demolished tbe delusive shibboleth, "Force is no remedy," which certainly has been used with great effect by one Itld;cal orator of renown. Equally effective has been the exposure of Mr. e Ghapinan's impracticable doctrines, according to which every man is as good as his neighbour, and, to indulge in a Ilibernieism, "a great deal better." It requires but litde tricrital effort to see the fallacy of such teacnina.. It wotild be manifestly unfair if the industrious and the indo- lent, tile skilled and the unskilled, the learned and the ignorant, were to be equally provided for. Society formed on such a basis could not hope for longth of life, if, indeed, it escaped strangulation at birth. The very nature of man is opposed to such a Utopia. Our selfish nature has not , been sufficiently subdued, nor our moral and benevolent feelings cultivated to such a degree to enable us to bear the infliction with anything like complacency. And wisely too ; we have only to re&ct on the destruction of all incen- tive tive to exertion which would ensue, and the consequent deterioration of our whole nature, to bring its absurdity prominently before our minds. (o doubt your correspon- dent would piefor to designate the guiding principle of sae) a community with the brief sentence,---.! right is might," the justice of which I entirely repudiate. As a princiole the centence rever,ed is niuh more sound and logical, and one upon which our forefathers have acted since the creation of the world, and which is also the guiding principle of our own though many of us are loth to aeknewledge it. Might is right. A keen observer, if he is also reflective, will per- ceive it in the little affairs of every-day life. As an in- stance which will be fresh in eYerybocly's mbar!, I will just

mention the recent Socialist riots in London. We find there might or force, which, right or airong, considered as an act solely, has resulted in right being done to thousands of suf- fering and deserving people. Had it not been for those strongly-condemned riots, we should not have had a relief fund established ha Warrington at the present time, and 1,300 people (sometimes) daily receiving food and clothing at the Drill Ha'!. On the ruins of demolished property and 1 the blasted reputation of a Chief Commissioner, "our I honest, industrious poor" are having a high old time of it; 1 but it was always thus, is all ag-s and in all countries, and so it will continue to the end of the world. Upon a tree a sparrow caught a fi .6 fat fly, and despite the entreaties of the poor victim, made a good feast, because the sparrow's beak was strong, the tly's but weak. A hawk, after a remon- strance at the sparrow's cruelty, made quite as good a feast ; because his beak was stronger. The eagle killed the hawk, , a hunter the eagle, and a bear the man. .
'ls Might not right, here. everywhere, From fly to eagle. man to bear?" —Yours, dtc.,
M. I. R.

SOCIAL EQUALITY. Sir,—Wheri I read " Jaques" first reply to my interroga- tion anent Communism, I wondered whether I was repeat- ing Don Quixote's mad freak with the windmills, or that I bad played the part of the oyster in the crab and oyster business. I confess to a little bewdderment at the first, caused by the complacent, self-satisfied air, of my critic. However, on recovering my equilibrium, I was fain to have another tilt at my antagonist. So I penned my second and third letters ; and if " Jaques' " rent's is te be taken seri- ously, it would almost appear that I have only pricked his balloon, and released a little harmless carburetted hy- drogen in the shape of playful irony and thinly veiled Satire. " To clear up matters "so.as to enlighten " Jaques'" un- derstanding, I admit the distinctions he lays down between land and capital ; also that lam a believer in evolution. But this will not help" Jaques" out of the bog he floun- dered into when he stated " that if a man creates his own fortune he takes nothing from anybody else." I I-eve I challai,ed " Jaques" to produce such a man, and lam Ie still " thirsting after this very elementary information ;" and I maintain, sir, that capitalists who obtain large fortunes do so by conventional legal frauds. As well let man try to lift himself above the clouds by laying hold of the sides of a balloonless car, as try to create a fortune from the produce of his own unaided labour. The existence of large fortunes are proof of the existence of a large mass of ill-fed, ill- ciothed, and ill-paid labour. I therefore re-affirm that there is no distinction in the existence of a landlord and capitalist, b :cause both exist 'upon the produce of other people's lahour,"and I contend there can be no such thing as "social equality ' where society admits of two such opposite classes as rich and poor, or as " Jaques " put it, where " distinc- tion and fortune" are to be acquired. To call such a state of society "social equality" is to call it what it is not. Oa the question of Communism. I fear "Jaques" has gone out of his deptli; certainly he does not appear to be posted up in the Pracrical application of its principles as ex- emplided in the United States. Take "Oneida Com- munity," State of New York, as the most scientific commu- nity of this generation. In 1878 it contained 145 males and 161 females of 311 ages; 60 were under 14 years, and 82 under 21 years. Up to 1878 they had been 30 years .in exietence ; commencing with about 40 persons. It will be seen that during the last 14 years its increase of population was a little over four children per annum, as the deaths of children _were nil during that period. This low birth-rate arose from this recognition of "the great principle lying at the foundation of stirpiculture, or the scientific propogation of human beings having been evolved." —American Co»zmunities,by W. A. Hinds, Oneida. Evolution then "is not utterly fatal to communistic theories," as " Jaques " would have it, seeing that this com- munity does not allow their numbers to increase above their means of subsistence. I may say that they are a rick com- munity and could support a largtr population. It is " J2ques "that is "unfortunate " in his statements, which are at variance with ascertained facts.
in future let me advise " Jaques " to deal with my state- ments, and nut with his own "elementary " ideals. W. H. CIIAPINIAN.
Warrington, March 12th, 1836.
OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.

Sir,—ln your last issue I find the names of three promi- nent Liberal gentlemen of Warrington who seem to have gone some little out of their way to pronounce against the Disestabliehment and Disendowment of what is called the National Church. I ceateinly grant the right of these gentlemen to form conclusions for themselves, and to act upon them, but that upholders of a State Church should find araongst Unitarians and the Society of Friends col- leagues and helpers is somewhat beyond my comprehension. The occasion taken hold of hy the gentlemen to whom I refer seems to me to have been not the happiest. With the Rev. W. Tuckwell I Lope Warriogton audieeces will grow in friendliness and sympa.hy. He is a splendid dreamer, and if none of us live to see either his New Utopia or Church of the Future, at leaet we have the satisfaction of knowing him as a mighty Image Breaker. Listening to the rev. gentleman's lecture, I could not gather what opinions he held respecting Disestablishment. He need not have been shy or diffident at pronouncing them, for I am sure he had sufficient enconfagement given to him by his chairman, Mr. John Crosfield. The first question I should ask myself respecting the Church as a" State-controlled ecclesiastical system" would be—Does this Church give back to the people an equiva- lent for the revenue she derives from them? Again—Does this Chureh teach the truth, and nothing but the truth, to the people ? If these ceeestione are not answered in the affirmative, the sooner the whole system is toppled over the better for all parties. I care not one jot for her endowments, if her disendow- anent is to be followed up by the endowment of the other nine hundred and ninety-nine shibboleths, but if they are to be diverted i nto channels whereby the people shall he made to feel the innumerable pleasures that may be crowded into this life, then am I anxious that a wise and speedy settlement of the question shall come about, How can a fair equivalent be given to the people in return for the monies absorbed by the Church, when we are told by the well-informed lecturer that her clergy are "intel- lectually incompetent?" Is it not a fact that, for a great number of years past, there has been one constant wail for Church Reform? Did not Mr. Disraeli try his hand with a Public Worship Regulation Act, at reconciling the various schools of thought within the Church? ' Still further back, did not Parliament, by appointing a permanent committee—the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, try to give the Church a self-governing power, more or less secular, but still in sympathy, yet what has come of it all? Mr. Tuckwell tells us that but the "dregs" of our University men "take orders." The late Bishop Fraser, speaking of the things that are fatal to the Church, says "that an ignorant, grasping, self-seeking clergy, with a fierce intolerance against those who differ from us, and who commit blunders that are worse than crimes, are they who are giving over the Church to the spoiler." If, after all these attempted reforms, there still remains amongst the clergy such a large amount of "selfish ignorance," how can we feel justified in waiting for reform from within? But, sir, there is a widespread feeling that what these gentry preach is not true. Hence may it not be possible that Mr. Crosfield, Mr. Monks, and the Rev. R. Filcher, in their anxiety to perpetuate a State Church, are helping to rivet the chains of ignorance still closer that bind the in- tellect of man? If " nine-tenths" of the clergy are una- ware that there .is "any valid objection to the literal ac- ceptance of the six days' creation," bow is it possible for the intellectual classes to accept them as teachers? Or how is it possible for them to commence reforming them- selves? Is it with men of this class that Mr. Filcher would ally himself? Of course ram aware that in the" Church of the Future" all these things will have passed away. lam willing to be-. have this, and also to believe that the Unitarians of Cairo- street and the Trinitarians of Sankey-street may bridge over the gulf that now separates them in their anxiety to build up the Church of the Future; that the Frederic Har- risons and Herbert Spencere of the future may find sweet consolation in communing with the Cardinal Mannings and Cardinal Newmans of the future ; but I ask, will a thought-fettered Church help to bridge over the innumera- ble gulfs that now separate the people. Mr. Crosfield ought to have left the dreaming business to the lecturer. No one wishes to pull down the churches, or to have " the streets paved with their stones," nor yet to hive them "put up to auction and sold to the highest bidders." I should recommend a re-perusal of 'The Radi- cal Programme," and it will there be found (p. 162) that it may possibly, some day, should tha Church persist in her Present alliance, come within the duties of the House of Commons to look upon all churches as National property, and deal with them accordingly.—Yours, Am,

div.p: Ti4E I4AAMINER. SATURDAT, MARCH 13, 1886. --'OUR LONDON LETTEk.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The familiar figure of Mr. Gladstone has been absent from the Treasury Bench throughout the week. He spoke with his accustomed energy on Friday night in the debate on the House of Lords; but he caught cold on Saturday, and on Sunday took to his bed with the determination to stop there till he is better. It is not a very serious affair. He has of late years been peculiarly su•sceptible to cold, and when attacked promptly places himself under the motherly care of Mrs. Gladstone, who on these occasions assumes the airs ef a despot. It , happened that there came to town on Monday, all unconscious of Mr. Gladstone's indisposition, a deputation from the Scottish Liberal Club of Edin- burgh, charged with the commission of handing to Mr. Gladstone an address voted to him when be visited that city in November. They waited on till yesterday, when Mr. Gladstone was anxious to re- ceive them, protesting he felt quite well enough, but Mrs. Gladstone would not hear of it. She went out to meet the deputation herself, and made them a little speech in which she expressed the Premier's thanks for the address.

The necessity for Mr. Gladstone's absence from the House of Commons comes at a convenient time. Everything is going on very quietly, and the Pre- mier might just as well be at home as in the House. Perhaps he did not find it altogether inconvenient to be absent on Tuesday night, when Mr. Dillwyn's resolution with respect to the Church in Wales came forward for discussion, It would have been hard for him to speak against the motion, still more so to vote against it. The case of Wales with respect to the Church of England is scarcely better than was that of Ireland at the time the Church was disestab- lished. Mr. Gladstone has, however, guarded him- self against misapprehension, having repeatedly stated in Scotland and elsewhere that the present Parliament would not be able to deal with the dis- establishment question. Its turn will come, though its time is not yet. How near at hand it is was tes- tified to by the critically narrow majority by which Mr. Dillwyn's resolution was negatived. A majority of twelve for the preservation of the Establishment , in Wales is, like the majority of 36 for the retention of the House of Lords, "the writing on the wall." Delay in settlement of the Irish question commends itself for two reasons to.the Conservatives. It not only keeps back reforms which they hate, but it oc- cupies the attention of Parliament, and prevents it dealing with other questions. There have been through the week all kind of rumours with respect to the Cabinet deliberations on Ireland. Statements, full of detail and clothed with an imposing air of authority. have been put forward on one day, only to be contradicted upon official authority on the next. The simple fact is that now, as at the opening of the session, the plan is not to be described for the sufficient reason that it is not yet drawn up. Mr. Gladstone is still going, forward with his mission of examination and in- quiry. But ty time is now drawing near when all the threads will be gathered up and the scheme completed. Mr. Gladstone is pledged to communi- cate his plan to the House on or about the close of the financial year, which terminates on the 31st of March. There thus remains less than three weeks at his disposal, and we shall shortly be hearing of daily Cabinet Councils. . How the matter will end it would be rash to predict; but I know that at the present moment the prospects of unanimity in the Cabinet are re- garded most hopefully. It would be half the vic- tory won if Mr. Gladstone could bring forward his scheme supported by the united force of the Cab- inet. The Conservatives are eagerly watching the movements of Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyttn, and in their eagerness have gone ,in advance of events, publishing reports of :their atual or closely proximate resignation. I believe it is quite on the cards that when the scheme is formulated Mr. Tree velyan may find himself unable to support it. He is a man of keenly sensitive mind, the very pink of honour, and would for conscience sake sacrifice any- thing, even the companionship of Mr. Gladstone, whom he deeply reverences. He would be more than human if, after his experience of the Irish office, he could regard with favour any extension of the power and influence of the Nationalists. He has seen it work evil to Ireland and will be hard to convince that a further extension of it may be so tempered as to result in unqualified good. Mr. Tre- velyan may therefore possibly retire, but I think Mr. Chamberlain will not. If he leaves the Treasury Bench, where;is he to tzo to? He cannot join the Whigs, and there js as yet no evidence of the crea- tion of a party of Radicals opposed to the policy of doing full justice to Ireland. Ir.there were, Mr. Chamberlain's course is clear. He would put him- self at their head and make things uncommonly uncomfortable for Mr. Gladstone. As there is not, he will stay where he is. No indication of the line of defence that will be taken in the Pimlico poisoning case has yet been given, nor is it likely to be disclosed before the magistiate. It is evident that the case must be sent for trial, and in accordance with custom the defence will be reserved. It is likely to be of a somewhat startling character. The charge against Mrs. Bartlett is that she poisoned her husband by administering chloroform, traces of which, accord- ing to the medical testimony for the prosecution, have been found in the body. The counsel for the defence has sat quietly by whilst the prosecution have committed themselves altogether to this theory. The defence will be that such procedure as that charged is impossible. I heard two of the most eminent surgeons in England discussing the case the other night, and they agreed beyond controversy that chloroform could not have been administered to Mr. Bartlett without his knowing it and being a determinedly consenting party. Chloroform is to the taste a liquid considerably stronger than over- proof whisky. If it were administered to a patient, the immediate effect would be a gasping, choking, burning sensation that would effectually prevent his continuing the draught. Among the rumours of the day put forward with circumstance is one that would send Lord Rosebery to undergo treatment at the hands of the German doctor who reduced Prince Bismarck from uncomfortable corpulency to ordinary girth. A fortnight or three weeks ago I referred to this doctor, and mentioned the report that the Czar had borrowed his services, finding himself, in spite of the daily perils that surrounded him, getting too stout. The rumour with respect to Lord Rosebery, which has been gravely copied in most of the papers, was, I believe, originally put forward as a joke. Lord Rosebery, it is true, is plump in person, but is certainly in no need of a specialist to bring down superabundant fat. Somebody playfully re- marked that the labours of the Foreign Office had not reduced his weight, and that if 'things did not improve he must go to Germany and see Bismarck's doctor. The not very brilliant joke was repeated, finally got in the papers, and was accepted as a matter of fact much, I believe, to Lord Rosebery's annoyance. He is just stout enough to make the topic a delicate one. The weather, which continues to be abominable, has a serious responsibility at its door. The morn- ings in London have for the past six weeks been SO dark that it has frequently been impossible for painters to get forward with their work. There was, a short time ago, talk of postponing the Academy in order to give painters an opportunity of making up for lost time. It was found, after brief discussion, that this course was impracticable, and the Academy will open on the uval day. But it will be a hard race against time. An A.R.A. tells me that he is at least three weeks behind with his work, and does not quite see how he is to make it up before sending-in day. Lord Richard Grosvenor and Lord Kensington have at length received the reward of many long and weary nights spent in the service of the party. Whilst the term of office lasts, there is nothing more thankless than the office of Whip. If things go wrong the Whip is held responsible. If all goes well it is accepted as a matter of course. But men will do a good deal for a peerage, and the bestowal of one upon the late Liberal Whips/will prove an incentive to the light-hearted young gentlemen who have now succeeded to the office. It is a puzzle to some people that whilst Lord Kensington is said to. be raised to the peerage he is Lord Kensington The mtplanation, of course, is that he has hitherto been a member of the Irish peerage, and is now a peer of the realm. Lord Kensington owns a vast amount of house property in the district of London, whence he takes his name. Within the last fifteen years this has gone up marvellously in I3ut i n e truism h rt ume 'value, making him a very rich man. Lord Richard ' s a Grosvenor bore his title by courtesy. DISCUSSION ON HOME RULE AT RUNCORN.

The discussion on Home Ririe, adjourned a week ago from a meeting called by the Runcorn Liberal Association, was resumed on Thursday night in Bethesda Lecture Hall. There was again a goad attendance, and Mr. S. Pope presi- ded. Mr. H. Hill, who lectured on the subject on the last occasion, again opened the debate with an able speech, in which he reviewed to some extent the history of Ireland with regard to its bearing upon Home Rule. At the last meeting Mr. Kniveton asked that some definite statement of the Irish demand should be laid before them, and the speaker said he bad got an aathoritative, and he believed definite, proposal of the Irish party. (Applause.) The Irish party asked that the internal affairs of Ireland should be regulated by an Irish Parliament consisting of the Queen, Lords, and Commons of Ireland. All imperial affairs, all that related to colonies, foreign states, and the common in- terests of the Empire, continue to be regulated by the Im- perial Parliament—(hear, hear,)—in which Ireland should have some representation. It was clearly undesirable to separate two countries politically, so nearly connected geo- graphically, socially, and which had so many common interests, commercial and international. It was not the less clearly undesirable that one country should control the do- mestic affairs of another country whose genius, likes and dislikes, it confessedly did not understand; and to whose business it admittedly had not time to attend. The Irish Parliamentary party wished, in fact, to retain every guar- antee for the real and •effective union of the Einnire— , (applause)—but let each transact its own private business as each deem best. (Hear, hear.) Let both neighbours combine for every neighbourly purpese, and pull together, if hands be against theirs, as neighbours should— (applause)—and let England'once for all give up the arro- gant pretension to dominate:over the hearthstone and domestic economy of the other. (Applause.) As to the Crown, it was not proposed to affect its prerogative at all. As for the Irish Parliament, it would have supreme con- trol of the internal affairs of Ireland. Its juris- diction would include every exclusive Irieh inter- est; education, agriculture, commerce, manufac- tures, public works, courts of justice, the magis- tracy, railways, post office, and every detail of Irish busi- ness and Irish national life. If deemed desirable the altera- tion of the Acts which settled Irish property in the reign of Charles 11. should be plac,d beyond the jurisdiction of the Irish Parliament. He did not think this a very radical de- mand. (Hear, bear.) He narrated some of the injustices and hardships inflicted upon Ireland by English law, and the starvation that was taking place there at the present time. He hoped that every one present would say these things must cease, and that justice must be done to Ireland. Let this be done, and they would have one Ireland at home and a greater Ireland in America to call upon in time of danger to the Empire. (Applause.) The Chairman, in throwing open the discussion, said he had been struck by the ability and moderation displayed by Mr. Hill. ( Hear, hear.) Mr. 0. Leak agreed entirely with Mr. Hill in the view he took, and after quoting some facts with regard to Ireland from Mr. Giffen's book, said they simply proved that the country had been misgoverned. (Hear, hear.) He con- demned the system of coercion by which the sister isle had been ruled, and contended that unless we were prepared to perpetuate that policy Ireland must have some measure of self-government. (Applause.) Mr. G. Bellamy declared himself as a Home Ruler for one reason because he was a Radical. (Hear, hear.) The spirit of the age demanded that Ireland should have that measure of self-government which the country bad a right to expect —(applause)—and considering the muddle England had made in its government, he really thought we should let Ireland govern itself.

Mr. Millington also spoke in favour of Home Rule. Mr. W. Handley said the sooner the question was dealt with in a satisfactory manner the better it would be for the United Kingdom. (Hear, hear.) He remarked upon the rapid development of public opinion on the sub- ject during the past few years. The great mistake England had made in this Met) question was in trying to rule Ire- land for England's good, and that was a bad principle of government. We had posseeseil Ireland for 700 years, and Vet its state was to-day a disgrace to a civilised country, because if it had been governed for Ireland's good it would have been happy, prosperous, and contented. After several apposite references to hiotorv, Mr. Handley referred to the evils inflicted upon the sister isle by absentee landlordism. Out of a rent roll of ten millions fully one half went out of Ireland every year. In a place of business if one half the capital went out every year, could they expect that busi- ness to prosper? No more could they expect Ireland to prosper so beg as its landlords impoverished the country by being absentees. (Applause.) There was no doubt that the Liberal party had tried honestly to put matters right for a number of years--(applause)—and he spoke favoura- bly of the scheme of Home Rule put forward by Mr. Chem. erlain and Mr. Joseph Cowen. Mr. Williamson dealt with the wrongs of Ireland, and quoted resolutions passed by Orange lodges prior to the Act of Union, showing that even the Orangemen were against the measure. Mr. H. D. Kitto also spoke in favour of Home Rule. Mr. Hill replied to the observations made by the various speakers The Rev. W. Vause moved, "That this meeting, called by public advertisement to consider the question of Home Rule, urges upon the Government and its illustrious leader, Mr. Gladstone, the necessity of granting to Ireland such and so large a measure of Horne Rule as may be compatible with the maintenance and integrity of the British Empire; and that copies of this resolution be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Brunner." (Loud applause.) It was unnecessary, he said, to say much in support of the re- solution, because the whole tenour of the discussion had been favourable to Home Rule. In the past many politi- cians bad been frightened at Home Rule, but it had sow come to be looked upon, not as a bugbear, but as some- thing which was clear, simple, and thoroughly practical, which would bring good not only to Ireland but to Eng- land. (Hear, hear.) He weuld not support a Parliament for Ireland if he thought it was going to be one such as they bad before. (Hear, hear.) A Parliament which was constituted only by one religious sect would not have his support, and he quoted statistics to show that at present' Ireland was really governed by one sect, and as an advocate for religious liberty, as well as an advocate for political liberty, he had great pleasure in moving that resolution. (Applause.) Mr. Faulkner seconded the resolution, which was car- ried unanimously. Mr. W. Handley moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Hill for the clear, intelligent, and temperate manner, in which he had placed the question before them. Mr. Bellamy seconded the proposition, and it was carried by acclamation. A vote of thanks was also accorded to Mr. Pope for pre- siding, on the rnotien of Mr. Hill.

The charge of nepotism against the Premier is . clearly disproved, and that fat living of close on a thousand a year is not to be given, or at all events has not been offered, to his son-in-law. It was at Mr. Drew's house that a well-known Oxford "coach" was stopping a little time ago. If Ido not give his name my reason will be obvious,though indeed he is himself the retailer of the story, which illustrates how many things are said which were better unsaid. The parson's wife was consulting the Oxonian on the prospects of her son, and said she did hope that he would be a clever boy. The boy's father was present. "Oh," said the professor, "you need have no fears about that. I have ob- served that intellect, like gout, always skips a generation."

LATEST NEWS.

- - The Duke of Argyll is confined to bed at Inverary from an attack of gout. The funeral of Mr. John Brooks, the late member for the Altrincham Division of Cheshire, took place on Friday at Swallowfield, Reading. A fire, resulting in damage to the estimated extent of £34,000, occurred on Thursday night at the clothing factory of Messrs. Dunes, Chatham. The South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire gas tube titters have decided to strike work in several works against the threatened reduction in wages. Mr. Lacaita, M.P. for Dundee, is suffering from an attack of whooping cough, aggravated by a bronchial affec- tion, and will have to austain from his parliamentary duties for some weeks.

HEAVY DAMAGES —The New Zealand libel case, in which Mr. Bryce, formerly a New Zealand minister, sued Mr. Rusden, author of the history of New Zealand, concluded on Friday, the jury finding for the plaintiff; damages £5,000.

The Central News is officially ihformed that the Queen has been pleased to approve the appointment of Sir Charles Warren, G.C.M.G., to be Chief Commissioner of the Metropolitan police, in the place of Sir E. Henderson, re signed.

MRS. WELDON AGAIN.—Mrs. Georgina Weldon com- menced an action in the Queen's Bench, on Friday, against Mr. St. John Wontaer to recover £lO,OOO damages for negligent conduct of a case in which he acted as her solici- tor, and £5OO damages for detention of documents.

THE BELT CASE.----At the Central Cri;;;;;1-.Court, on Friday, Mr. Walter Belt, the sculptor, and his brother, Mr Richard Bel' were charged with conspiring to obtain £5,000 from Sir Neville Abdy by fraud and false pretences. The prosecutor having repeated the evidence given by him before the magistrates, the Court adjourned. THE IPswicu ELEcriorr PETITION.—At the resumed bearing on Friday afternoon of the Ipswich election peti- tion, Mr. Garrard Ward, secretary of the Liberal Associa- tion, denied bribing electors, but admitted wr:ting to a voter saying some lucre would find its way to his house for expenses. The witness fainted, and was carried out of court.

DISASTROUS FIRE AT OLDHAM.—A POLICEMAN KILLED. —About half-past nine on Thursday night the goods ware- house belonging to the Lancashire and Yoikshire Railway Company at Werneth, Oldha:n, was discovered to be on fire. The fire brigade were quickly on the scene, but the flames had obtained a mastery of the building, which was stored with cotton and other inflammable material. With- out any warning the front wall suddenly fell outwa,cls, kill- ing,Constable Schofield, who was playinc, from a hydrant in Rochdale-road. The origin of the fire has not been ascer- tained. The damage is extensive, the premises being a complete wreck. The damage is estimated at £70,000. of which it is believed a large portion is insured. The two men injured are improving.

THE PIMLICO TRA—GEDY.—The magisterial investigation into the Pimlico mystery was continued on Friday, at the Westminster Police Court, when Mrs. Bartlett and the Rev. George Dyson were further charged with the murder of the husband of the first named prisoner. The whole bearing was occupied with additional medical testimony. Drs. Dud- ley and Green gave evidence that all the internal organs were healthy, excdpt that there was fatty degeneration of the heart. When the stomach and intestines were opened, there was a strong smell of chloroform and garlic. The centents of the stomach were preserved, and the prisoners told of the suspicions circumstances. In cross-examination, the witnesses admitted they had never known cases of poisoning from liquid chloroform, which was most volatile. The case was adjourned for a week. SAD Ice FATALITY NEAR Sr. HELENS.-013 Thursday evening a sad accident occurred on Garr Mill Dam, an ex- tensive sheet of water situate two miles from St. Helens, on the Garswood estate of Lord Gerard. About half-past six o'clock, a young man named John Eves, aged 17, a collier, son of a blacksmith residing at Billinge, went down to the dam with several others and commenced skating. Eves was about forty yards from the side when he found that he had ventured too near a dangerous • spot, and irhmPdiately threw himself on his :back. But too late, for the velocity he was travelling at was too great, and he elided forward into the water. Several young men came as near as possible, and taking off their scarves tied them together and threw one end to him. Eves seized it, and was being slowly drawn to the strong ice when one of the knots gave way and he fell back again and was drowned.

div.head: FIVE LIVWS LOST AT AN ORPHANAGE.
div.p: FIVE LIVWS LOST AT AN ORPHANAGE.

ELBERFELD, FRIDAY.—The Elberfelder states that the boys' orphanage at Voerde, in the district of Heiz4en, was destroyed by fire last night. Five of the in- mates perished in the flames,. the remainder, SO in number, being saved.

—THE VATICAN AND PRINCE BISMARCK. A telegram dated frem Rome states that a Papal courier has left Rome for Berlin conveying an autograph letter from Leo XIII., thanking Prince Bismarck for the eulo- gies passed on the Papacy at the recent Parliamentary dinner.

div.head: SEVERE GALE. AT GIBRALTAR.
div.p: SEVERE GALE. AT GIBRALTAR.

GIBRALTAR, FRIDAbIt.—A severe gale raged here last night. causing great damage on shore and to the shipping. A steamer is reported ashore six miles frorn the Rock, with her funnel gone and her crew in the rigging. It is impos- sible to reach them by sea. Two sailing vessels are ashore behind the Rock.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met :t—f4;u—r—o.cio—ck:

NEW PUBLIC OFFICRS,—EarI MORLEY, replying ts Lord Larnington, said plans for erecting new public offices in Parliament-street, were under consideration. The plans of the Institute of British Architects would cost nearly half a million more than the plans selected. No information could be given as to the ertction of a new National Portrait Gallery. •TRB BRITISR MUSRLIC, &C.—Earl HARROWBY moved an address in favour of opening the British Museum and Na- tional Gallery and National History Museum to the peblic three evenings each week.—Lord SUDELEY said the expense which would be incurred would be certain, but the author- ities were divided as to the advantages to be derived by the working classes.—After considerable discussion, Earl Harrowby's motion was agreed to.
• Returns, as to boycotting in Ireland, asked for by Lord Cranbrook, were agreed to, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The House met at 4 o'clock.

QUESTIONS, &c.—Mr. EVERETT gave notice, on an early day, to call attention to the enormous sums raised annually in tithes on agricultural produce of the country, and to move a resolution.—Sir L, PLAYFAIR, replying to Mr. Fry, said no special Act was required to extend the hours of polling at School Board elections, and the Education De- partment had no desire te increase the hours of poll ing.— Mr. HIBBERT, replying to a question, said he was not aware that an order bad been issued for the discharge of 400 workmen from the Devonport Dockyard. HARBOURS OF REFtGI3.-011 the motion to go into COM- mittee of Supply on the civil service estimates, Mr. DAWSON called attention to the present depression of trade and the large numbers of persons out of employment, and moved that the Present was a favourable time foot' the Government to carry out certain valuable and necessary public works, more especially the formation of harbours of refuge at vari- ous points upon the coast. He insisted on the necessity of constructing Harbours of Refuge on oar coasts, and west of Ireland, having a minimum depth of ten feet at low water. The want of harbours was clearly shown by lose of life and property that annually took place, which in ships amounted to from 300 to 350, ie- life from 800 to 900, and in property to over two millions sterling. He thought in face of such facts, there was no defence for the scandalous apathy with regard to the provision of harbour accommoda- tion.—Mr. BORLASE seconded the resolution, and pointed out that they were not subsidizing trade in anything they /inked. Their object was the saving of human life.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN pointed tut the difficulties that surrounded the subject, as there was no agreement as to the kind of har- bour required. He did not believe that building harbours would reduce the loss of life at sea. Therefore be considered on humanitarian grounds no case had been made out for State assistance. As to relieving the existing distress, pauperism was now less per thousand than it had been for years past, but there was no doubt great distress amongst better classes of citizens. He believed the ultimate remedy for the existing distress was to be found in the increased activity of local authorities and the liberal loans to be gran- ted them to carry out local works. Mr. C. DAW. SON supported the resolution, and Mr. A. BAL meet said if harbours of refuge were required there could be no better time for constructing them.— Mr. BRADLAUGE opposed the resolution. He ben-eyed there was no more dangerous tendency at the present time than the tendency of many democratic advisers to urge that I was the duty of the State to provide in seasons of distress and misery, for the relief of that distress by Government action. State interference destroyed and neutralised self- reliance and the individual action of local authorities.—Mr BLAKE supported the resolution, but Mr. CONYBERB agreed in tho views expressed by Mr. Bradlaugh.—Sir J. PEASE thought assistance might ba given to those that helped themselves, but not to tbaio who had dons nothing in that direction.

• THE GesCOMPANY.—At a special meeting of the directors of this company on Thursday, the following tenders for the construction of a gasholder tank, 52 feet by 19 feet, were received :--White, Liverpool, £1,086 5s 4d• Holme and King, Liverpool, X6S6 is 3d; T. Simiiin, Runcorn, £561 15s; T. Davies, Froishamt £550; J. Littler, Frodsham, £548 103 (accepted); and Dawson, of Bury, £543. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, KINGSLEY.—The Rev. EL B. Blogg, M.A., vicar of Frodsham, has appointed the Rev. A. P. Rey- nolds t') the living of this parish, which has been rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev. A. Grier, B.A. The Rev. A. P. Reynolds, who is a student bf St. Aiden's Theo- logical Coileae, has in succession held the miracles of Christ Church', Everton, Liverpool, and of St. Lawrence, Frod3ham. He left the latter position two years ago, on his appointment as curate-in-charge of All Saints', Thornton Hough, near Chester.

A fire broke out in Denham-yard, Strand, London, on Thursday morning. An old man named Calnan was snf- , focated. Mr. Gladstone continues to improve in health, but the severity of the weather necessitates his remaining indoors. At the London Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, Jacob Reigelruth, a German, was sentenced to death for the murder of his wife. The crime was committed under the influence of jealousy. Mae. GLADSTONE'S SYMPATHY WIT'S A BERNAvED FARMER—Mrs. Gladstone writes to the father of the young Merionethshire farmer killed in sheep rescuing :—" Our heart bleeds for you, poor father of Henry Davies. My hus- band and myself desire to sympathise with you deeply. Your son was doing his duty nobly. This thought will help you ' to bear the tridnendous trial, though I know in some way it will make it harder. We pray God to help and conafort.— Your friend, CATHERINB GLADSTONE."

THE -VACANCY IN THE ALTRINCHA3.II DIVISION. SELECTION OF THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE. Last night a crowded and enthusiastic meet- ing of the Council of the Liberal Asso- ciation of the Altrincham Division was held in the Reform Club, Altrincham, to decide upon the action of the Liberal party in connection with the Parliamentary election rendered necessary by the death of the late Mr. John Brooks, M.P. The chair was taken by/Mr. T. W. Killick. A telegram was read from Mr. Joseph Lee, of Stockport, the president of the Association, regretting that he was prevented by a severe cold from being present. The CHAIRMAN then moved that the Council ex- press its admiration of the ability and courtesy of the late Mr. John Brooks, the first member of Par- ' liament for the division, and its deep regret that his life, which promised to be full of honour and use- fulness, should have been so suddenly -termi- nated ; and that the resolution be sent to the family of Mr. John Brooks, with assurances of most respectful and sincere sympathy. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) said that the contest of a few months ago was fought without bitterness or ill- feeling, and this was mainly due to the courtesy of Mr. Brooks, who showed throughout it the forbear- ance and manliness that so constantly marked his character. (Hear, hear.) If they had to be repre- sented by a Conservative, they could not have an abler or more promising member, and they all felt that in his sudden and early removal they had lost a gentleman whose early death Liberals united with Conservatives in sincerely deploring. (Hear, hear.)

Sir J. C. LEE, in seconding the proposal, said he had met Mr. John Brooks in London last week in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal, and, whilst he regretted to observe his health was not then strong,. yet-he could not fail to notice his great ability and the attention he gave to the interests of the constituency without reference to party. His early death was a public loss, and one that was felt by all classes and all parties, who would unite in the heartfelt expression of condolence and sym- pathy with the bereaved family and relatives. (Hear, hear.). Mr. G. ROOKE, in supporting the resolution, said that no one who had met with their late member could fail to recognise the kindness of heart,. tho abilities, and the vigorous and well-trained intellect with which he was endowed, and they must all greatly regret that a career of such bright promise had so suddenly closed He was glad to t'A.nk that the Liberals of the division were not so blinded by partisanship as to be unable to recognise the loss the county had sustained and to join in the sincere expressions of regret and esteem embodied in the resolution. (Hear, hear.) The vote of condolence was then unanimously carried.

A very full discussion as to the advisability of con- testing the coming electionthen took place,. and it was ultimately agreed with unanimity and enthu- siasm that the election should be contested, and that Mr. I. S. Leadam should be invited to he the candidate. Mr. Leadam, we need hardly say, is the gentleman who so gallantly fought the last battle of the Liberal party. He will begin the campaign where he left off in November-last, and there is good reason to hope that on this-occasion his efforts will be successful. The Conservatives have not yet held a meeting; but there is some talk of asking Sir 117".. Cunlifio Brooks to become their candidate.,

div.head: PROPOSED NEW SCITOOL IN WARRINGTON..
div.p: PROPOSED NEW SCITOOL IN WARRINGTON..

In order to avert the establishment of a School Board in Warrington, steps are being taken by a number of gentlemen to erect a new school to ac- commodate about 500 children, for the district around Battersby-lane, the Crossley-street schools having been closed owing to the intimaiion. of Iler Majesty's inspector for the district (Mr. W.. S. Cow- ard) that they would no longer be recognised. as Government schools. The Warrington Training College Committee have resolved to contribute 1'1,600 towards building and furnishing schools of the nature required, provided the Training College Committee are permitted to use the same as prac- tising schools, and that the inhabitants and:rate- payers of the borough, with those interested in vol- untary education will provide about £1,400 more, which it is estimated will be required to complete and furnish the schools, including the cost of land. At a meeting of the gentlemen referred to recently held, it was decided on the motion of Mr. R. W. Francomb, seconded by the Rev. E. J. Wilcocks, to adopt the proposal of the Training College Commit- tee, and a committee was appointed to give effect to the resolution, Mr. J. E. Wright being appointed secretary pro tem. The site for the proposed schools which was before the meeting was one in the Six- penny Fields, belonging to Colonel Blackburne. Since the meeting, the Rector (the Rev. W. Que- ke,tt) has made public various objections which he has to the site,referred to, the chief of these .beingthat it is -within3ooyards of the present National Schools in Church-st. The Rector expresses the opinion that " the Training College have enough to do at home with their money if they would look to their-own re- quirements." Some surprise at this opposition by the Rector has been expressed, as he has himself spoken of the necessity there was for new.schools, in the district in question. We understand that efforts have been made for some time back by.-the promoters of the proposed new schools to.obtain a site in Battersby-lane, and it was because of their inability to do this that the site. in Sixpenny Fields was fixed upon. But now,.we• learn, a more .suitable site has been obtained fronting Hamilton- street and near to Battersby-lane, belonging to Mr. Sharpe, and at a meeting of the. committee held on IThursday this site was adopted.

WARRINGTON. A SUCCESSFUL ARCHITECT.—The. plans prepared by Mr. Robert Curran, architect,. of this town, have been selected in connection with. the St. .Alban's Church restoration and new rectory building com- petition, Blackburn.

- EVANGELISTIC SERVICES.-Mr. Wiggan, assisted by Mrs. 'Wiggan, has this week-been holding Ha-ions services at Legh-street Primitive, Methodist CI-impel (pastor, the Rev. J. Calvert), which. have been well attended. The services are to: be. continued. Mr. and Mrs. Wiggan have recently been at Widnes, where their meetings attracted considerade atten- tion, and in Warrington they appear to be doing a good work.

- ALARM OF FIRE.—On Monday afternoon, an alarm of fire was raised in Dannett-street. It appears that in one of the houses a woman who. had been using a hot iron had put it in a cupboard. before it had become cold and some inflammable material was ignited. P.C. Dean, who happened to be near at the time, succeeded, with the assistance of ' a neighbour, in extinguishing the fire befOre much damage was occasioned. I ELECTION' OF OITARDIANS.NOtiCOS Of the elec- tion of Guardians have been issued by Mr. J. C. Sutton, the returning officer. Nominations are to be sent in not before the 15th inst., and not later than the 26th. There are ten Guardians to be elected for Warrington township, and two for the township of Latchford. It may be mentioned that since 1872 there has been a contest at every election of Guardians in Warrington. CONVERSAZIONE.—On Monday evening a conver- szione was held in Holy Trinity Schools, Museum- street. in connection with Holy Trinity Literary and Debating Society. There were a large number of guests present. The room had been tastefully de- corated with plants and banners in honour of the occasion. The proceedings opened with a miscel- laneous concert, and dancing was afterwards indul- ged in to the accompaniment on the piano of Mr. R. Ford. Suitable refreshments were provided, and a very pleasant evening was spent. VEGETAItIANISIST.—A meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society was held on Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. H. Jones presiding, when an interesting essay on "Vegetarianism "was read by Mr. C. George. The essayist was supported by Mr. W. 11. Chapman, who practically demon- strated the subject by providing a sample of the vegetarian diet, which was partaken of by the members. In the debate which ensued the follow- ing joined :—Messrs. W. Broadhurst, J. Storey, J. S. Green, J. Swift, • J. Horton, A. Rathbone, and the Ch airman. THE GAlETY.—Considering the slackness of the times, this place of entertainment comes in for a good share of patronage, the various companies en- gaged being such as to secure appreciaition. The , company this week has included :—Mts. 3 Lizzie Elton, serio comic singer and dancer ; Mr. Fred Newby, comic vocalist; Mr. Tony Sinelair, negro artiste and dancer; Zenora, acrobat and contor- tionist; Miss Florence Hayes, vocalist ; Yankee Bos- well, negro artiste; Mr. Will Atkins, character singer; Mr. Henri Foden, in a performance on the' "enchanted staircase."

----- pRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BARS, LONDON. Thirty-seventh Annual Report for the year ending 31st December, 1885. The Directors have mrch pleasure in presenting their report and accounts for the year 1885. The Assurance Fufids have been increased during the year by the sum of £990845: namely, ties Ordinary Branch £232,425, and the Industrial Brasich £757,920. The total assets of the corepany amount to 25,702 862. ORDINARY BRANCH. The number of policies issued (luring the yesr was 17,553. assuring the sum of £1.887,890, and producing a New Annual Premium Income of £85,374. The Premiums of the year were £.303.275, being an increase of £64,407 over tfae year 1884. The total irctease for the first four years of the quinquennium is £162,018. The claims of the year amounted to £108,771. The number deaths was 712, and 38 endowment assurances matured. The rate of expenditure of the brawn was little more than 10 per cent. on the premium income. The number of policies in force was 415,483. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The Premiums received during the year were £2,794,622. be- ing an increase of £150,006. The claims of the year amounted to £1,069,878. The number of deaths was 119,846. The nnmber of policies in force, including 36,671 free policies, was 6,695,890. The Directors are happy to report that the duration • policies in this Branch is still steadily increasing. The average duration of all policies now in existence exceeds five years. The rate of expenditure of the Branch upon the Premium Income shoWs a further reduction of more than one-half per cent.
